question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't support fixing it secretly. They require written notice to the owner, and they say repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. They don't cover insurance.

**Documents used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf," dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf," dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 October 2026. The filenames show versions v115 and v009, but the excerpts don't use the words "Authorised Version," so I can't confirm that label from the text.

## What the law says

- **Damage:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to rented premises, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewing counts as negligent damage would depend on the facts, and the documents don't answer that.
- **Notice:** A renter must give written notice to the provider "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage, stating the fact that it occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice may be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can repair:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter-arranged repairs:** The renter may arrange urgent repairs only after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and being unable to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage doesn't appear to be urgent, and the documents don't list it as such.
- **Owner's options:** The provider may give a written repair notice for damage caused by the renter's failure to comply with the damage duty. It must state the damage and allow 14 days to repair it in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If that isn't done, the provider may repair it at the renter's expense and must give written particulars of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Leaving the property:** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider's final inspection must be completed within 10 days after the end date, and the renter should be given an opportunity to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets:** A renter may keep a pet only with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the renter can do or ask

1. **Notify the owner in writing now,** describing the damage (chewed skirting boards) and when it happened, as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the owner to arrange the repair,** or ask whether they will agree to the renter arranging it. The documents don't say whether an owner can agree to renter-arranged repairs outside the urgent-repair process, so check that with the owner or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
3. **Keep records:** Photos and any quotes or invoices from a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Form 4 also says photos should be dated and labelled [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the condition report** from the start of the tenancy, since it records the premises' condition at the start [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents don't address the owner's insurance, so I can't answer that part. The owner or their insurer would be the right source.

(2) Responsibility: it states the renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage (fair wear and tear excluded), must leave the premises 'in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear,' and that the owner can repair at the renter's expense. The hedge on whether chewing is negligent still leaves the overall direction clear. (3) Insurance: it says 'The retrieved documents don't address the owner's insurance.' question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say how many circuits a rental must have. They do set an electrical safety standard that starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after today, and a general duty to keep the premises in good repair.

**What the law says**

- **Circuit protection (not yet in force):** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of several listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This concerns protection, not the number of circuits.
- **Current duty:** A rental provider must ensure the rented premises are provided and maintained in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). This applies regardless of the age of the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety check:** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician . The renter can ask in writing for the date of the most recent check .
- **Repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs . Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering .
- **Heating (relevant to the heater):** Until 28 March 2023, a fixed heater in good working order must be in the main living area of a Class 1 building . From 29 March 2023, an energy efficient fixed heater in good working order must be installed there .

**What you can ask for**

1. **A written request for the electrical safety check record.** Ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing . The provider must give you a copy of the most recent check within 7 days of your written request .
2. **An inspection and repair of the circuit.** Notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable of the breakdown . Repairs are not in the documents as "urgent" unless they fall within the urgent categories, so ask for the provider to look at the fault. The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time .
3. **If repairs are not done:** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs if the provider has not carried out non-urgent repairs within 14 days of receiving notice .
4. **From 29 March 2023:** Ask that the outlets and lighting circuits be connected to the circuit breaker and residual current device required by the standard above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Limits of the documents**

- The documents do not state a minimum number of circuits or the load each circuit must carry, so I can't say whether one circuit is too few.
- A breaker tripping under combined load may mean the circuit is overloaded or faulty. An electrician should confirm this, and the documents don't say who pays for it.
- **Version details:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 document is Authorised Version No. 101, incorporating amendments as at 7 September 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 document is marked S.R. No. 3/2021, and its title indicates a version dated 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I did not find an Authorised Version number for the Regulations in the retrieved text.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the number of circuits, the answer states "The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have" and "The documents do not state a minimum number of circuits." On next steps, it advises "A written request for the electrical safety check record. Ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing," and also an inspection and repair of the circuit with written notice to the provider.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer gives no minimum number of circuits and does not say the RCD standard already applies: it says 'The documents do not state a minimum number of circuits' and labels the circuit breaker/RCD requirement 'Circuit protection (not yet in force): From 29 March 2023'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with versions: the Act as "Authorised Version No. 101, incorporating amendments as at 7 September 2022", and the Regulations by the link "21-3sra002" and as "a version dated 1 June 2022". Every rule it applies is cited to these in-force versions, and the 29 March 2023 circuit-protection standard is drawn from the in-force Regulations version 002 rather than a later version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They don't mention coin-operated laundry at all, so I can't confirm either way. The nearby rules below do limit how service charges can be set and billed.

**What the law says**

- **Separately metered rooms:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays the utility and the room is separately metered. The charge must not exceed the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This covers utilities, not washing machines.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must give an itemised account of that individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency:** These bodies may impose a service charge for "laundry or utility services or facilities" only in a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3). This applies only where it is not possible or practicable to measure the resident's use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service, and written notice is required. The resident can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your operator is one of these bodies is not stated in your question.
- **Prohibited terms:** A fixed term rooming house agreement must not include a term that "unreasonably limits the resident's use of utilities" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Under section 94A, a resident can apply to the Tribunal to declare invalid or vary a term of a non-fixed-term rooming house agreement, or a fixed term agreement, if the term is harsh or unconscionable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether that machine must be free of charge.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the operator in writing for the separate schedule of charges for services, as required by section 109 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask for an itemised account of your own use if you are charged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. Check your agreement for any term that unreasonably limits your use of utilities, which is prohibited in fixed term agreements [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. If the charges seem harsh or unconscionable, you can apply to the Tribunal under section 94A [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
5. Find out who operates the house. If it is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, the section 109A limits apply.

**Document versions**

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file is labelled v115 and is dated 13 October 2026, which is before 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text doesn't state an Authorised Version number on its face, so I'm relying on the file label.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 file is labelled v009 and is dated 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 file I found is labelled v002 and is dated 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). It may not be the latest version.

For a definite answer on coin-operated machines, you may need to check the rooming house agreement and house rules, or get advice from a tenancy service. Those documents weren't in my search results.

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, file rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf (1 Dec 2024)

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents show that mould breaches the rental minimum standards. They do not say whether a rental ad may show mould, and they do not say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

## What the law says

- **Mould is a minimum-standards issue.** Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Regulation 29(1) applies these standards to rented premises, other than community housing or specialised housing program premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider must comply before the renter moves in.** Under section 65A(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, a provider "must ensure that rented premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day on which the renter enters into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould is an urgent repair issue.** The Act's definition of "urgent repairs" includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** Section 89A allows a provider to enter to produce advertising images and video, but the renter can object to images that show certain possessions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved do not say whether a provider may advertise a property with visible mould, or what rules apply to misleading advertising.
- **Proof:** The documents do not say what evidence is needed to prove a breach of the minimum standards, or whether a photo is enough. That would be decided by the Tribunal, and the documents do not cover its evidentiary approach.

## What the renter can do or ask

1. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the premises do not comply with the minimum standards on or immediately after the day the renter moves in, "the renter may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Refuse to move in.** A renter is not required to enter into occupation of premises that do not comply with the requirement that they be vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If they do not, the renter is not required to pay rent for the period before they actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Terminate before possession.** If the renter has not yet taken possession, they can give notice of termination on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the disclosure rules.** For applicants, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards, and, from 31 December 2021, whether they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Document versions

The retrieved documents are labelled with version numbers in their file names:
- Residential Tenancies Act 1997: file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", version 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021): file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", version 004, dated 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Both versions predate 1 October 2025, so they are the ones that apply on that date. The documents do not state these as "Authorised Version" numbers, so I have taken them from the file names.

## Not covered by the documents

- Whether the advertisement itself is permitted or misleading.
- What evidence (such as photos, reports, or inspections) proves a mould breach.
- How a dispute over mould would be decided.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer quotes the mould and damp standard: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." (2) It says "The documents do not say what evidence is needed to prove a breach of the minimum standards, or whether a photo is enough", which the rubric accepts as covering the photo-proof point. (3) It gives next steps, including requesting urgent repairs and giving notice of termination before possession.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** If the friend is sub-letting or taking over part of your rental without written consent, your landlord (the rental provider) can give you a notice to vacate. The documents don't say how you would remove the friend yourself, so you'll likely need to deal with the friend directly and get advice.

**What the law says**
- Under the Regulations, a renter "must not assign ... or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider cannot unreasonably withhold consent to assign or sub-let, and cannot charge a fee for consent beyond reasonable expenses [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The Act allows a rental provider to give a notice to vacate if the renter "has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The termination date must be "not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZV).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and specifies the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZO).
- If the renter doesn't leave, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
- **Ask for written consent.** Because consent can't be unreasonably withheld [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), you could ask your landlord or agent in writing whether they will consent to your friend's occupancy. Whether a friend living with you counts as "sub-letting" is not defined in the retrieved documents.

- **Challenge options are limited.** The 30-day challenge right in s 91ZZS covers notices under ss 91ZX–91ZZC, and the family-violence challenge in s 91ZZU doesn't list s 91ZV [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Form 6 says you may challenge a notice if you believe it "was not given to you properly" or the information is incorrect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't give a specific deadline for challenging a s 91ZV notice.
- **Getting the friend out.** The retrieved documents don't cover how a renter removes an occupant who isn't a party to the agreement. I can't confirm the steps from these sources.
- **Get advice.** Form 6 directs renters to community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or to call 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** If the notice was given because you asked for repairs, the Act may make it "of no effect." The retrieved text does not say whether a verbal follow-up counts as exercising a right, so keep written evidence of your request.

**Source:** The retrieved document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf," dated 2 July 2019. The "v088" in the filename is the only version marker I found. I have not found any later amendment in the retrieved material, and the excerpts are partial.

### What the law says

- **The notice type:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate "without specifying a reason" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For an ordinary periodic tenancy, the termination date must be "not less than 120 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because no reason is required, the timing and context of the notice matter.
- **Retaliation rule:** "A notice under section 261 or section 263 is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repair rights:** A tenant may ask the Director to investigate non-urgent repairs if the tenant has "given the landlord written notice advising the landlord that repairs... are required" and the landlord has not carried out the repairs "within 14 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Tenants can also apply to the Tribunal for repair orders [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge deadline:** For a s 263 notice, a person may not apply to challenge its validity "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice to vacate is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, that is about 31 December 2019.
- **Landlord's conduct:** A landlord "must not... require or compel or attempt to compel the tenant... to vacate the rented premises" except in accordance with the Act. The penalty is "60 penalty units in the case of a natural person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What to check

1. **Written or verbal request:** Did you give the landlord written notice of the leaking fixtures? The Director route requires written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), so keep copies, emails, or texts. Whether a verbal request counts as exercising a right is not addressed in the retrieved text.
2. **Timing:** The notice came the same day as your follow-up. Note the exact times and any messages.
3. **Termination date:** It must be at least 120 days after the notice date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A shorter date is a defect.
4. **Form:** The notice must be in writing and signed, addressed to you, and state a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For s 263 notices, the reason is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Tenancy type:** Confirm whether you are on a periodic (month-to-month) agreement, since the 120-day rule applies to that type [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Any other reason given:** Keep a record of anything the landlord said about why you were asked to leave.

### What you can do or ask

- **Dispute the notice:** Apply to the Tribunal challenging validity, within 60 days of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The argument is that the notice "was given in response to" your exercise of a repair right under s 266(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Request repairs:** Give written notice of the repairs. If they are not done within 14 days, you may ask the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice:** A notice "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given," which must be in writing and signed by both you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Do not move out on the landlord's say-so:** A landlord cannot compel you to leave except under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents do not say how a Tribunal would weigh the evidence of motive, so consider getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' legal service before the deadline.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law prohibits the conduct you describe, but the documents don't tell me whether you can win a challenge on your facts or how to bring one. I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That is the latest version in my search results and the one in force on 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **Advertised rent must be fixed.** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30F(1)).
- **No inviting higher offers.** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30F(3)).
- **No false or misleading rent representations.** A provider or agent who advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30G(2)).
- **No inducing a tenancy by misleading conduct.** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter an agreement by false or misleading representations about "the rent payable under the agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30E(3)(b)). This applies to providers not acting in trade or commerce, and it does not limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30E(1), (4)).

Penalties for these offences are 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Can you challenge it?

- **Possibly, under s 30E or s 30G.** If the email falsely said you withdrew, that may be a misleading representation, but that is a factual question. The documents don't say whether a false withdrawal notice is itself a breach.
- **Higher offers.** Hearing that someone offered more does not prove an offence. The offence is the provider or agent *soliciting or inviting* a higher offer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30F(3)). You would need evidence that they did so.
- **Compensation.** The Act's compensation provision (s 210AA) is mentioned in the context of **discrimination** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't show that it applies to these facts.
- **Enforcement and process.** The note to s 30E says that s 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make on an application for contravention of that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 472, so I can't tell you who can complain, the process, time limits, or what orders are available. The documents also don't say whether the Director or another body handles complaints about these offences.

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list specific evidence requirements for these offences. The following is general practical advice, not drawn from the Act:

1. **The original advertisement** (screenshot or PDF, with the URL and date), showing the advertised rent. This matters because s 30F and s 30G turn on what was advertised [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Your application form and any correspondence** showing when and how you applied.
3. **The withdrawal email in full**, with full headers, plus your replies and any record that you did not withdraw.
4. **Any other communications** from the agent or provider about price, offers, or the rent.
5. **The current listing** showing the higher rent, with dated screenshots.
6. **Any information about the other offer**, such as who told you and when, written down while fresh. Hearsay is weaker, so note the source.

If the Act requires a separate notice or form for this situation, the documents don't say.

## Gaps

I don't have the text of s 472, the complaint process, time limits, or any Tribunal guidance on these offences. For those, check the Act's remaining provisions or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or Victoria Legal Aid.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not on the owner's allergy alone. The Act says a provider must not unreasonably refuse, and if the provider doesn't apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, they are taken to have consented. Your timing matters here.

Based on the Act as in force on 15 October 2026, the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Consent is needed, but can't be unreasonably withheld.** A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent.** The provider is taken to have consented "unless, within 14 days after being given the request, the residential rental provider applies to the Tribunal" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The request form.** A renter must make the request "in the form approved by the Director" and give it to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal factors.** If the provider applies to VCAT, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises and its fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The Regulations** repeat the principle: the renter must seek consent, and "the rental provider must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This is from the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 document dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Applying this to your situation

- **Timing:** Your request was about three weeks ago, roughly late September 2026. If it was given around 24 September, the 14-day window closed around 8 October. Unless the owner applied to VCAT within that window, the Act treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Please confirm the exact date you gave the form.
- **The refusal:** The documents I retrieved don't say whether an informal refusal stops deemed consent. Under the wording quoted above, only a Tribunal application within 14 days does [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also couldn't find anything on whether an agent's refusal counts for these purposes.
- **The allergy:** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground to refuse, and they don't address how an owner's infrequent visits affect that. The Tribunal's listed factors don't mention allergies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So I can't say whether the refusal is "unreasonable" under the Act.

## What you can do

1. Check the date you gave the form and whether the provider has told you they applied to VCAT.
2. If there's no Tribunal application, put in writing that consent is deemed under s 71C(2) and ask the provider to confirm it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If the provider disputes this, you can ask VCAT for an order permitting the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

I couldn't find any retrieved material on VCAT's process or fees, or on whether a provider can later try to exclude a pet that was kept with deemed consent. This isn't legal advice; for a firm answer, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate.

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026, ss 71A–71E.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, standard-form pet clause (file dated 30 June 2026).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice probably still stands unless the landlord has formally withdrawn it. Your landlord would still need a VCAT possession order before you could be made to leave. The documents don't say whether a sale falling through ends a notice automatically, so that point needs legal advice.

**What the law says**

- A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. If there is a contract of sale, the landlord must give the notice within 14 days after the last sale condition is satisfied, or within 14 days after the contract is entered into if it isn't conditional in that way. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the landlord or their agent, states the reason, and, for a sale notice, is accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A notice "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because the landlord hasn't withdrawn it, the notice appears to remain in effect on the documents I have.
- The landlord cannot get a possession order unless the notice has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You also have to leave by the termination date only if the notice is valid. If you stay past that date, the landlord must apply to VCAT. VCAT decides whether to make a possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Check the notice.** Confirm the termination date is at least 60 days after it was given, and that it includes the required form and documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge it if it's defective.** You can apply to VCAT challenging validity on or before the hearing of a possession application, but only within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Check when you received it, because this deadline may already have passed.

- **Leave early if you wish.** Form 6 says that, for a sale notice, you can end the agreement earlier by giving at least 14 days' notice of intention to vacate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The Act allows this for a renter given a sale notice under section 91ZZB [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek advice quickly.** The Regulations' form says that if you want to challenge a notice, you should seek legal advice as soon as possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The Act document is titled "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), but the retrieved text does not state an Authorised Version number, so I can't confirm one. question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, you probably do not have to pay the higher rent. A rent increase needs a formal written notice, and an email saying the rent is going up does not appear to meet that requirement.

**What the law says**

- A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase made in breach of these requirements is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5, which states that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 also says rent cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement provides for it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Email is only an approved delivery method if the renter has consented to it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What this means for you**

- Your agent's email, with no prescribed notice, does not appear to start a valid increase. The documents do not say how a court or tribunal would treat an informal email in every case, so you should check this if the agent pushes back.
- The documents do not give a start date for an increase that has not been validly notified, so I can't tell you "from when" you would owe it.
- If a valid Form 5 notice arrives later, the notice period is at least 60 days from the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You then have 30 days to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate whether the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If the Director reports, you have 30 days after receiving that report to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says that, while this is pending, you will generally need to pay the increased rent from the date in the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Versions used**

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (version 110, dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf" (version 004, dated 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The excerpts do not state an "Authorised Version" number on their face. I have taken the version numbers from the file names. Both versions are dated before 1 October 2025, so I have treated them as the versions in force on that date.

**What you can do**

- Reply in writing that you have not received a valid rent increase notice in the prescribed form, and ask the agent to confirm in writing whether one will be issued.
- Keep paying the current rent until a valid notice is given.
- If you receive a Form 5 notice, check the 60-day period, the stated amount and calculation method, and the start date. Diary the 30-day deadline to apply to the Director.
- Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 for advice. This number is listed in Form 5 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The law requires you to tell the owner about the damage in writing, and only a suitably qualified person may do repairs. The documents don't say whether the damage would affect the owner's insurance.

## What the law says

- **Damage and notice:** A renter must not damage the premises, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the provider written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Written notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Repair notices:** If the damage was caused by the renter's failure to take care, the provider may give a written repair notice. It can require you to repair the damage at your expense within 14 days, in a proper and tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you don't, the provider may do the repairs and recover the reasonable cost from you, provided they give you particulars in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Moving out:** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the owner or agent in writing about the damage to the skirting boards and what it is. Since you are moving out soon, do this before you vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to repair it through a suitably qualified person.** Get a quote and ask the owner's permission or agreement, since the provider may choose to repair it themselves or require you to repair it within 14 days under a repair notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Don't arrange repairs without the owner.** The urgent-repair route in section 72 requires that you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair the damage immediately and that they couldn't or didn't do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage may not be "urgent," and the documents don't list which repairs count as urgent beyond the examples given, so check the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance referred to in the regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Keep records.** Keep receipts and documentary evidence of any repair. VCAT considers whether the provider was notified and given a reasonable opportunity to repair, and whether documentary evidence was provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Insurance:** The documents do not say whether the damage would affect the owner's insurance on the property, so I can't answer that part.
- **Whether the owner can be bypassed:** The documents don't address whether a renter can have repairs done without telling the owner. They only set out the notice and repair-notice process above.

## Version of the law

Both documents were in force on 15 October 2026. The Act file is labelled v115 (dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations file is labelled v009 (dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents do not explicitly state an "Authorised Version" number, so these labels come from the file titles.

(2) Responsibility and condition, the hardest point: the answer says the renter 'must not damage the premises, but fair wear and tear is excluded' and can be required to 'repair the damage at your expense'. It also says the renter must leave the premises 'in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'. (3) Insurance: 'The documents do not say whether the damage would affect the owner's insurance.' (4) Next step: 'Give written notice now' and offer to repair.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found contain no rule on how many circuits a rental needs. They do set a rule about how power outlets must be protected, but it starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after your date. Your landlord still has general repair duties now.

## What the law says on 1 March 2023

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 002 (as at 1 June 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file dated 7 September 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I found. I did not find anything later.

- **Electrical protection rule (not yet in force):** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and to a switchboard-type residual current device that meets one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This rule does not apply on 1 March 2023.
- **Maintenance duty (in force now):** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies regardless of the rent or the age of the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks (in force now):** The landlord must ensure an electrical safety check is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs (in force now):** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and the landlord must ensure anyone doing repairs is suitably qualified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## Number of circuits

The retrieved documents do not say how many circuits a rental must have. They only regulate how outlets and lighting circuits are protected, from 29 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Written notice:** Tell your landlord in writing as soon as practicable about the breakdown. The renter must notify the landlord in writing of a breakdown of facilities or equipment supplied by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Repair in a reasonable time:** The landlord must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time. You may apply to VCAT for an order if repairs are not done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Electrical safety check record:** You can ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check, in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you moved in, the landlord must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The landlord must also keep and produce records of these checks [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not clearly say whether a tripping circuit breaker counts as an urgent repair. The full list is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, which is not in these documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If it is urgent, the landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. If they don't, you may arrange them if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act, and you may be reimbursed up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Practical note:** Keep a written record of each trip and of what appliances were running. Your written report to the landlord should say the breaker trips when the kettle and heater run together, and ask for an electrical safety check by a licensed or registered electrician.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't expressly say whether coin-operated washing machines can be charged for. They do set rules on charging for rooming house services, and those rules apply here.

**What the law says**

- **Charges for services:** If a rooming house operator charges for services, they must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in. If you use a service, they must give you an itemised account of your own use [1, s 109].
- **Water, central heating, laundry or utility services:** Only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for these, and only in a declared rooming house, where it isn't possible or practicable to measure your use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service, and it must be backed by written notice [1, s 109A]. If your operator is a private operator rather than Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, this provision doesn't apply.
- **Excessive usage:** If a fault causes excessive usage charges for a service at your room, the operator may be liable for the excess, provided you notified them as soon as practicable [1, s 120AA].
- **Unreasonable limits on utilities:** A rooming house agreement cannot include a term that unreasonably limits your use of utilities [2, reg 39(h)]. (Note: this is from the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 document, which is labelled S.R. No. 3/2021 and dated 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).)
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide laundry facilities in good working order, including a washing machine, for every 12 or fewer residents [4, reg 14(2)].

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the schedule of services.** Ask whether the washing machine charge is listed in the written schedule given before you moved in [1, s 109(a)]. If it wasn't, ask why.
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you're being charged, you can ask for an account showing your individual use [1, s 109(b)].
3. **Check whether the charge is excessive or unreasonable.** If the charge seems to unreasonably limit your use of the machines, you can raise the regulation on utilities above [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the machine count.** Compare the number of machines with the number of residents. The standard is one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents [4, reg 14(2)]. If the machines aren't working, report it in writing, as the Act requires residents to report broken facilities [1, s 116(2)].
5. **Seek help if needed.** For disputes about service charges, the Tribunal can order a service charge to be withdrawn or varied, but only where Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency imposes it [1, s 109A(3B)–(3C)].

**Documents used**

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (reprint dated 13 October 2026, labelled v115). This is the version in force on 15 October 2026.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, S.R. No. 10/2023, file dated 1 December 2024. This is the only version retrieved. It may not be the latest version, so check the current version before relying on it.
- [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021, file dated 30 June 2026.
-  Same as [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf), reg 14.

If you tell me whether your operator is Homes Victoria, a registered housing agency, or a private operator, I can say which of these provisions applies more precisely.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say that showing mould in an ad is banned. They do bar misleading ads about a property's characteristics. A photo can show that mould exists, but the documents don't say a photo alone proves the property breaches the minimum standards.

*Version note:* The retrieved copies are the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file labelled "v110," dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file labelled "v004," dated 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Both predate 1 October 2025. The text doesn't print a separate Authorised Version number, so I can only point to those file labels.

### What the law says

- **Advertising:** A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter a tenancy by misleading or deceptive conduct, or by a false or misleading representation about "the characteristics of the premises." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Honestly showing mould is not, on its face, misleading. Hiding it or describing the home as mould-free would be [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), Schedule 4, clause 8.
- **Duty to comply:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units (natural person) or 300 (body corporate) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 65A(1).
- **Disclosure:** Before the agreement is signed, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards. They must also disclose any repair notice received in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by the building structure (on and from 31 December 2021) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), reg 16(2)(b)–(c).

### Is the photo enough?

The documents don't answer this directly. Two points matter:

- The standard covers only mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould, but not its cause. That is a separate question.
- A condition report is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition only if it is signed by both the provider and the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 36(1). The documents don't say how a photo would be treated by the Tribunal.

### What the renter can do

- **Ask for urgent repairs:** If the premises don't comply with the standards when the renter moves in, the renter may request urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 65A(2). Mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" that makes the premises unsafe or insecure is included in the definition of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 3(1).
- **Terminate before moving in:** If the renter has not yet taken possession, they can end the agreement by giving a termination notice on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 91L(f).
- **Record the condition:** Put any mould in the condition report before or when moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), ss 35–36.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether a photo alone is enough to prove a breach at the Tribunal.
- Any rule on how mould must be shown or described in listing photos.
- How the ad photos were taken or whether the renter consented (s 89A covers advertising images, but the documents don't link it to mould).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the mould and damp standard is stated ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'). The hardest point, that a photo alone is not proof, is covered by 'the documents don't say a photo alone proves the property breaches the minimum standards' and 'A photo shows mould, but not its cause.' Next steps are given, including requesting urgent repairs and ending the agreement before moving in under s 91L(f).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer makes neither claim: it says "a photo can show that mould exists, but the documents don't say a photo alone proves the property breaches the minimum standards," and "the documents don't say that showing mould in an ad is banned," citing only the existing ban on misleading representations rather than a ban on advertising non-compliant premises.

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "v110," dated 6 August 2025 (link 97-109aa110), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "v004," dated 1 July 2025 (link 21-3sra004). These are the versions in force on 1 October 2025, and every rule it applies, including s 65A, s 91L and Sch 4 cl 8, comes from them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I have don't say how to remove a friend who moved in without consent. They do show that letting someone move in may breach your own duties as renter, and that your landlord may then be able to end your tenancy. I've assumed you are the renter, since your friend moved into your rental.

## What the law says

- **You must not sub-let or assign without written consent.** "A renter under a residential rental agreement must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Consent can't be unreasonably withheld, but you still need it.** The provider "must not unreasonably withhold consent" to a sub-letting. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Breach can lead to a notice to vacate.** A provider "may give a renter a notice to vacate rented premises if the renter has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The notice "must specify a termination date that is not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Notices must be valid.** A notice to vacate "is not valid unless" it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reason(s), and specifies the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **The Regulations say the same in summary.** The rental provider "may give the renter notice to vacate if the renter assigns or sub-lets the premises without consent." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Whether a friend living with you without paying rent counts as sub-letting or "part" of the premises being assigned is a question of fact. The documents don't answer it.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask your friend to leave** and agree a move-out date. The documents don't cover the process for a non-party occupant.
- **Ask your landlord or agent for written consent** if you want your friend to stay. Consent is required, and the provider must not unreasonably withhold it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice before acting** if the agent serves a notice. The documents don't set out a challenge period for a s 91ZV notice. The 30-day challenge right in s 91ZZS applies only to notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB and 91ZZC [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so it does not clearly cover this kind of notice.

## What the documents don't cover

- How to remove a non-party occupant who won't leave.
- Whether a friend living with you counts as sub-letting in your case.
- Any tribunal process for a s 91ZV notice beyond the notice requirements above.

## Versions

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file labelled "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (dated 13 October 2026). The text does not state an "Authorised Version" number; "v115" is the file label. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file labelled "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (dated 30 June 2026). Again, "v009" is the file label. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Both were in force on 15 October 2026 as far as the documents show. Please check the official Authorised Version on the Victorian legislation website, and consider speaking to a tenancy advisor (for example, Consumer Affairs Victoria) about your specific situation.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The arrangement point is the harder one, and it is met by the words "Whether a friend living with you without paying rent counts as sub-letting or 'part' of the premises being assigned is a question of fact," which say the outcome depends on the facts and name payment as a deciding fact. The written-consent point is stated directly: "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four failure statements appear: the only fixed period, 14 days, applies to a landlord's notice to the renter, not to ending the friend's stay; the answer says to "Ask your friend to leave and agree a move-out date" and that "The documents don't cover the process for a non-party occupant"; and it says nothing about lockouts, the friend having no rights, or VCAT adding the friend to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 by file name "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (dated 13 October 2026) and link 97-109aa115, which is Authorised Version No. 115, and every other rule it applies comes from the in-force Regulations version ("rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", link 21-3sra009), with no reliance on any other version.
