question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- A landlord could give a **periodic—month-to-month—tenant** a notice to vacate without stating a reason, but the termination date had to be **at least 120 days after the notice was given**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- That notice had **no effect if it was given in response to the tenant exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly decide whether asking for repairs constitutes such an exercise of a right, so they do not conclusively answer whether your particular notice is retaliatory.
- The landlord had a duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**.  For non-urgent repairs, after the tenant gave written notice and the landlord failed to repair within **14 days**, the tenant could apply to the Director to investigate.  For urgent repairs, the tenant could arrange repairs after taking reasonable steps to obtain the landlord’s immediate action, or apply to the Tribunal in specified circumstances. 
- If the notice relied on the landlord intending to repair, renovate or reconstruct the premises, the landlord needed all necessary permits and consents, and the work had to be work that could not properly be carried out unless you vacated; the notice had to give at least **60 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- Any notice to vacate had to be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason if applicable, and specify the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should check or ask

1. **Check the stated basis of the notice.** If it is a no-reason notice, check that the termination date is at least **120 days** after the notice date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
2. **If it claims repairs or renovations**, ask for evidence of the necessary permits and consents, and whether the work genuinely cannot be done while you remain. Also check that it gives at least **60 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
3. **Preserve evidence of retaliation:** your repair requests, dates, replies, photographs, and the notice showing that it was issued the same day. The documents support checking whether the notice was given in response to exercising an Act right, but do not specify what evidence proves that. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
4. **Check the notice’s formal validity:** prescribed form, correct address, signature, stated reason where required, and termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
5. If it is a **no-reason periodic notice** and you believe it was retaliatory, note that a challenge to its validity could not be made after **60 days from the date it was given**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not specify the precise application procedure for challenging that notice, so they do not provide further procedural steps.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all three points: the 120-day no-reason notice; that such a notice has 'no effect if it was given in response to the tenant exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act'; and the challenge window, in the words 'a challenge to its validity could not be made after 60 days from the date it was given'. It does not name VCAT as the forum, but the 60-day challenge right is clearly conveyed.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the landlord could give a periodic tenant a notice to vacate "without stating a reason" (and requires a reason only "if applicable"), and the only challenge deadline it gives is that "a challenge to its validity could not be made after 60 days from the date it was given." The 14-day, 60-day and 120-day figures elsewhere are repair and notice periods, not challenge deadlines.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019" (linked as 97-109aa088), and every rule it applies is sourced from that in-force version, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer the property at a **fixed amount of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not **solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent**. A breach carries penalties of up to **60 penalty units for an individual** or **300 penalty units for a body corporate**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not make a **false or misleading representation about the rent** in an advertisement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved Act does **not specifically say** that falsely telling an applicant they withdrew is unlawful, nor does it set out a specific applicant appeal process for a rejected application. The misleading-conduct provision retrieved applies to conduct inducing someone to **enter a residential rental agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the evidence shows that the agent or rental provider replaced your application with a higher offer, or invited someone to pay more than the advertised rent, that may raise an issue under **sections 30F or 30G**. The documents do not establish from these facts alone that a breach occurred.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent or rental provider, in writing:

1. why your application was recorded as withdrawn;
2. when and why the advertised rent changed;
3. whether any applicant was invited or permitted to offer more than the advertised amount; and
4. that they correct the record if you did not withdraw.

The retrieved documents do not specify what evidence an applicant must preserve or a particular process for challenging this conduct. As a practical matter, retain the original advertisement showing the rent, your application and submission confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, all correspondence, and dated screenshots or other records showing the later higher listing—but the documents do not prescribe this evidence list.

If the conduct involved unlawful discrimination based on a protected attribute, the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version current to 1 July 2025**, states that an affected applicant may apply to VCAT for compensation under section 210AA or complain to VEOHRC. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) No discrimination is stated in your question, so the retrieved documents do not show that this pathway applies.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the ban on inviting offers above the advertised rent and says the Act does 'not specifically say' that a false withdrawal email is unlawful. It never states that relisting at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself. It also omits that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not banned, and instead suggests that replacing the application 'with a higher offer' may itself raise an issue.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted. The answer does not say relisting at a higher rent is illegal by itself; it limits the issue to soliciting: "They must not solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent." Its closest statement, "replaced your application with a higher offer, or invited someone to pay more than the advertised rent, that may raise an issue under sections 30F or 30G," is hedged with "The documents do not establish from these facts alone that a breach occurred," so it does not claim that accepting an unsolicited higher offer is illegal. It also never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025" (link 97-109aa110) and applies ss 30F/30G from it. The only other document it relies on is the in-force Regulations, cited as "Authorised Version current to 1 July 2025" (link 21-3sra004). No out-of-date version is used.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You used the approved form, as required. The rental provider must not **unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) An owner’s allergy may be relevant, but the documents do not say that an allergy automatically justifies refusal. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Most importantly, the rental provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days after receiving your request**, they applied to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Since you sent the request three weeks ago—21 days—the documents indicate that consent is deemed **unless the rental provider made that Tribunal application within the 14-day period**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The fact that the owner hardly visits is not, by itself, decisive; the documents do not specify how much weight that fact must receive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing:

1. **Whether the rental provider applied to the Tribunal within 14 days** of receiving your request; and  
2. If not, confirm that consent is deemed under section 71C(2) of the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If an application was made in time, the Tribunal can decide whether refusal is reasonable and may order that you are permitted to keep the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You can put forward the owner’s limited visits and any measures addressing the allergy, but the retrieved documents do not give a specific procedure or deadline for your response. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed rental-agreement form also states that you must seek consent and that the rental provider must not unreasonably refuse a pet request. This form is from the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (30 June 2026)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)**, a notice to vacate for sale may be given if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession** immediately after the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice is **not withdrawn merely because the buyer pulled out**. It is withdrawn only when a withdrawal notice is given **in writing and signed by both the person who gave the original notice and the renter**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

So, unless the landlord gives you a properly signed withdrawal notice, you should **not assume the notice has been cancelled**. However, the documents do not say whether the buyer’s withdrawal, by itself, makes an already-issued sale notice invalid. The documents therefore do not establish definitively whether you must leave in your particular circumstances. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord in writing to provide a signed withdrawal notice under section 91ZZQ. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check whether the notice was in the prescribed form, gave at least **60 days’ notice**, stated the sale reason and termination date, and included the required supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If you believe the notice is invalid, you may apply to **VCAT within 30 days after it was given** to challenge it; you may also challenge it on or before a hearing if the landlord applies for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Do not treat the notice as cancelled without written withdrawal or a VCAT determination. If you do not leave by the stated date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order, and only Victoria Police acting under a warrant can carry out a forcible eviction. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. Most points are covered: the 60-day minimum, withdrawal only by a written notice signed by both parties, and next steps (ask for a signed withdrawal, or apply to VCAT within 30 days). The first point is missing, though. The answer never explains that the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice and its evidence, meaning a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract of sale. Instead it says the documents 'do not establish definitively whether you must leave,' which leaves the reader unable to tell which way that point falls.

It rejects automatic cancellation ("not withdrawn merely because the buyer pulled out"), requires a joint withdrawal ("signed by both the person who gave the original notice and the renter"), and states the correct period ("at least 60 days' notice").

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the applicable documents are:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version v110**, dated **6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version v004**, dated **1 July 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days’ notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase. A valid notice is required for **all** rent increases, and a rent increase made contrary to that requirement is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed **Form 5** must state the current rent, new rent, proposed start date, calculation method and delivery details. It may be sent by email **only if you have consented to electronic service**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- If you receive a valid notice and consider the proposed rent excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within **30 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do not state that a failed negotiation creates any separate obligation to accept the increase.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?

## What the law says

You **must give the rental provider written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage, stating that it occurred and describing its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Dog-chewed skirting boards are damage, not fair wear and tear on the information provided. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You should not simply arrange a concealed repair without telling the owner. The renter must avoid damaging the premises, and the prescribed rental-agreement summary says that **only a suitably qualified person may do repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider may give you a written repair notice requiring you to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days**, and the repair must be done in a **proper and tradesman-like manner**. If it is not, the provider may arrange the repair and recover the reasonable cost from you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider may also claim from the bond the reasonable repair or restoration cost for damage caused by the renter or a renter’s visitor, taking fair wear and tear into account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not say whether repairing the skirting boards without notifying the owner would affect the owner’s insurance**, or whether an insurer must be notified. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Send the owner or agent written notice now, with photographs and a description of the damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Ask in writing whether they want to arrange the repair, or whether they agree that you may arrange it.
- If they agree, confirm who will do the work, obtain a written quote or invoice, and use a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Keep the notice, agreement, photographs and invoices. The owner may still seek reasonable repair costs or claim against the bond. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 March 2023**, the retrieved documents do **not** specify a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points that a Victorian rental must have. The electrical minimum standard then required was only to commence **on and from 29 March 2023**; it required all power-outlet and lighting circuits to be connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device, but did not prescribe a number of circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must nevertheless maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, and any repair work must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that one circuit, or a breaker tripping when a kettle and heater run together, automatically breaches that duty. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide **every 2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician.  The renter may request the date of the most recent check in writing, and may request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record; the provider must supply it within **7 days**. 

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Give the rental provider written notice** describing the tripping breaker and asking them to have the circuit and relevant outlets assessed by a licensed or registered electrician. A renter must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment supplied by the provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask in writing for**:
   - the date of the most recent electrical safety check; and
   - a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record.  
   The record must include the electrician’s name and licence or registration number, the inspection date, results, required repairs and actions taken, and an AS/NZS 3019 report. 

3. If the problem is not fixed within a reasonable time, the documents say you may apply to the Director for an investigation after giving written notice and waiting **14 days**, or apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified non-urgent repairs after the provider has not repaired it within **14 days** of receiving notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that you can require the provider to install a particular number of circuits. Do not attempt electrical work yourself; the documents require repairs to be carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

**Documents in force on 1 March 2023:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version v002** (1 June 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version v101** (7 September 2022). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the first, the answer says 'the retrieved documents do **not** specify a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points that a Victorian rental must have'. On the second, it advises giving written notice asking the provider to have the circuit assessed by a licensed electrician, and asking in writing for 'the date of the most recent electrical safety check'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer states that the documents "do **not** specify a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the circuit breaker and RCD standard was "only to commence **on and from 29 March 2023**", so it neither asserts a minimum circuit count nor claims the standard already applies on 1 March 2023.

It does not apply rules from any other version, and the 29 March 2023 electrical standard is mentioned only as not yet in force.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
### What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (dated 13 October 2026). It requires a rooming house to provide **one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, in good working order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** expressly say that a rooming house operator may or may not use coin-operated machines. However, if the operator charges residents for a service, section 109 requires the operator to:

- give the resident a **separate schedule of the service amount before residency begins**; and
- provide an **itemised account showing the resident’s individual use** if the resident uses the service. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The special rule allowing a “service charge” for laundry facilities applies only to **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, and only where use cannot be accurately or practicably measured; the charge cannot exceed the cost of providing the facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that this special rule applies to an ordinary private rooming house operator.

### What you can do or ask

Ask the operator in writing for:

1. the **separate schedule** explaining the laundry charge; and  
2. an **itemised account** showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask why the machines are coin-operated and whether the charge is included in, or additional to, your rent. The retrieved documents do not provide enough information to conclude that the coin charge itself is unlawful, but they do set out the operator’s disclosure and itemisation obligations.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. The answer states the requirement of 'one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order.' For the hardest point, it says the documents 'do not expressly say that a rooming house operator may or may not use coin-operated machines' and 'do not provide enough information to conclude that the coin charge itself is unlawful.' It notes that the operator must give 'a separate schedule of the service amount before residency begins.' As a next step, it advises asking the operator in writing for 'the separate schedule explaining the laundry charge.'

It does not say there are no rules, since it cites section 109's requirements for "a separate schedule of the service amount" and "an itemised account". It also limits the cost cap, saying the special rule "applies only to Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency" and not to "an ordinary private rooming house operator."

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004 (1 July 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110 (6 August 2025)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Each room must be **free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) A residential rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards **on or before the renter enters occupation**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** say that a rental provider is prohibited from advertising premises merely because an advertising photo appears to show mould. They do require the provider to disclose to a rental applicant **whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards** and, if the provider received a repair notice in the previous three years concerning structural mould or damp, that fact. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A photo alone is **not stated in these documents to be conclusive proof** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The standard depends on whether there is mould or damp and whether it is caused by or related to the building structure; the documents do not prescribe what evidence is sufficient to prove that. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter or applicant can do or ask

Before applying, ask the provider or agent:

- whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- whether they received a repair notice in the last three years relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If the person becomes the renter and the premises do not comply on or immediately after occupation, they may request **urgent repairs** to bring them into compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

All three points are covered: the output states the standard that each room must be 'free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'; it says 'A photo alone is not stated in these documents to be conclusive proof that the premises fail the minimum standard', which covers the hardest point; and it gives next steps (ask the provider or agent about compliance and repair notices, and request urgent repairs after moving in).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** — *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009** — *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A renter must not **assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider’s written consent**. The rental provider may give the renter a notice to vacate if this occurred without consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do **not** say whether a friend who merely moved in—without paying rent or receiving exclusive possession—is legally a sub-tenant, guest or another type of occupant. They therefore do not provide a definitive answer about your friend’s status.

You cannot personally force the friend out. If a person does not leave after a valid notice and VCAT makes a possession order, only Victoria Police may carry out a forcible eviction under a warrant for possession. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the rental provider or agent in writing for consent** to the friend’s occupation, or explain that you want the friend to leave. The required consent for assigning or sub-letting is written consent from the rental provider—not merely informal permission from the agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

2. If the friend is a renter or sub-tenant, the documents do not set out a separate procedure for you to terminate their occupation. A notice to vacate form is directed to the renter who is a party to the residential rental agreement, and must identify that renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. If the rental provider gives you a notice to vacate and you do not leave, the provider may apply to VCAT for a possession order. An application under section 322(1) may be made after the notice is given and no later than 30 days after the notice’s termination date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. The documents do not state that you can independently remove a friend who is not named in the rental agreement. **They do not contain enough information to say exactly what notice, if any, you must give your friend.**

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the relevant version was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019**—the document titled *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act required the residential rental provider to keep the premises in good repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) A renter also had to give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of fixtures or facilities. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate based on **repairs, renovation or reconstruction** was valid only if the provider:

- intended to carry out the work;
- had obtained all necessary permits and consents; and
- could not properly carry out the work unless you vacated. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

That notice had to give at least **60 days’ notice** and be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, specify the termination date, and include approved documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved provisions do **not** state a general rule making a repairs-based notice invalid merely because it was issued in retaliation for requesting repairs. They do state that a notice under section 91ZZD—concerning the end of a fixed term—has no effect if given in response to exercising a right under the Act or reporting damage or a breakdown under section 72AA; that provision concerns a **fixed-term** agreement, not a month-to-month periodic agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can check or ask

1. **Check the notice’s stated reason.** If it says repairs, check whether the proposed work genuinely requires you to leave, rather than merely being ordinary maintenance that could be done while you remain. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the timing.** A repairs notice must allow at least **60 days**. A same-day termination date would not meet that requirement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Check the form and evidence.** Confirm that it is the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, gives the reason and termination date, and includes documentary evidence supporting the repairs reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Preserve evidence of possible retaliation:** your repair request, photographs, messages, dates, the provider’s responses, and the fact that the notice was issued the same day. The retrieved documents do not specify a separate retaliation application or test, so they do not establish what remedy is available solely on that basis.

5. **Challenge the notice at VCAT if it is a repairs notice.** You may apply to challenge a notice given under section 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC within **30 days after the notice was given**, and no later than the hearing of an application for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does not expressly confirm that section 91ZZS applies to every possible notice issued to a month-to-month renter, so it does not provide a complete answer for a notice relying on another section.

6. **Continue pursuing the repairs separately.** For non-urgent repairs, after giving written notice and waiting **14 days** without repairs, you could apply under the Act’s repair procedures; the Tribunal could order specified repairs and compensation. question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document on **1 October 2025** is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, incorporating amendments as at **6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental property must generally be advertised or offered at a **fixed rent amount**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The provider or agent must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. A breach carries a penalty of **60 penalty units for an individual or 300 penalty units for a body corporate**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising or promoting the property with a **false or misleading representation about the rent** is also prohibited in the circumstances covered by section 30G, with the same penalties. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The fact that another applicant allegedly offered more does **not, by itself, establish** that the agent solicited or invited a higher offer. The documents do not state that an applicant must be accepted at the advertised rent, nor do they specifically make an unexplained “withdrawn” email unlawful.
- The Act also prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct, or false or misleading representations about rent, where that conduct induces a person to enter into a residential rental agreement; section 30E applies where the provider or agent is not acting in trade or commerce. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing, to explain:

1. why your application was recorded as withdrawn;
2. who withdrew it and when;
3. whether the property was re-advertised at a higher rent; and
4. whether the agent or provider requested, encouraged or invited any applicant to offer more than the advertised rent.

You can ask the relevant regulator or tribunal about the conduct, but **the retrieved Act does not set out a specific complaint process for a prospective applicant in this situation**, and it does not state what evidence an applicant must preserve. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

As a practical matter, preserve the original advertisement showing the rent, the application and submission confirmation, all emails or messages—including the “withdrawn” email—screenshots showing dates and URLs, any later advertisement showing the increased rent, and any communication indicating that a higher offer was requested or invited. The retrieved document does not prescribe this evidence list, so this is evidence-preservation advice rather than a requirement stated in the Act.

It only suggests asking the agent 'whether the property was re-advertised at a higher rent', which leaves the reader unable to tell whether that is lawful. The other three points are covered: soliciting is banned, the documents do not require acceptance at the advertised rent, and the documents do not 'specifically make an unexplained "withdrawn" email unlawful'.

It states 'the documents do not state that an applicant must be accepted at the advertised rent', so it does not claim the applicant can force the agent to rent to them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You had to request consent using the **form approved by the Director**, and give it to the residential rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Most importantly, the provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within **14 days** after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Three weeks is 21 days, so the 14-day period has passed.

The owner’s allergy could potentially be considered by the Tribunal, because the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the nature of the premises and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not say that an owner’s allergy automatically justifies refusal, nor do they say that the owner’s infrequent visits determine the issue. A refusal must still be reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing:

1. **Whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal within 14 days** of receiving your request; and  
2. If so, for the application details or evidence of that application.

If no application was made within the 14-day period, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations also state that a renter must seek consent before keeping a pet and that the provider must not unreasonably refuse the request. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Do not rely only on the agent’s verbal refusal without checking whether a timely Tribunal application was made. The retrieved documents do not specify a separate procedure for enforcing the deemed consent beyond the Tribunal provisions.

The hardest one, the three-week application, is handled by "Three weeks is 21 days, so the 14-day period has passed" together with "If no application was made within the 14-day period, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented". The answer also gives the deemed-consent rule and the next step of asking the agent in writing whether a Tribunal application was made within 14 days.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The landlord’s notice is **not automatically withdrawn merely because the buyer pulled out**. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a written notice of withdrawal is given, signed by the person who gave the notice and by the person to whom it was given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, you do **not automatically have to leave solely because the notice date has passed**. If you remain, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order; VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the order is reasonable and proportionate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form also says that the landlord cannot personally force you out; forcible eviction can occur only through Victoria Police acting on a VCAT warrant for possession. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state whether the buyer’s withdrawal itself makes a sale-based notice invalid. Therefore, they do not provide enough information to say definitively that you must leave or that the notice is invalid.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, using the formal written withdrawal process. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies to VCAT, **attend the hearing and challenge whether the notice was valid**, including whether the stated sale reason still exists. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Do not treat the buyer’s withdrawal as automatically cancelling the notice, but do not leave solely because the landlord says you must: the retrieved documents say VCAT decides whether a possession order should be made. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

It does cover the signed written withdrawal and the next steps.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), together with the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

A rental provider must give at least **60 days’ notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed form must state the current and new rent, the start date, the amount and calculation method, and how the notice was delivered. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, an ordinary email saying the rent will increase—and your unsuccessful negotiation—does **not by itself** make the increase payable if it was not the prescribed rent-increase notice. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is **invalid**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to pay the higher rent from 1 October 2025, or from any other date based only on that email. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Continue paying the existing rent and ask the agent to provide a valid **Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If a valid notice is later given, the higher rent can begin no earlier than **60 days after the notice is given**, subject also to the rule that rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If you receive a valid notice and consider the proposed rent excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within **30 days** after the notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state a separate rule calculating the exact calendar start date where a valid notice is issued on 1 October; they establish only the minimum **60-day notice period**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. It says a renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises; damage caused by a dog would generally fall within this rule, unless it is fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of the damage, stating that it occurred and describing its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Moving out soon does not remove the obligation to leave the premises in substantially the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You should **not simply arrange a repair secretly**. The documents do not expressly say that a renter may independently repair non-urgent damage without notifying or obtaining the rental provider’s agreement. They do say that repairs—urgent and non-urgent—must be done by a **suitably qualified person**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider may issue a written repair notice requiring you either to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days**, in a proper and tradesman-like manner, or stating that the provider will arrange the repair and that you are liable for the reasonable cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A provider may claim from the bond the reasonable cost of repairing or restoring damage caused by the renter or a renter’s visitor, taking fair wear and tear into account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not address whether repairing the skirting boards without telling the owner would affect the owner’s property insurance**, so I cannot say what the insurance consequences would be.

## What you can do or ask

1. Send the owner or agent written notice now, describing the chewed skirting boards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
2. Ask whether they want to arrange the repair or consent in writing to you arranging it.  
3. If they agree that you arrange it, use a suitably qualified person and keep the written approval, invoice and repair details. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
4. Ask whether they want the damage repaired before the tenancy ends or intend to issue a repair notice. The provider may require repair within **14 days** or arrange it themselves and seek the reasonable cost from you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
5. Ask the owner or agent directly about any insurance notification requirements; the retrieved tenancy documents contain no answer on that issue.

It says dog damage "would generally fall within this rule, unless it is fair wear and tear" and that the renter must leave the premises "in substantially the same condition". It states that the documents "do not address" the insurance question. It gives next steps, such as sending written notice and getting written consent for the repair. The hardest point is responsibility for pet damage, and it is covered by the words "damage caused by a dog would generally fall within this rule, unless it is fair wear and tear."

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 March 2023**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at **1 June 2022** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101**, dated **7 September 2022** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents **do not specify a minimum number of power-point circuits** that a rental must have. They therefore do not establish that having most power points on one circuit is unlawful merely because the breaker trips. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical rental minimum standard requiring power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual-current devices applied **“on and from 29 March 2023”**—so it was not yet in force on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider must maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. Any repair must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing** that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and request that a **licensed or registered electrician inspect and rectify the electrical installation**, including assessing whether the circuit is safe and adequate. The renter must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities, fixtures, equipment or facilities provided by the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Request the most recent electrical safety-check record.** The provider must arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by the provider every two years. On your written request, the provider must give you the most recent record within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

3. If the provider does not carry out the repair, give written notice identifying the repair required. For a **non-urgent repair**, you may apply to the Director if it has not been done within **14 days**, or apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that a breaker tripping in these circumstances is automatically an **urgent repair**. Do not attempt electrical work yourself; the documents require repairs to be carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. It requires a rooming house operator to provide **one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the rooming house can accommodate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version 002 (1 December 2024)** contains the same laundry standard. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The operator must also provide access during all reasonable hours to facilities for residents’ use and must not unreasonably restrict or interfere with residents’ proper use and enjoyment of those facilities. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The Act permits the operator to make house rules about using facilities, but the rules must be reasonable and applied consistently and fairly. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved documents **do not expressly say whether a private rooming-house operator may charge a coin fee for using a washing machine**. They therefore do not establish that the charge is either definitely lawful or definitely unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

- what legal or contractual basis they rely on for the coin charge;

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Each room in rented premises must be **free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards **on or before the day the renter enters occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not say that it is automatically unlawful to advertise a property showing apparent mould**, nor do they say that the image must be removed from an advertisement. They do provide rules for producing advertising images—for example, giving the required entry notice and making a reasonable attempt to agree on a suitable time with the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The provider must also disclose to a rental applicant whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and, if applicable, whether the provider received a repair notice in the previous three years concerning mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A photograph may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the premises, but the retrieved documents **do not state that a photograph alone conclusively proves** that the premises fail the minimum standard. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter or applicant can do or ask

- Ask the agent or rental provider **whether the apparent mould is structural mould or damp**, whether it has been repaired, and whether the premises currently comply with the minimum standards. The provider must disclose compliance with the standards to an applicant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether a mould/damp repair notice was received in the previous three years and, if so, for the relevant details. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Preserve the advertisement and photograph, including its date and the property address. The regulations state that dated, labelled photos identifying the location or room may be useful in a condition dispute. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If the renter takes occupation and the premises do not comply with the minimum standards, the renter may request **urgent repairs** to bring them into compliance. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a rule that the advertisement photograph, by itself, proves non-compliance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (dated **13 October 2026**). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If your friend is **subletting part of the property**—for example, paying you rent or having an arrangement giving them occupation—you must not sublet without the residential rental provider’s **written consent**. An unauthorised subletting is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent is unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate if you have sublet, or purported to sublet, all or part of the premises without consent. The notice must specify a termination date at least **14 days after it is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You cannot simply remove your friend by force. If you do not leave after a valid notice, the rental provider may apply to VCAT for a possession order; a forcible eviction can occur only under a possession order and warrant, carried out by police or an authorised person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state whether merely allowing a friend to live with you, without payment or a subletting arrangement, legally amounts to subletting. They therefore do not provide a definite procedure for removing a friend who is only a guest or occupant.

## What you can do or ask

- Check whether your friend’s arrangement is a **sublease**. If it is, ask the rental provider or agent for written consent immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If consent is refused and you believe the refusal is unreasonable, you may apply to VCAT for a determination that consent is not required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If you receive a notice to vacate, the prescribed **Notice to Vacate** form must identify the relevant reason and section of the Act, explain the specific details, state the termination date and comply with the delivery requirements. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If you want your friend to leave but the documents do not establish that they are a sub-renter, the documents do not say what notice or other step you must use.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer makes the outcome depend on the arrangement and names payment as a deciding fact: "for example, paying you rent or having an arrangement giving them occupation" versus "merely allowing a friend to live with you, without payment or a subletting arrangement". It also states that "you must not sublet without the residential rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer sets no certain notice period or process for the friend and says "the documents do not say what notice or other step you must use"; its only fixed period ("at least 14 days") applies to the rental provider's notice to the renter, and it never says the renter may lock out the friend, that the friend lacks rights, or that the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088 (2 July 2019)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- A residential rental provider must keep the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Leaking water-using fixtures may be **“urgent repairs”** if they are malfunctioning in a way that results, or will result, in a substantial amount of water being wasted. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- The provider may give a notice to vacate for **repairs, renovation or reconstruction** only if the work cannot properly be done while you remain, all necessary permits and consents have been obtained, and the notice gives at least **60 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and state the termination date. For a repairs notice, it must also include approved documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- The document expressly says that a notice under **section 91ZK (threats and intimidation)** has no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved document does **not** state a general rule making every ordinary periodic-tenancy notice invalid merely because it followed a repair request. It therefore does not, by itself, establish that your notice is retaliatory or invalid.

## What you should check or ask

1. **Identify the statutory ground stated on the notice.** Check whether it claims repairs, threats/intimidation, rent arrears, or another ground. The reason must be stated on the notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the timing and evidence.** Because the notice was given the same day as your repair follow-up, keep the repair messages, emails, photographs, call records and the notice. Ask for the documentary evidence supporting the stated reason, especially if the provider claims the premises must be vacated for repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Check the termination date.** If the notice relies on repairs, it must give at least **60 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not provide the general notice period for an ordinary month-to-month residential rental agreement, so I cannot state that period from these documents.

4. **Continue using the repair procedures.** For non-urgent repairs, the renter’s written notice is relevant: if repairs are not done within **14 days**, the renter may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For urgent repairs, the renter may arrange them after taking reasonable steps to have the provider or agent do them immediately; if unable to get them done, the renter may apply to the Tribunal. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Consider challenging the notice at VCAT.** The document provides a specific challenge process within **30 days** for notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB and 91ZZC, with the application made on or before the hearing of the possession-order application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state an equivalent general 30-day challenge process for every periodic notice.

6. **Ask VCAT to determine validity if the notice fits one of those grounds.** The Tribunal may determine whether the notice is valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Keep evidence showing the repair request immediately preceded the notice and showing that the stated reason is unsupported or inconsistent with the provider’s conduct.

Finally, it gives a 30-day challenge window for other notice sections rather than a 60-day VCAT challenge, so all three required points are missing or materially different.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental property must be advertised or offered at a **fixed amount of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or otherwise invite an offer higher than the advertised rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Promoting or advertising the property with a **false or misleading representation about the rent** is prohibited where the provider or agent is not acting in trade or commerce. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Misleading or deceptive conduct about the rent is also prohibited in inducing someone to enter a residential rental agreement, in the circumstances covered by section 30E. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent or provider invited applicants to offer more than the advertised rent, that appears to be the conduct specifically prohibited by section 30F(3). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish whether merely increasing the advertised rent after your application, or falsely recording that you withdrew, itself breached one of those provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent or provider, in writing, to explain:

1. why your application was recorded as withdrawn;
2. who withdrew it and when;
3. whether anyone was asked or permitted to offer more than the advertised rent; and
4. why the advertised rent was later increased.

The retrieved Act does **not** state the procedure for challenging this particular application decision, nor does it specify what evidence a prospective renter must preserve. It also does not provide enough information to say whether you can obtain compensation or another order on these facts. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

As a practical matter, preserve the original advertisement showing the rent, the complete application and submission confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, all messages with the agent, and dated screenshots showing the later higher listing. Also keep any message or witness account indicating that a higher offer was requested or received. The retrieved document does not prescribe these items, so this is evidence-preservation advice rather than a statutory requirement.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never says that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not banned on this date (only inviting one was). It covers the ban on inviting higher offers, and its statement that 'the documents do not establish whether merely increasing the advertised rent... or falsely recording that you withdrew, itself breached one of those provisions' arguably covers the relisting and false-email points, but the unsolicited-offer point is missing.

On relisting, the answer says "The documents do not establish whether merely increasing the advertised rent after your application... itself breached one of those provisions." It also never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.
