question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must request consent to keep a pet using the form approved by the Director and give it to the residential rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days** after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Because you sent the form three weeks ago, the 14-day period has passed. On the documents, the agent’s refusal alone does not prevent deemed consent if no Tribunal application was made within that period. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does not specifically say whether an owner’s allergy—or the fact that the owner rarely visits—makes refusal reasonable. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the nature of the premises, fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal **within 14 days** of receiving your request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no such application was made, you can state that the provider is taken to have consented under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the provider disputes this or seeks to prevent you keeping the dog, you can apply to the Tribunal; the Tribunal may order that you are permitted to keep the pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not state any separate procedure for challenging the agent’s refusal or any specific rule about allergies, so I cannot give further steps on those points.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
### What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate because the premises are being sold is permitted if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The notice must also be in the prescribed form, state the reason and termination date, and include supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, **if the notice was valid when given and has not been withdrawn, you should not assume you can ignore it**. However, the documents do not say that a failed sale automatically makes an existing notice valid or invalid. Whether the original notice remains valid may depend on the facts—for example, whether the landlord genuinely intended to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession and whether the notice met all formal requirements. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

Ask the landlord in writing to provide a **signed notice of withdrawal**. Until that is done, the notice is not withdrawn under section 91ZZQ. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If you believe the notice was invalid—for example, because the sale reason or supporting evidence was inadequate—you may apply to VCAT challenging its validity, generally within **30 days after the notice was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) If you do not leave by the stated date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order; only VCAT can decide whether you must leave, and a forcible eviction requires a VCAT possession order and warrant executed by Victoria Police. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed notice form is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025), Form 6**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On the documents provided, **you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed that rent would increase**. The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days’ notice in the prescribed form**, and a rent increase that does not comply is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed **Form 5** says that a valid notice is required for **all** rent increases and must state the current rent, new rent, start date, amount and calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) It may be sent by email only **if you have consented to electronic service of notices**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the email was only an informal proposal and was not a valid Form 5 notice—or you had not consented to receiving notices by email—the higher rent cannot start on the date mentioned in that email. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Continue paying the current rent and ask the agent to provide a valid **Form 5 Notice of Proposed Rent Increase**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Ask them to confirm the date they say you consented to electronic service, if they rely on the email as formal notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If a valid notice is later given, the increase can start **no earlier than 60 days after that notice is given**, subject to the other rules: rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months, and special restrictions apply during a fixed term. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- You may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within **30 days after a valid notice is given** if you consider the proposed rent excessive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide enough information to calculate the exact commencement date because no valid notice date has been supplied.

**Applicable documents:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **v110**, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf); *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **v004**, dated 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers every point: Form 5 is required ('a valid notice is required for all rent increases'), at least 60 days' notice is needed, the email alone does not oblige the tenant to pay ('you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed... a rent increase that does not comply is invalid'), and it gives a next step ('Continue paying the current rent and ask the agent to provide a valid Form 5').

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable Act is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises. Dog-chewed skirting boards would likely be treated as damage, not fair wear and tear, although the retrieved documents do not specifically address dog damage. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The renter must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable**, stating that the damage occurred and describing its nature. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The renter must leave the premises in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Repairs must be done by a **suitably qualified person**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider can issue a written repair notice requiring the renter to repair the damage at the renter’s expense **within 14 days**, in a proper and tradesman-like manner. Alternatively, the provider can state that they will arrange the repairs and that the renter is liable for the reasonable cost. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

So, **you should not simply arrange the repair and conceal it**. You must notify the owner or agent in writing as soon as practicable. The documents do not expressly say whether you may independently arrange a repair before receiving a repair notice, so they do not establish that you can do so without the provider’s agreement.

## What you can do or ask

Write to the owner or agent promptly, describe the damage, and ask whether they want:

1. you to arrange a suitably qualified repairer; or  
2. them to arrange the repair and provide the reasonable cost.

Keep photographs, written communications, the repairer’s qualifications and the invoice. If the provider arranges the repair under the Act, you may be liable for its **reasonable cost**, and the provider must give you written particulars of that cost; reimbursement is generally due within **14 days after completion**, subject to the statutory hardship provisions. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On insurance: **the retrieved documents do not say whether repairing the skirting boards without telling the owner would affect the owner’s insurance**. You should therefore ask the owner or agent, and not make any insurance-related assumption.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 March 2023**, the retrieved documents contain **no rule specifying how many electrical circuits a Victorian rental must have**. They therefore do not establish that having most power points on one circuit is, by itself, unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical minimum standard then in force required—**from 29 March 2023**, not 1 March—all power-outlet and lighting circuits to be connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not say that the rental must have separate circuits for a kettle and heater, or specify how much load a circuit must handle. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider nevertheless had to maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, with repairs or works carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing** that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and request that a suitably qualified person investigate and rectify the electrical problem. A renter must report damage or a breakdown of facilities, fixtures, furniture or equipment provided by the rental provider as soon as practicable. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Request a copy of the most recent electrical safety check.** The provider must give it to you within **7 days** of receiving a written request. The record must include the electrician’s name and licence or registration number, the check date, results, required repairs and actions taken, and an AS/NZS 3019 report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

3. The prescribed agreement terms required an electrical safety check of the rental provider’s electrical installations, appliances and fittings **every 2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician; if no check had occurred within the previous 2 years when you moved in, the provider had to arrange one as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

4. If the tripping is a **dangerous electrical fault**, it is an **urgent repair**. After taking reasonable steps to have the provider or agent act immediately, you may arrange the repair if they do not do so; reimbursement is available for the reasonable cost up to **$2,500**, subject to the Act’s conditions. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) If it is not urgent and the provider does not repair it within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director for an investigation or to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** say that you can require the provider to install a particular number of circuits. You can ask for the fault to be professionally investigated and repaired, rather than simply asking for an additional circuit.

**Documents and versions applicable on 1 March 2023:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 101**, incorporating amendments as at 7 September 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

Both points are covered: the answer says the 'retrieved documents contain no rule specifying how many electrical circuits a Victorian rental must have,' and it says that if the tripping is a 'dangerous electrical fault, it is an urgent repair,' alongside advice to request a copy of the most recent electrical safety check.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rooming house must provide **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the house can accommodate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The regulation does **not** say that use of the machine must be free. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

However, if the operator charges an amount for a service, they must have given you a **separate schedule of the service charge before you became a resident**, and if you use the service, they must give you an **itemised account showing your individual use**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the rooming house is operated by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, a laundry service charge is allowed only where it is not possible or practicable to measure each resident’s use accurately, and the charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator in writing for:

- the schedule of charges that was provided before you moved in; and
- an itemised account showing your individual laundry use. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask why the machines are coin-operated and how the charge was calculated. The retrieved documents do **not** state a general rule that an ordinary private rooming-house operator is prohibited from charging per use, or set a specific maximum coin charge.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant versions are:

- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 004, 1 July 2025**; and
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110, 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Each room in rented premises must be **free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) A rental provider must also ensure that the premises meet the prescribed minimum standards **on or before the renter enters into occupation**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** expressly prohibit an advertisement from showing apparent mould. However, a rental provider or agent must not induce someone to enter a rental agreement through conduct that is misleading or deceptive, or by a false or misleading representation about the premises’ characteristics. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) They must also give applicants prescribed information, including whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and, since **31 December 2021**, whether the provider received a repair notice in the previous three years about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A photo is relevant evidence, but the documents do **not** say that a photo alone conclusively proves that the minimum standard is breached. The standard concerns mould or damp **caused by or related to the building structure**, and a photograph alone may not establish that cause, the extent of the problem, or the condition of the premises when you would occupy them. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

Before applying, ask the provider or agent, in writing:

1. **Does the property currently comply with the rental minimum standards?**
2. **Is the apparent mould being treated or repaired before occupation?**
3. **Has the provider received a mould or damp repair notice in the last three years?** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask to inspect the bedroom and request an explanation of what the photograph shows. If the advertisement or answers conceal a known defect or create a misleading impression, that may engage section 30E of the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If you enter into an agreement and the premises do not meet the minimum standards, you may request urgent repairs to make them compliant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) If you have not yet entered into possession, the Act also allows termination of the agreement on the ground that the premises do not meet a rental minimum standard. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

All three points are covered: the output states rooms must be 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'; on the hardest point it says 'the documents do not say that a photo alone conclusively proves that the minimum standard is breached... a photograph alone may not establish that cause'; and it gives next steps such as asking the agent in writing, inspecting the bedroom, requesting urgent repairs, and terminating before possession.

## What the law says

If your friend is legally a **sub-tenant**, the Act says a residential rental provider may give the renter a notice to vacate where the renter has sub-let all or part of the premises without consent. A rental provider cannot personally use force; forcible eviction requires a VCAT order and a warrant carried out by Victoria Police. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

On the documents provided, I cannot say that you can simply serve your friend with a notice to vacate or change the locks. The documents do not explain the legal status or removal procedure for a friend who is merely an occupant rather than a sub-tenant.

You should first establish whether your friend has a sub-tenancy or another residential agreement with you. The relevant documents in force on **15 October 2026** are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 9 (30 June 2026)**. question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088 dated 2 July 2019, which was in force on 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about retaliation for repairs
The retrieved documents do not contain any provision that specifically prohibits or addresses a landlord giving a notice to vacate in retaliation for a tenant requesting repairs as of November 2019. 

### What you should check regarding the notice
Even without a specific statutory prohibition on retaliatory notices, you can verify whether the notice itself is legally valid by checking the following requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf):
* **Form & Signature:** Ensure the notice is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, and signed by the residential rental provider or their agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **Reason Specified:** Verify that the notice clearly specifies the reason(s) for giving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
* **Documentary Evidence:** If the notice is given under specific grounds (e.g., sections 91ZW, 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB, or 91ZZC), check that it is accompanied by documentary evidence approved by the Director that supports the stated reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **Termination Date:** Check that the termination date specified in the notice complies with the timeframes required by the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
If you believe the notice fails to meet these formal requirements, you can apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity. You must make this application **on or before the hearing of an application for a possession order**, and it must be lodged **within 30 days after the notice to vacate is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will then determine whether or not the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: If you are renting month-to-month, landlords generally have broader rights to issue notices without providing a specific reason under section 91ZW, though the notice must still meet the formal validity checks listed above.)*

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses all three points. It never states that a no-reason notice requires at least 120 days' notice, and only says landlords 'generally have broader rights to issue notices without providing a specific reason.' question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 110, as at 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), which was in force on your date of 1 October 2025, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### **Can you challenge what happened?**
Yes. The agent's actions likely breach several specific provisions of the Act regarding rental advertising and conduct:
* **Fixed Rent Requirement:** Rented premises must be advertised or offered at a fixed rent amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **No Soliciting Higher Offers:** It is an offence for a rental provider or their agent to solicit or invite an offer of rent that is higher than the advertised amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Misleading Conduct:** Providers and agents are prohibited from inducing someone to enter a rental agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, or by making false/misleading representations concerning the rent payable under the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They must also not make false or misleading representations in relation to the rent for the premises when promoting them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**How to challenge:**
* **Apply to VCAT:** You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) regarding this conduct. The Act explicitly notes that the Tribunal may make orders under section 472(1A) in respect of a contravention of the misleading/deceptive conduct provisions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Australian Consumer Law:** The Act states that these tenancy provisions do not limit the operation of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria), which also prohibits misleading and deceptive conduct [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### **What should you save as evidence?**
While the documents do not provide a specific checklist for this exact scenario, to prove the statutory breaches outlined above (soliciting higher rent, false advertising, and misleading conduct), you should immediately preserve:
* **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or links showing the property was advertised at the fixed, lower rent amount.
* **Proof of your application:** Copies of your submitted rental application and any confirmation emails/receipts proving you applied at the advertised price.
* **The false withdrawal email:** The full email (including headers/timestamps) falsely stating you withdrew, as this directly evidences the misleading representation.
* **Proof of the new listing:** Screenshots or records showing the property was re-listed at a higher rent.
* **Evidence of the higher offer:** Any communication or proof that another party offered more than the advertised price (if available).

*Note: The documents do not cover specific procedures for withdrawing a rental application, but the agent's false claim and subsequent actions fall squarely under the prohibited advertising and conduct rules listed above.*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can they refuse?
No, not outright. Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider (or their agent) **must not unreasonably refuse** consent for you to keep a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

They cannot simply say "no" and stop there. If they refuse your request, they are legally required to apply to VCAT within **14 days** of receiving your official form to prove that their refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they do not file an application with VCAT within those 14 days, the law automatically treats them as having **consented** to you keeping the dog [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### How the "Allergy" and "Rare Visits" Factors Work
If the agent does take the matter to VCAT within the 14-day window, a Tribunal member will decide if the refusal is reasonable. The Tribunal may consider factors such as the nature of the premises, the type of pet, and **any other relevant matters** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

While an owner's allergy can be considered, your point that they "hardly ever visit" is highly relevant to this decision. You can argue that because the owner rarely enters the building or your apartment, the risk of triggering an allergic reaction is minimal, making their blanket refusal unreasonable.

### What You Can Do
1. **Check the 14-day deadline:** Count exactly 14 days from the date you sent the official request form. If that period has passed and they have not applied to VCAT, you are legally deemed to have permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can formally notify the agent in writing that consent is now deemed given under the Act.
2. **Challenge the refusal:** If they refuse within the 14-day window without going to VCAT, or if they do apply to VCAT, you can also apply to VCAT yourself to challenge the decision [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Present your case clearly, emphasizing the owner's infrequent visits and any steps you will take to manage pet-related issues (e.g., regular cleaning, keeping the dog contained).
3. **Request clarification:** Ask the agent in writing whether they intend to file an application with VCAT under section 71D of the Act within the next 14 days. If they do not, their refusal has no legal standing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: This information is based on Victorian residential tenancy law as of 15 October 2026. For free legal advice or to file an application, you can contact Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) or visit VCAT (vcat.vic.gov.au).*

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria), version 110 as at 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes.** The fact that the buyer pulled out does not automatically cancel or invalidate the notice. Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate remains legally binding until it is formally withdrawn by the landlord or successfully challenged at VCAT. 

### What the Law Says
* **Notice for Sale:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if they intend to sell the premises with vacant possession immediately after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This notice must specify a termination date of at least 60 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Withdrawal Requirements:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn *only* if a formal "notice of withdrawal" is provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Crucially, this withdrawal notice must be in writing, signed by the landlord (or their agent), **and also signed by you** (the renter) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because your landlord has not provided this signed document, the original notice remains valid.

### What You Can Do
1. **Request a Formal Withdrawal:** Contact your landlord or agent immediately and ask them to provide a written notice of withdrawal that is signed by both parties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Once you sign it, the notice will be officially withdrawn.
2. **Challenge the Notice at VCAT:** If the landlord refuses to withdraw it, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge its validity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Since the sale has fallen through, you may argue that the ground for the notice (that the premises are to be sold with vacant possession on the termination date) is no longer established. You must make this application within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Negotiate a New Agreement:** If you wish to stay, you can try to negotiate a new residential rental agreement with your landlord for a different termination date or convert it to a periodic agreement.

*Note: This information is based strictly on the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria), version 110 as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). For specific legal advice tailored to your lease, you should contact a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version dated 6 August 2025) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version dated 1 July 2025), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under section 44(1) of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a rental provider must give a renter at least 60 days' notice **in the prescribed form** (Form 5) of a proposed rent increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The regulations strictly require this specific form to include details like the calculation method and your right to challenge the increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Because your agent only sent an informal email and never provided the official prescribed notice, the rent increase is legally invalid under section 44(5) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You are not required to pay the higher amount.

### From when does it apply?
Because the increase is invalid, **there is no valid start date for the higher rent**. The agent must issue a proper Form 5 notice giving you at least 60 days' notice before any new rent amount can legally take effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### What you can do or ask for:
*   **Request the official notice:** Ask your agent to provide you with a completed **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Continue paying current rent:** You can continue paying your existing rent amount until a valid, prescribed notice is properly served [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
*   **Challenge the increase:** If they do provide a valid Form 5 and you believe the increase is excessive, you have 30 days from receiving that notice to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation, or apply directly to VCAT under certain conditions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:

**1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?**
No. You have a strict legal duty to notify your rental provider in writing as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard residential tenancy agreement also explicitly states that where damage occurs, you must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Fixing it secretly would breach this notification requirement and could lead to disputes over your bond refund at the end of the tenancy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Who is responsible for the repair?**
Because your dog caused the damage, it is not considered "fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner's legal duty to maintain the property in good repair does not cover damage caused by you or your visitors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Therefore, **you are legally responsible** for repairing the skirting boards or compensating the owner for the cost. 
*   If you arrange the repair yourself, it must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
*   You should keep all receipts and get written confirmation from the owner that the matter is resolved so it does not negatively impact your bond refund when you move out.

**3. Would it affect the owner's insurance?**
The retrieved documents do not contain information regarding how tenant-caused property damage impacts a landlord's home insurance policy (such as excess fees or premium increases). You would need to ask the owner directly about this.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026)** and the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023 (Authorised Version No. 2, dated 1 December 2024)**, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
**Yes, rooming house operators are generally allowed to charge for coin-operated washing machines**, but they must strictly follow disclosure and access rules:
* **Disclosure & Accounting:** If a private rooming house operator charges you for any service (including laundry), they must give you a separate schedule of those costs *before* you take up residency [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, whenever you use the service, they must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Government/Registered Housing Agencies:** If your rooming house is operated by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they may impose a "service charge" for laundry only if it is not practicable to accurately measure individual use, and the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Access Requirements:** The operator must provide you with access to all facilities during "all reasonable hours" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Minimum Equipment Standards:** Under the Rooming House Standards Regulations, a rooming house is legally required to provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The law mandates the *provision* of the machine but does not require it to be free.

### What You Can Do
1. **Check your move-in paperwork:** Verify that you received a schedule of service charges before signing your agreement, and that you are receiving itemised accounts for your laundry use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they haven't provided these, they are breaching the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Monitor access:** Ensure the machines are accessible during reasonable hours as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Unreasonable restrictions on access could be challenged.
3. **Challenge excessive charges:** 
   * If you live in a Homes Victoria or registered housing agency property and believe the charge is too high, you can apply to VCAT to have the service charge withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   * For private operators, if the charges are unfair, hidden, or violate your agreement, you can raise this with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT for relief regarding unreasonable house rules or breach of duties.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
Based on the documents in force on 15 October 2026, the relevant laws are the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version dated 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version dated 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### How the law addresses your situation
The provided documents do not contain a specific section detailing the exact process for removing a mere guest or unauthorized occupant from a tenancy. However, if your friend’s stay is considered an assignment or sub-letting of part of the premises without consent, **section 91ZV of the Act** applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under this section, a residential rental provider may give you a notice to vacate if you have assigned or sub-let any part of the premises without consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard agreement also notes that renters must not assign or sub-let without written consent, and doing so allows the rental provider to issue a notice to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Important distinction:** Under the provided texts, the statutory power to issue a Notice to Vacate for this breach lies with the **rental provider**, not you as the tenant. The documents do not outline a process for a tenant to unilaterally evict an unauthorized occupant from their own lease.

### What must happen to end the tenancy
If the rental provider decides to act on this breach, the following steps apply:
1. **Use the correct form:** The notice must be given using the prescribed Form 6 from the Regulations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Provide a valid termination date:** The notice must specify a termination date that is at least 14 days after the date the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Explain the reason clearly:** You (or the provider) must explain why the notice is being given with specific details. Simply quoting general rules is insufficient, and VCAT may find the notice invalid if it lacks sufficient detail or required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Delivery:** The notice can be delivered personally, by registered post, or by email (if you have consented to electronic service) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### If your friend refuses to leave
If the termination date passes and your friend does not vacate, the rental provider must apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT will decide if you must leave and on what date. Importantly, you cannot personally use force to remove them; only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT warrant for possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Limitations of the provided documents
The retrieved texts focus strictly on the rights and obligations of rental providers and renters regarding formal notices and breaches like unauthorized subletting. They do not contain specific guidance on how a tenant internally manages or removes a guest who is not formally subletting the property, nor do they cover a landlord revoking permission for their own friend. For matters outside these specific statutory notice requirements, you would need to consult broader tenancy guidelines or legal advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version dated 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says
Under Victorian tenancy law, rental providers and their agents must advertise rent as a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They are strictly prohibited from soliciting or inviting offers that are higher than the advertised price [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, they must not engage in misleading or deceptive conduct to induce you to enter an agreement, nor make false representations concerning the rent payable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Making false or misleading representations about rent in advertisements is also a specific offence [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Can you challenge what happened?
Yes. The Act treats these actions as offences with penalties (60 penalty units for a natural person, 300 penalty units for a body corporate) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). While the provided documents do not outline a specific private compensation claim for this exact breach (unlike unlawful discrimination under section 210AA), they explicitly note that these provisions do not limit the operation of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can report the misleading conduct and false advertising to Consumer Affairs Victoria or seek advice on your consumer law remedies.

### What evidence you should save
To support a challenge, you should preserve:
* **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or records showing the advertised fixed rent price [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **The false withdrawal email:** The exact email claiming you withdrew (to prove the misleading conduct) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Proof of higher offers/listings:** Evidence of the property being listed at a higher rent and any information regarding others offering more than the advertised price (to demonstrate solicitation of higher offers or false advertising) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent for you to keep a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Crucially, there is a strict **14-day rule**: If the agent or owner refuses your request, they must apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within 14 days of receiving your official form to prove that refusing is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they do not apply to VCAT within those 14 days, the law automatically treats them as having **consented** to you keeping the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Regarding the owner's allergy: When deciding if a refusal is reasonable, the Tribunal considers factors like the type of pet, the nature of the premises, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While an owner's health condition could be considered, the agent cannot simply say "no" outright. The fact that the owner "hardly ever visits" is a highly relevant factor that strongly supports your case that the refusal is unreasonable.

### What You Can Do
1. **Check the 14-day deadline**: Count 14 days from the date you sent the official request form. If that period has passed and they have not applied to VCAT, consent is legally deemed given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may proceed with keeping your dog.
2. **If they applied to VCAT within 14 days**: They are required to notify you of a hearing. You can attend and present evidence (e.g., proof that the owner rarely visits) to show the Tribunal that refusing consent is unreasonable.
3. **Apply to VCAT yourself**: If you believe their refusal is unreasonable, or if they have not responded properly, you can apply to VCAT for an order permitting you to keep the pet on the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: This information applies to standard residential tenancies in Victoria as of 15 October 2026. For specific legal advice, contact Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) or your local Tenants' Union.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Do you still have to leave?**
No, you do not automatically have to leave just because a notice was issued. If the buyer pulled out and the contract of sale was terminated, the legal reason for your notice (the sale) no longer exists. This means your landlord is likely no longer entitled to enforce it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

### What the law says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a landlord can only give you a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the contract of sale was conditional (e.g., subject to finance or inspections), the landlord can only issue the notice within 14 days after those conditions are satisfied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

If the buyer pulls out, the ground for the notice ceases to exist. When a landlord applies to the Tribunal for a possession order, the Tribunal will only make an order if it is satisfied that the landlord "was entitled to give the notice" and that the notice "has not been withdrawn" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because the sale fell through, the landlord likely lost their entitlement to the notice.

### What you can do
* **Request a formal written withdrawal:** You can ask your landlord to formally withdraw the notice. The Act generally requires a notice of withdrawal to be in writing and signed by both the person giving the notice and the person receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If your landlord applies to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order because you haven't left, you have the right to challenge the validity of the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can argue that the information in the form is incorrect or incomplete, or that the landlord was not entitled to give the notice because the sale fell through [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* **Seek immediate advice:** If you think you have grounds to challenge the notice, you should seek advice immediately from a community legal organisation or call Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how your situation is handled:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under section 44 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), a rental provider **must** give a renter at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A valid official notice is required for all rent increases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Because you never received an official rent increase notice, any attempt to raise your rent is legally invalid [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You are only required to continue paying your current rent.

### From when would a higher rent apply?
Since the increase is invalid without a proper notice, it cannot take effect at all right now. If your agent decides to issue a valid official notice in the future, the new rent can only start on the date specified in that notice, provided that date is **at least 60 days after** the notice was given to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), here is how the law addresses your situation as of 1 March 2023:

### 🔌 Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The retrieved documents do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points that a rental property must have. 

### ⚡ What can you ask for?
While the law doesn't mandate a specific number of circuits, it does set strict safety standards and maintenance duties that you can use to address your issue:

**1. Ask for an upgrade to meet new electrical safety standards (effective 29 March 2023)**
Although these rules do not come into force until just over a month from now, you can ask your rental provider to proactively upgrade the switchboard to comply. From **29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Request repairs if the system is faulty or unsafe**
Your rental provider has a legal duty to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the breaker trips because of outdated wiring, a defective breaker, or an electrical fault (rather than simply overloading it with high-power appliances), this counts as a breakdown of facilities. 
* **If it's an immediate safety hazard** (e.g., sparking, burning smells, or complete loss of power): This may be classified as an **urgent repair**, which the provider must fix immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* **If it's a non-urgent fault:** You should notify your rental provider in writing about the breakdown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They are required to carry out the repairs within a reasonable time. If they do not fix it within 14 days of receiving your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### 💡 Practical Tip
Before requesting upgrades or repairs, try using the kettle and heater at different times to see if the breaker stops tripping. If it only trips when both are used simultaneously, the electrical system may simply be underpowered for modern appliances rather than being "broken." In that case, your strongest leverage is asking for the RCD/Circuit Breaker upgrade mandated by the new 29 March 2023 safety standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says
Yes, rooming house operators are allowed to charge residents for using coin-operated washing machines. However, they must strictly follow these legal requirements:
* **Facility Standard:** The operator is legally required to provide a washing machine in good working order as part of the standard laundry facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
* **Pre-Occupancy Disclosure:** If the operator charges for services like laundry, they must give you a separate schedule detailing these service amounts *before* you take up residency [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Itemised Accounts:** If you use the charged services, the operator must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of those services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Homes Victoria/Registered Agencies:** If your rooming house is operated by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they may impose a service charge for laundry if it is not possible to accurately measure your individual use, but the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask
* **Ask for the schedule:** If you were never given a schedule of service charges before moving in, ask your operator to provide one immediately.
* **Request itemised accounts:** If you are charged but haven't received an itemised account showing your specific usage, request one from the operator.
* **Check facility compliance:** Ensure the washing machines are kept in good working order as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
* **Seek help if needed:** If the operator refuses to provide the required schedules or accounts, or if you believe a charge is unfair, you can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for advice or apply to VCAT to resolve the dispute.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 110 as at 6 August 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 4 as at 1 July 2025)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation on 1 October 2025:

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?
**No, not if it misrepresents the property's condition.** 
The rental minimum standards explicitly require that each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Additionally, residential rental providers are prohibited from making false or misleading representations regarding the characteristics, condition, or facilities of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Advertising a property with visible mould could therefore be considered a breach of these rules.

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the standards?
The retrieved documents do not state that an advertisement photo alone is definitive proof of non-compliance. However, you can use it as initial evidence and take formal steps to document the issue:

* **Complete the Condition Report:** Within 5 business days of moving in, you must fill out and sign the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You should note any mould or dampness, indicate that you disagree with the rental provider's assessment if they claim it is clean/undamaged, and attach your own photos to support your assessment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Request Urgent Repairs:** If the rented premises do not comply with the rental minimum standards on or immediately after the day you enter into occupation, you may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs to ensure the premises comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Withhold Rent (if applicable):** If the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean when you are supposed to move in, you are not required to enter occupation or pay rent for that period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

By documenting the mould on the condition report with your own dated photos, you create a formal record that can be used if a dispute arises later.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 15 October 2026, here is what you need to know and do.

### The Law
Under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version dated 30 June 2026), a renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Letting a friend move in without your knowledge breaches this rule.

Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version dated 13 October 2026), you are entitled to issue a **Notice to Vacate** if the renter assigns or sub-lets (or purports to assign or sub-let) any part of the premises without your consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Must Do
1. **Issue a Notice to Vacate:** Provide the renter with a formal Notice to Vacate stating that it is being given because they assigned or sub-let part of the premises without your written consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Set the Termination Date:** The notice must specify a termination date that is **not less than 14 days** after the date you give the notice to the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Provide Specific Details:** You must explain in the notice why it is being given. It is not enough to simply quote a section of the Act; VCAT may find the notice invalid if it lacks sufficient detail or required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Deliver the Notice:** The notice can be delivered personally (e.g., by hand) or by registered post. Keep proof of delivery [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What Happens Next
- **If they leave:** If the renter vacates by the termination date, the matter is resolved.
- **If they stay:** If the renter does not leave by the termination date, you must apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT will hold a hearing to decide if it is reasonable and proportionate to make the order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Enforcement:** You **cannot** personally use force or change the locks to remove your friend. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT warrant for possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*Note: If the situation involves family violence, different timeframes and protections may apply. You should seek immediate legal advice from a community legal organisation or Victoria Legal Aid.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), No. 110 of 1997 (Authorised Version dated 6 August 2025) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Vic), S.R. No. 4 of 2021 (Authorised Version dated 1 July 2025):

### Does the notice still stand?
**Yes.** Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate given because the landlord is selling the property does not automatically expire or become invalid just because the buyer pulls out. The notice remains legally valid until it is formally withdrawn. 

### How can the notice be withdrawn?
According to section 91ZZQ of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a formal "notice of withdrawal" is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This document must:
* Be in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* Be signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* Be signed by you, the renter (the person to whom it was given) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What can you do?
1. **Request a formal withdrawal:** Contact your landlord and ask them to provide you with a signed notice of withdrawal. Until you receive this document, the original notice to vacate is still in effect.
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If you believe the reason for the notice is no longer valid (e.g., the premises are no longer being sold) or the information on the form is incorrect, you can challenge it at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
3. **If the landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order:** If your landlord tries to force you out through VCAT, the Tribunal must first be satisfied that the notice has not been withdrawn before making an order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can explain to VCAT that the sale fell through and ask if you can stay longer or if you would experience hardship by having to leave [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?

*   **Continue paying your current rent** until a valid notice is served and the 60-day period has passed.
*   **Ask your agent for the official form.** Request they provide you with the "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (Form 5) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Check the date on the notice.** Ensure the start date listed is at least 60 days after the date the notice was sent to you.
