Every rule it applies (ss 263 retaliation, the 120-day notice period, the 60-day challenge window, form requirements and possession orders) is cited to v088. It mentions v089 (4 December 2019) only to say it was not in force and was not applied.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents support a challenge at VCAT on the ground that a notice was given because you exercised your rights as a renter, but they don't contain the specific retaliation section, the minimum notice period, or a deadline for your challenge.

**Which versions apply:** On 15 October 2026, the in-force Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file labelled v115 and dated 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file labelled v009 and dated 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The text doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version No." label, so I'm using these file version labels. Older versions in the search results don't apply.

---

### What the law says

- **Grounds to challenge:** The Form 6 notice to vacate says a renter may challenge a notice at VCAT if they believe it was given "because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs are a protected right:** The Regulations say renters must notify the landlord in writing of breakdowns of facilities or fixtures, and the landlord must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord's possession application:** The landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order only after giving a notice to vacate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The application must be made no later than 30 days after the termination date in the notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must be satisfied the notice "has not been withdrawn" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and that it is "reasonable and proportionate" to make the order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must consider the nature, frequency and duration of the renter's conduct, and whether any breach is trivial [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity:** The Form 6 notice must state a reason with specific details. VCAT may find a notice invalid if it lacks enough detail or required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What to check

1. **The stated reason and details:** Does the notice give a specific reason with section number and details, or only a general statement? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
2. **The termination date:** The notice must allow the minimum notice required under the Act, plus time for delivery [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't state the minimum number of days for a month-to-month agreement, so I can't confirm whether a same-day notice with a termination date is valid.
3. **Timing:** Your repair request and the notice date. The notice was given the same day you followed up, which is relevant to your retaliation argument, but the documents don't set a rule about how close in time counts.
4. **Documentary evidence:** Whether the notice says evidence is attached, and whether any is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Delivery:** Whether it was delivered properly (in person, post, or email with consent) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

- **Keep records:** Save your written repair requests, the notice, and any messages or photos.
- **Challenge at VCAT:** Form 6 says you can challenge a notice at VCAT if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your renter rights [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Watch for deadlines:** The documents say "specific timeframes may apply to certain reasons to challenge a notice" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but the retrieved text doesn't give the deadline for a retaliation challenge. The 30-day VCAT deadline in Form 6 applies only to notices linked to family violence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Treat the deadline as unconfirmed and act quickly.
- **Stay in the home while it's contested:** If the landlord applies for a possession order, VCAT decides whether to make it. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice now:** Form 6 advises seeking advice immediately from a community legal organisation, via consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act as it stood on 1 October 2025, the advertised fixed rent could not be solicited to be exceeded, and the Act prohibits false or misleading rent advertising. However, the retrieved documents don't cover the withdrawal email, and they don't show a complaint process for this situation.

## What the law says on 1 October 2025

The applicable version is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file dated 6 August 2025, labelled "v110" ( [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)). The excerpt doesn't print a separate Authorised Version number, so "v110" is the only version identifier I can give you.

- **No bidding:** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" ( [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 30F(3)). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate ( [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)).
- **Accepting unsolicited offers:** The 6 August 2025 version does not contain a provision barring providers from accepting an unsolicited higher offer. A later version (dated 25 November 2025) adds s 30F(4), which says a provider "must not accept an unsolicited or otherwise uninvited offer" of higher rent ( [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)). That version was not in force on 1 October 2025, so I can't apply it to your situation.
- **False or misleading advertising:** A provider or agent "who promotes or advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent" ( [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), s 30G(2)).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** why your application was recorded as withdrawn, and ask for the rent they advertised and any offers they received. This is a practical step; the documents don't set out a formal process for it.
2. **Check the Tribunal route.** The excerpt notes that s 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of s 30E (misleading conduct inducing a person to enter an agreement) ( [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)). The excerpt doesn't show a specific Tribunal remedy for breaches of s 30F or s 30G, so I can't confirm one from these documents.
3. **Seek advice.** The documents don't say whether a withdrawal email or a higher offer, on its own, breaches the Act. Please check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisory service.

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence requirements, so this is general practice:

- The advertisement or listing showing the fixed rent, with the date and a screenshot.
- Your application form and any emails or messages you sent.
- The "withdrawal" email, with full headers and date, and any replies.
- Any messages or listings showing the new, higher rent, with dates.
- A note of anything you were told about other offers, including who told you and when.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether the withdrawal email itself breaches the Act.
- Whether accepting the higher offer breached the Act on 1 October 2025 (the explicit prohibition appears only in the later version).
- The Tribunal process or remedies for breaches of s 30F or s 30G.

This is general information based on the documents, not legal advice.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?

- **Consent is required.** A renter may keep a pet only if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The request must be in the approved form.** A renter must request consent in the form approved by the Director and give it to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You used that form, so this step appears to be met.
- **The provider must not unreasonably refuse.** The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent after 14 days.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal factors.** If the provider does apply, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- Three weeks ago is roughly 24 September 2026. The 14-day window would have closed around 8 October 2026, assuming the request was given on that date.

- The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal, or whether the owner rarely visiting changes that. The Act only says a refusal must not be unreasonable and lists factors the Tribunal may consider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Consumer Affairs Victoria can be contacted on 1300 55 81 81 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises "are immediately after the termination date to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Where a contract of sale has conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied, or within 14 days after the contract is entered into if it is not that kind of contract [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum notice:** The termination date must be "not less than 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity requirements:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and is accompanied by documentary evidence approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, an increase without a valid written notice is invalid, so you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet. The start date depends on a valid notice, which you haven't received.

## What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice must state the amount of the increase and the method used to calculate it, and must mention your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Only one increase per notice, and no more than once every 12 months** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **An invalid increase has no effect.** A rent increase made in contravention of these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements:** The rent generally can't go up before the term ends unless the agreement provides for a set increase or a calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed form:** The notice must be Form 5 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an email from an agent counts as a valid notice, so you should check whether anything you received follows that form.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for a formal Form 5 notice.** Check that it states the current and new rent, the start date, and the calculation method [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the notice period.** The 60-day requirement applies to the version of the regulations in force on 1 October 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Later versions of Form 5 say 90 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but those postdate your date, so I haven't applied them.
3. **Ask the Director to investigate.** If you receive a valid notice and think the rent is excessive, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to VCAT.** After a Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it. Without a report, you can apply with VCAT's leave after 30 days from the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 notes that you will generally pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get help.** Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting information line is 1300 558 181 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- The notice may provide for only one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase and the method used to calculate it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase made in contravention of these requirements is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form (Form 5) says the rental provider must give at least 90 days' notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This conflicts with the 60 days in the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't explain the discrepancy, so I can't tell you which period a tribunal would apply. The safer reading for you is the longer 90-day period.
- Form 5 also requires the current rent, the new rent, the start date and the calculation method. The rental provider's name must be given, and it "cannot be the agent's name" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask for**

- **Ask for a proper notice.** An informal email is not in the prescribed form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Ask the rental provider to serve a Form 5 notice. The documents don't say whether an email could ever count as service. Form 5 mentions email delivery only if the renter has consented [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the timing.** If a valid notice were given on 1 February 2026, the earliest start date would be about 2 April 2026 under the 60-day rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), or about 2 May 2026 under the 90-day rule [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). These are my calculations from the stated periods, not figures from the documents.
- **Object within 30 days.** You may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given if you think the increase is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT.** After a Director's report, you may apply to VCAT within 30 days. Without a report, you may apply to VCAT with leave, if there are reasonable grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says you will generally need to pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Get help.** Form 5 gives Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting website (www.consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) and phone number (1300 558 181) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** Your current lease terms (for example, whether you're on a fixed term, or whether a rent increase is already provided for in it), and whether the rental provider has served any notice that isn't in the documents. The Act says a rent increase during a fixed term is not allowed unless the agreement provides for one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Check your agreement.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The Act requires you to tell the owner in writing, and you can only arrange repairs yourself in limited urgent cases. The documents don't say whether insurance is affected.

## What the law says

The Act in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file labelled Authorised Version 115 (dated 13 October 2026). A renter must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage to the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version dated 30 June 2026) add that renters must avoid damaging the premises and, where damage occurs, must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The same Regulations say that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Telling the owner is required.** Getting the skirting boards fixed quietly would not satisfy the written-notice duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Arranging the repair yourself is limited.** You may arrange urgent repairs only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to carry them out immediately, and you cannot get them to do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether chewed skirting boards count as urgent. The full list of urgent repairs is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, which isn't in the documents I retrieved [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Don't assume the repair qualifies.
- **If you do arrange urgent repairs,** you must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations describe reimbursement of up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Expect the owner may seek the cost.** In a dispute, the Tribunal must consider whether the repairs are needed because of the renter's act or omission or a breach of the duty not to damage the premises, and whether the renter provided documentary evidence of the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep receipts and written records.
- **Practical next step:** Tell the owner or agent in writing now, describe the damage, and offer to arrange a suitably qualified tradesperson with their agreement.

The documents I retrieved don't cover how the owner may recover the cost from your bond or what the Tribunal would order in your case.

## Insurance

The documents don't address the owner's property insurance or whether the damage would affect it, so I can't answer that part.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set a number of circuits for a rental. They don't cover the law as it stood on 1 March 2023 for this issue, so I can't confirm what applied that day.

**What the law says**

- The circuit-protection standard is in Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021. It says: "On and from 29 March 2023, in relation to electrical safety, all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to—(a) a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000... and (b) a switchboard-type Residual Current Device that complies with" one of three listed standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This text also appears in the 2025 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Because 29 March 2023 is after 1 March 2023, the documents indicate this clause was not yet in force on the date you gave. The retrieved documents don't show the version in force on 1 March 2023 that covers this point.
- The clause doesn't say how many circuits a rental must have. It sets a protection requirement for the outlets and lighting circuits.

**What the renter can ask for**

- **Electrical safety check records:** The regulations require the rental provider to ensure an electrical safety check is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and to give the renter the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The earliest version I retrieved is dated 1 June 2022 and is labelled v002. Its page doesn't show an Authorised Version number, and I can't confirm it was in force on 1 March 2023.
- **Compliance after 29 March 2023:** From that date, you can ask the provider to confirm the outlets and lighting circuits meet clause 9 above [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set a procedure for this request or a deadline for the provider to respond.

**What I couldn't confirm**

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 versions I retrieved are dated 2025 or later, so I couldn't check the Act's wording as at 1 March 2023.
- The documents don't cover urgent repair procedures or any remedies for the tripping breaker.

Because the breaker trips under normal use, you may want to raise it with your provider in writing now, describing the problem and asking for an electrical check. Keep a copy of the request.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a number of circuits for a rental or say how much load a circuit must carry. They do require that power outlets be protected by circuit breakers and safety switches, and they give you specific things you can ask your landlord to do.

**Versions applied (as at 15 October 2026):** The Act is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file `rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13`) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file `rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30`) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm the Authorised Version numbers from the text of these documents, so I've used the version numbers in the file names.

### What the law says

- **Electrical protection:** The rental minimum standards say that "all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device complying with one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This has applied since 29 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to comply:** The landlord must ensure the rented premises comply with the minimum standards on or before the day you move in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Good repair:** The landlord must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** If the agreement doesn't contain a prescribed safety term, the landlord must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations and fittings they provided is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can ask for

1. **Compliance with the standards.** Ask the landlord to make sure the wiring meets the electrical safety standard above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a single-circuit setup with an overloaded circuit breaker breaches this standard, so you'd need an electrician to assess it.
2. **Urgent repairs.** If the premises don't comply with the minimum standards when you move in, you can issue a request to the landlord for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't set out a full list of urgent repairs, so check that electrical faults count before relying on this.
3. **The date of the last electrical safety check, in writing.** At your request, the landlord must give you the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **An electrical safety check.** If no check has been done in the last 2 years at the time you first occupied the premises, the landlord must arrange one as soon as practicable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Any required number of circuits, or the load a circuit must carry.
- Whether the tripping breaker counts as a breach of the standard.
- The current list of urgent repairs, and any reimbursement or VCAT details, because the 2026 version of the regulation's forms wasn't in the retrieved text.

Because the breaker is tripping, I'd suggest asking a licensed electrician to check the circuit and report in writing. You can ask the landlord to arrange this.

It says power outlets must be connected to a Circuit Breaker and a Residual Current Device. It gives next steps, including asking for 'the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing' and a repair request.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't directly say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They set rules for utility charges and for service charges, but neither covers laundry machines specifically.

**Version applied:** The latest version in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in the file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't state the version number on the page, so I'm taking it from the file name.

**What the law says**

- **Utility charges don't cover washing machines.** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used *in the room*, but only if the operator pays for them, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge. This doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Nothing in this section covers laundry machines.
- **Service charges are restricted.** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of the amounts before the resident moves in. If the resident uses those services, the operator must give an itemised account of the resident's individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The laundry service charge rule applies only to public and community housing providers.** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may charge for laundry services in a declared rooming house, but only if it isn't possible or practicable to measure the individual use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This doesn't appear to apply to a private operator, but the documents don't say what coin-operated charges by other operators are allowed.
- **Washing machines are a required standard.** From 26 February 2024, the rooming house standards require a washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the house's maximum occupancy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The operator must also ensure that facilities and services meet the applicable standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). (That obligation appears in the 2020 version of the Act I retrieved [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf); I did not confirm it in the 2026 excerpt.)

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the schedule of services.** If the operator charges for the machines, ask for the written schedule of charges. You're entitled to it, and it should have been given before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you're charged for using the machines, you can ask for an account showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the machines work.** Under the standards, there should be a working washing machine for your house's residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). If there isn't, raise it with the operator.
4. **If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or change a service charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a private operator may charge for coin-operated machines, and at what price.
- Whether a coin charge counts as a "service charge" under these sections.
- Whether the 2023 standards (dated 1 December 2024) are the current version as of October 2026. This is the only version I found [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

If you tell me who operates your house (a private landlord, a community housing provider, or Homes Victoria), I can search for the rules that apply to that situation.

---

The hardest one, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is covered by 'The documents I found don't directly say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines.' The answer also states the 'washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents' standard, says the operator 'must give the resident a separate schedule of the amounts before the resident moves in', and gives the next step 'Ask for the schedule of services.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents suggest that advertising a property with known mould in a bedroom may breach the law. They do not say whether a photo alone proves a breach.

**What the law says**

- **Advertising:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises to let unless they reasonably believe, at the time, that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The mould standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is Schedule 4, clause 8 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough?**

The documents don't answer this directly. The clause refers to mould "caused by or related to the building structure," and a photo shows the mould but not its cause. The documents don't say whether a photo is sufficient evidence of a breach, or how a dispute would be decided.

Record-keeping may matter. A later version of the Act says a provider or agent who advertises must keep records "sufficient to demonstrate compliance with section 65B," and the Director may publish guidance on what those records are [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This provision appears only in the Act version dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** Advertising the flat with mould photos isn't automatically unlawful, but the provider must reasonably believe the premises meet the standards. A photo alone doesn't settle whether the place fails them, and the documents don't say how much weight a photo carries.

## What the law says

- **Advertising:** A provider or agent must not advertise premises to let unless, when they advertise, they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The mould standard:** Each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Note that the photos show mould but don't show its cause. The standard only covers mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure.
- **Records:** A provider or agent who advertises must keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the advertising rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Director may publish guidance on what records are sufficient [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and can require the records to be produced. Failing to produce them carries a penalty of 150 penalty units for a natural person or 750 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?

The documents don't say. They don't state that a photo proves or disproves compliance, and they don't set out how a dispute is decided. What they do show is that the question is whether the mould is caused by or related to the building structure, and whether the provider reasonably believed the premises complied when advertising. A photo showing mould is relevant evidence, but the documents don't say whether it is conclusive.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Before moving in:** If the renter hasn't yet entered possession, they may give notice to terminate on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **After moving in:** If the premises don't comply on or immediately after the day the renter moves in, the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them up to the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Information requests:** The renter can ask the provider or agent for the records they must keep under the advertising rule, but the documents don't say the renter has a direct right to them. The renter can also ask the Director to require production of the records, though the documents don't say how a renter would do this.
- **Disputes:** The documents don't describe a dispute process for this situation beyond the termination and urgent repair routes above.

## Version caveat

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 text I retrieved is dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which is after 1 February 2026. The sections on advertising (s 65B) and records (ss 65C–65F) show amendment notes, but I can't confirm the exact wording in force on 1 February 2026.
- The Regulations text I used is "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25" (dated 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Newer versions exist, and I can't confirm from the retrieved material which version was in force on 1 February 2026. The documents also don't show an "Authorised Version No." field, so I can only identify the documents by their file references.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered, and the hardest one, that a photo alone doesn't prove a breach, is stated directly as "A photo alone doesn't settle whether the place fails them" and "the documents don't say whether it is conclusive."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states 'A photo alone doesn't settle whether the place fails them' and 'Advertising the flat with mould photos isn't automatically unlawful', and it requires only that the provider 'reasonably believe the premises comply' and 'keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance', never an inspection certificate.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer cites the Act as 97-109aa115 (version 115, dated 13 October 2026), not the in-force Authorised Version No. 111, and draws the advertising, records, termination and urgent-repair rules from that later version, so its substance depends on a version not in force on 1 February 2026. Its Regulations citation (21-3sra005, version 005) is correct.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't contain a specific process for removing a friend who moved in without consent. The closest rule is about subletting or assigning without consent, and the tenant can't remove the friend by force. I'm assuming you are the renter, since you say your friend moved in without telling the agent. If you are the landlord, let me know and I'll address that side.

**Which version I used:** For 15 October 2026, the most recent Act in the search results is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25", dated 25 November 2025). I can't confirm from these documents whether it was amended after that date. The earlier v110 (6 August 2025) is superseded [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The most recent Regulations retrieved are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01", dated 1 July 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I could not identify an "Authorised Version number" beyond these file labels.

---

### What the law says

- **Subletting or assigning without consent:** A landlord may give a renter a notice to vacate if the renter "has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The notice must give a termination date "not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Regulations on consent:** The renter "must not assign (transfer to another person) or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Gap:** The documents don't say whether a friend moving in and living there, without paying rent to you, counts as subletting or sub-let "any part of the premises." That depends on the facts and isn't defined in the retrieved text.
- **Breach process:** A landlord can use the faster successive-breach route only where the renter has breached the same duty provision twice before and the landlord gave a breach of duty notice each time [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the friend to leave.** The documents don't set out a process for this. I can't tell you what notice, if any, is needed for a non-party occupant.
2. **Tell the agent or landlord now.** Disclosing the arrangement and asking for consent, or agreeing on a way forward, may avoid a notice to vacate. The Regulations say consent must be in writing and the landlord "cannot unreasonably withhold consent" to subletting [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This applies to subletting or assignment, so it may not cover a friend who is simply staying.
3. **If you receive a notice to vacate,** you can challenge it at VCAT in some circumstances. Form 6 in an older 2022 version of the Regulations lists possible grounds, including that "it was not given to you properly" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Don't expect self-help.** The 2022 Form 6 text says "Rental providers cannot personally use force to remove you," and only Victoria Police acting on a VCAT warrant can carry out a forcible eviction [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That rule protects renters, but it shows the proper route is through VCAT.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether a friend who moved in without consent is an "occupant" the landlord can require to leave, and how that is done.
- The exact notice a landlord must give to remove a non-party occupant.
- Whether VCAT's approach changed after the 25 November 2025 version.

For case-specific advice, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the hardest point, the answer says the documents don't settle whether 'a friend moving in and living there, without paying rent to you, counts as subletting... That depends on the facts,' which names what they pay as a deciding fact. On consent, it says the renter 'must not assign... or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing statements is made. The answer says "I can't tell you what notice, if any, is needed for a non-party occupant" and that "the tenant can't remove the friend by force." It does not claim the friend lacks rights for not being on the lease, and it does not say the friend can apply to VCAT to be added. The 14-day period it cites applies only to a landlord's notice to the renter for subletting.

version-cited.reason: No. The rubric requires the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (dated 13 October 2026), but the answer instead names and applies 'rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25' (link 97-109aa111). It also relies on superseded Regulations versions ('rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01' and the 2022 version 21-3sra002 Form 6) for rules it presents as steps the user can take, rather than the in-force version 009.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't contain the 2019 provisions on retaliation or notices to vacate, so I can't say whether this notice is retaliatory under the law in force on 1 November 2019. They do cover the repair-request steps and remedies.

**Which version applies**

The version in force on 1 November 2019 is most likely the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **v088** (file `rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf`, dated 2 July 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The next version in the set, v089, is dated 4 December 2019 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), so it wasn't in force on your date. The documents don't state commencement dates, so this relies on the file dates.

**What the 2019 Act says that's relevant**

- **Urgent repairs:** A tenant may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and the landlord can't be reached or won't act. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** You may apply to the Director to investigate if you gave the landlord written notice that repairs are needed and they weren't done within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal orders:** After the Director's report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs, within 60 days of receiving the report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may also apply without the report if you haven't received it within 90 days of applying for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into Rent Special Account:** If you gave a notice requiring repairs and the landlord failed to carry them out, the Tribunal may authorise you to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The v088 excerpts don't include any provision on retaliatory notices to vacate, or the grounds and form for notices to vacate in 2019. I can't say what they required.
- Later versions have anti-retaliation rules, but they don't apply on 1 November 2019. For example, the 2025 version says a notice under s 91ZK is of no effect if given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The same version says certain other notices are of no effect if given in response to the renter exercising a right, or making a report under s 72AA [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It also gives 30 days to challenge a notice under s 91ZZS [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). None of this is confirmed for 2019.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 are not in force in 2019 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), so I have not relied on them.

**What you can check or do now**

1. **Confirm the version.** Check the full 2019 Act text (v088) for any retaliation and notice-to-vacate provisions. The excerpts I retrieved don't include them.
2. **Document the timeline.** Record when and how you reported the leaks (in writing, if possible), when the landlord was notified, and when the notice was given. The 14-day period in the repair provisions runs from the written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the notice itself.** Note any stated reason and termination date, and whether it was served the same day as your repair follow-up.
4. **Pursue the repairs.** If they remain outstanding, the written-notice and Director/Tribunal routes above are available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Get advice quickly.** Because I can't confirm the 2019 notice rules or any challenge deadline from these documents, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' legal service before the termination date. They can confirm the rules that applied on 1 November 2019.

It says it cannot confirm whether a retaliatory notice has no effect in 2019 ('The v088 excerpts don't include any provision on retaliatory notices to vacate'). It never mentions challenging at VCAT within 60 days, citing only a 30-day period from a 2025 version.

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version **v088** (file `rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf`, dated 2 July 2019)' and bases all its applied rules on that version (repairs, Director/Tribunal, Rent Special Account). It mentions the 2025 version (97-109aa110) and the 2021 Regulations only to say they 'don't apply on 1 November 2019' or are 'not in force in 2019'. Its recommended steps do not depend on them, so deleting that material would not change the substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act has a specific anti-retaliation rule, but in the version I found it covers only one type of notice. The documents don't show a general retaliation bar for a notice based on repairs, so the key question is which ground the notice relies on.

I'm applying the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as it stands on 15 October 2026. The most recent version in the search results is the Authorised Version dated 13 October 2026, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I haven't checked whether a later version applies on that date.

## What the law says

- **Notice to vacate for repairs:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate for repairs only if the works cannot be carried out unless the renter leaves, all permits and consents are obtained, and the notice gives at least 90 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The 90-day period is current under v115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An earlier version said 60 days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Retaliation rule:** A notice under s 91ZK (threats and intimidation) is of no effect if it was given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provision on notices given in response to a renter's rights, however, is limited to s 91ZK in the text I found [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I didn't find an equivalent provision for a repairs-based notice.
- **Discrimination:** A notice under the repairs section is of no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Form and content:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reason(s), and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a repairs notice, it must also be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice:** You may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) challenging the validity of the notice, and the application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the Tribunal finds the notice valid, you generally cannot challenge it again [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What to check

1. **The stated reason.** Does the notice rely on the repairs section, or on another ground such as a breach, damage, or sale? Check the cited section against the list above.
2. **The termination date.** For a repairs notice, it must be at least 90 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A date shorter than that is a defect.
3. **Documentary evidence.** Check whether the landlord attached evidence supporting the repairs reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Whether the works are real.** The landlord must intend the work, have permits and consents, and the work must need you to leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the works aren't planned, that suggests the stated reason is not genuine.
5. **Form and signature.** Check that the notice is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, and states the reasons [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Your repair request.** The Act requires you to give the landlord written notice of breakdowns or damage as soon as practicable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of your written request and the date it was sent. Note that this is from the 2025 version I found [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), not the v115 text, which doesn't include that section in the excerpt.
7. **Timing.** Note the date you received the notice. Your 30-day window to apply to the Tribunal runs from that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Apply to VCAT within 30 days** of receiving the notice, challenging its validity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Do this before the Tribunal hearing on any possession application, because the application must be made on or before that hearing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Raise discrimination or other defects** in your application if they apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek legal advice promptly.** The documents don't list specific services, so I can't name them from these sources.

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't contain a general rule that a repairs-based notice is void because it was given in retaliation for a repair request. The only express retaliation rule I found applies to s 91ZK notices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a retaliation argument succeeds for a repairs notice would depend on the discrimination ground or on case law, which I haven't searched.
- They don't say whether giving the notice on the same day as your repair request has any legal effect.
- Whether this notice is retaliatory is a factual question that the Tribunal would decide.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Every required point is covered. Form and reason: the notice is "not valid unless it is in the prescribed form... states the reason(s)" and, for repairs, must be "accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason." No general retaliation rule (the hardest point): "They don't contain a general rule that a repairs-based notice is void because it was given in retaliation for a repair request. The only express retaliation rule I found applies to s 91ZK notices." Next step: "Apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving the notice, challenging its validity."

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?

**Short answer:** The Act prohibits rental bidding, and it gives a route to the Tribunal (VCAT) for contraventions. The documents don't say how to dispute a withdrawal, and they don't list what evidence to keep.

**Version in force on 1 October 2025**

The latest retrieved version before that date is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, reprint labelled v110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I've used that version. The documents don't show an explicit "Authorised Version No." label, so I'm relying on the v110 file label.

The later reprints (v111, 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf); v115, 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)) postdate 1 October 2025, so I haven't relied on them. One caveat: the v110 text doesn't include s 30F(4), which bars accepting unsolicited higher offers. That subsection appears in v111, with an endnote saying it was inserted by No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't confirm when No. 6/2025 took effect, so I can't say whether s 30F(4) applied on 1 October 2025.

**What the law says (v110)**

- A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A provider or agent must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter an agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, or by a false or misleading representation about the rent payable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A provider or agent must not make a false or misleading representation about rent in promoting or advertising premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A residential rental provider must not unlawfully discriminate in refusing to let premises on a protected attribute [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Tribunal application:** The Act notes that s 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make for contraventions of the misleading-conduct section (s 30E) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't spell out the full VCAT process or time limits.
- **Discrimination:** If the withdrawal was based on a protected attribute, s 210AA allows an application to the Tribunal for compensation for loss suffered [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how this applies to your facts.
- **Asking the provider:** The documents don't set out a procedure for asking the provider to explain the withdrawal, so I can't say what a formal request must contain.
- **Higher relisting:** Relisting at a higher rent isn't itself addressed in the v110 text. The prohibitions I found concern advertising a non-fixed rent, soliciting higher offers, and misleading rent representations. Whether a breach occurred depends on what the provider did with the other offer.

**Evidence to keep**

The documents don't list specific evidence. These are my suggestions, not requirements from the Act:

- The advertisement showing the fixed rent, with the date you saw it.
- Your application and all correspondence with the provider or agent.
- The email saying you had withdrawn, with full headers.
- Any evidence that you did not withdraw.
- Anything showing the new listing price, and any information about the other offer.

**Not covered by the documents**

- The procedure and deadlines for a VCAT application.
- Who to contact for free advice or complaints. The later Regulations mention Consumer Affairs Victoria and Victoria Legal Aid [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), but those versions postdate 1 October 2025, so I haven't relied on them.

### What the law says

- **Fixed rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **No bidding:** A provider or agent must not solicit a higher rent offer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Act's note says the Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of this section [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **False rent advertising:** A provider or agent must not make a false or misleading representation about rent in advertising [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **No reasons required:** A provider does not have to give reasons for an unsuccessful application [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

2. **Ask about the higher offer.** The rules are about soliciting and accepting higher offers, so ask whether a higher offer was received and whether it was accepted.

- The **advertisement or listing** showing the fixed rent, with screenshots and dates. This is key for the fixed-rent and false-advertising rules [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not on the basis given. Under the Act in force on 15 October 2026, the provider can't unreasonably refuse, and if they didn't go to the Tribunal within 14 days, your request may now be treated as approved. Whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground is for the Tribunal to decide, and the documents don't answer that directly.

**What the law says**

- The renter must request consent in the form approved by the Director, and give the request to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You appear to have done this.
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse" consent to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, "within 14 days after being given the request," they apply to the Tribunal under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your request was made about three weeks ago, so that 14-day window has likely closed, unless the request was given to the agent later than you think. The documents don't say whether any Tribunal application was lodged.
- A provider can only refuse through the Tribunal. Under section 71D, they may apply for an order that it is reasonable to refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In deciding, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list an owner's allergy as a factor, so I can't say whether it would count.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the request date and any response.** Confirm when the agent received your form and whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days. If they didn't, the Act treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the agent in writing** to explain the reason for refusal and to confirm whether a Tribunal application was made. Keep copies of everything.
3. **Seek help if the refusal stands.** Victoria Legal Aid can advise on discrimination in relation to a rental agreement at 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT can be reached at vcat.vic.gov.au or 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the dog is an assistance dog,** the position is different. The Regulations state that refusing accommodation because of an assistance dog can be unlawful [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out the full rules, so please get advice.

**Documents used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 version named *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (dated 13 October 2026) is the most recent version and applies to 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number on its face, so I've identified it only by the file name, v115. Please check the official reprint for the exact number. The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (dated 30 June 2026) is cited for the discrimination guidance [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't clearly say whether a notice to vacate for a sale that fell through is still effective. Based on what I could find, the notice stays in place unless it is formally withdrawn, and the documents I retrieved don't cover the withdrawal rule that applied on 1 October 2025.

**Version applied:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110 (dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), is the version in force on 1 October 2025. A later version, v115 (dated 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), postdates your date, so I haven't relied on it for the main answer. I cite it only where it is the only text available on a point, and I flag that below.

**What the law says**

- A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession. Where a contract of sale is subject to conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. Otherwise it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** The retrieved v110 text doesn't include the withdrawal section. The later v115 text says a notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The buyer pulling out does not, on that wording, withdraw the notice by itself. Please check whether the v110 text says the same.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice.** A withdrawal only takes effect with a signed notice of withdrawal from both of you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the notice.** Under the v115 text, you can apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity on or before the hearing of a possession application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The v110 text on this point wasn't retrieved, so confirm the deadline before relying on it. The form notice also lists reasons to challenge, including that the notice "was not given to you properly" or that the information in it is incorrect or incomplete [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Whether the sale was genuinely planned when the notice was given isn't covered by the documents, but it is the key factual question.
3. **Wait for VCAT if the landlord applies for possession.** If you don't leave on the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know who can enforce it.** The landlord cannot personally use force to remove you. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **End the agreement early if you want to leave.** For a notice given because the premises are to be sold, you can end the agreement earlier than the termination date by giving at least 14 days' notice, using a Notice of intention to vacate form [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
6. **Get advice.** The form directs you to community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting, or 1300 558 181 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Bottom line:** Unless the landlord signs a proper withdrawal, treat the notice as still in effect. Don't assume it is void because the sale fell through. Get advice promptly, and check the 30-day challenge deadline against the date you received the notice.

The hardest, the dependence on the notice's ground and its evidence, is covered by the description of the sale-with-vacant-possession ground and its contract timing, plus 'Whether the sale was genuinely planned when the notice was given... is the key factual question.'
