question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice probably still stands, so you may still have to leave by the termination date. The buyer pulling out does not withdraw it. You may have options to challenge it, but the documents don't say whether a failed sale affects its validity.

The law in force on 1 February 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v111 (file dated 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The later v115 (dated 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the Regulations dated 30 June 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) post-date your question, so I haven't applied them. The Regulations version in force on your date is v005 (25 November 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The notice must give at least 60 days' notice. Where a contract of sale exists, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into, or after the last sale condition is satisfied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). (I could only retrieve this section's text from v110 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf); the v111 excerpts I have don't include it, so please check it against v111.)
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Since the landlord hasn't withdrawn it and you haven't signed anything, the statute doesn't treat it as withdrawn.
- **Validity:** A sale notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reasons, be accompanied by the documentary evidence approved by the Director, and specify the termination date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Enforcement:** The landlord cannot make you leave on their own. Only VCAT can order possession, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a VCAT warrant. Rental providers cannot personally use force [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice.** Withdrawal needs a written notice of withdrawal signed by both of you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You can apply within 30 days after the notice was given, on or before the hearing of any possession application [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You should check whether the notice was valid when given, since the documents don't address what happens after a sale falls through.
3. **Check the 6-month rule.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they must not let the premises for use as a home within 6 months of the notice. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a person or 750 for a body corporate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, an email saying rent is going up is unlikely to be a valid rent increase. You generally don't have to pay the higher rent unless you receive a proper written notice, and even then the increase can't start until at least 60 days after the notice is given.

## What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give the renter "at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v004) prescribe Form 5 for this, and the form states that "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases have no effect.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Form 5 content.** The notice must set out the current rent, the new rent, the start date, and the method used to calculate the increase [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It must also state that the rent "cannot be greater than the amount calculated using this method" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing limits.** The rent can't be increased "at intervals of less than 12 months" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and under a fixed-term agreement the rent can't rise before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What this means for you

- **Your email doesn't appear to be a valid notice.** Form 5 is a prescribed form that the provider "must use" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). An informal email saying rent is going up, followed by a refusal to negotiate, doesn't appear to meet that requirement. The documents don't say explicitly how an email is treated, so this is an inference from the prescribed-form requirement.
- **No start date applies yet.** Because no valid notice was given, the documents don't give a date from which a higher rent would be payable. If a valid notice is later served, the earliest start date would be at least 60 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Ask in writing** for the provider to serve a formal Form 5 notice if they want to increase rent. Keep copies of all communications.
- **If you receive a proper notice,** you have 30 days after it is given to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate the proposed rent if you think it is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT, and the form says you "will need to pay the increased rent amount from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your agreement** for any fixed-term rent increase clause, since that may affect what is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice** from a tenancy service if the agent insists on the higher rent without a valid notice. The documents don't list specific services, but Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting section is referenced in the form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Versions applied

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110 (dated 6 August 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) is the version in force on 1 October 2025. A later version, v111 (25 November 2025), exists [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) but does not apply to this date.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004 (dated 1 July 2025)** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) is the version in force on 1 October 2025. A later version, v005 (25 November 2025), changes Form 5 to require "at least 90 days notice" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That does not apply to this date.

*This is general information based on the documents retrieved, not legal advice.*

question: It is 1 February 2026. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?

The version of the Regulations in force on your date is the one dated 25 November 2025 (file version v005, Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form says the rental provider "must give you at least 90 days notice of any rent increase" and that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't explain how these fit together. Using 90 days is the safer reading, and you should check with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

During a fixed term, rent can only go up if the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Based on the documents, an email or a verbal statement that rent is "going up" is not a notice in the prescribed form. Form 5 requires specific details: the current and new rent amounts, the start date, and the method used to calculate the increase [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** Not without telling the owner first. The Act requires written notice to the owner, and the owner generally has to be given a chance to do the repair. The documents I found don't cover the insurance question.

**Version applied:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file `rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf` is the version in force on 15 October 2026. The file name gives the version as v115, but the text doesn't state an Authorised Version number separately, so please confirm that against the official reprint. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What the law says

- **You must notify the owner in writing.** A renter must give written notice to the owner "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **You can arrange repairs yourself only in limited cases.** Under the urgent repairs provision, a renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or agent to do the repairs immediately, and they cannot get the owner or agent to do them. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Renter-arranged urgent repairs need written notice.** You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving written notice of the repairs and the cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs.** This applies to both urgent and non-urgent repairs. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- **Chewed skirting boards are probably non-urgent.** The retrieved regulations list urgent repairs as including failure or breakdown of essential services or appliances for hot water, cooking, heating or laundry. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Damaged skirting boards aren't on that list, and the full statutory definition of "urgent repairs" isn't in the documents I retrieved. Confirm with Consumer Affairs Victoria.
- **Your duty to avoid damage.** A renter must avoid damaging the premises, and where damage occurs, must notify the owner in writing. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- **If the owner doesn't act.** For non-urgent repairs, the owner must carry them out within a reasonable time. You can apply to VCAT if the owner hasn't done the repairs within 14 days of receiving notice. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- **Damage you caused can count against you.** In a VCAT repairs application, the Tribunal must consider whether the repairs are needed because of an act of the renter, and whether the owner was notified and given a reasonable opportunity to repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage. Email is acceptable under the Act's electronic communication provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask the owner to arrange a suitably qualified person** to repair the skirting boards, and offer access so they can inspect. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

4. **Don't arrange repairs yourself without the owner's involvement** unless the repair falls within the urgent repairs rules above, which this likely doesn't.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a number of circuits for a rental. The electrical rule they do contain is about how outlets are protected, and it doesn't start until 29 March 2023, four weeks after today.

The later versions I found (2025 and 2026) are not in force yet, so I've relied on v002 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **The circuit rule starts later.** Clause 9 says "On and from 29 March 2023," all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Nothing in the documents limits outlets or appliances per circuit**, so I can't say whether one circuit for most outlets is non-compliant on its own.
- **The general repair duty applies now.** The landlord must ensure the premises are "provided and maintained" in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition, whatever the age of the property [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act text I retrieved is the 2026 compilation, not the 2023 version, so check the wording as it stood in March 2023.

## What you can ask for

1. **A written request for an electrical inspection and repair.** The landlord must make sure any repairs are carried out by a suitably qualified person [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Describe the tripping and the kettle and heater combination in your request.
2. **Confirmation that the wiring will meet the 29 March 2023 standard.** From that date, all outlets must be on the listed circuit breaker and RCD [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask the landlord to confirm this in writing.
3. **Record the problem.** Note any safety defect in your condition report and tell the landlord about it. The condition report guidance I found is from the 2025 version of the regulations, not v002, so check the 2023 form [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **If nothing is fixed.** The condition report guidance says that if the landlord doesn't carry out repairs within a reasonable time, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is also from the 2025 version.

**Safety note:** Don't keep resetting a breaker that trips repeatedly. Stop using the overloaded circuit and get an electrician to look at it. Any scorching, burning smell or warm outlets are urgent.

I couldn't find the 2023 text of the electrical safety check duty. The Act's two-yearly check duty in s 68A(1A) was inserted by No. 46/2025, so it likely wasn't in force on 1 March 2023 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

1. **An electrical inspection by a suitably qualified person.** The landlord must ensure repairs are carried out by a suitably qualified person [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **The date of the most recent electrical safety check, in writing.** You can request this [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **A repair, if the premises don't meet the minimum standards.** A landlord must ensure rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in. If they don't, you may issue a request for urgent repairs [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The number of circuits a rental must have.
- Whether tripping a breaker when two appliances run together is a breach. The documents don't address circuit capacity or appliance loads.
- The full urgent repair procedure. The Act refers to section 72AA for urgent repairs [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but that section wasn't in the material I retrieved.

**Version note:** As at 15 October 2026, I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (the latest regulations version in the material, dated 30 June 2026) and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (dated 13 October 2026). The version numbers come from the file names, as the text itself doesn't state them.

Because the wiring problem may be a safety issue, I'd suggest asking for an electrician's inspection in writing and keeping a copy of your request.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set limits on the charges an operator can make, and the rules for Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies are different.

**What the law says**

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays for those utilities, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge. This does not apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Washing machine use isn't covered by this section.
- **Service charges by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency:** These bodies may charge for "laundry or utility services or facilities," but only in a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3), and only where it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure the resident's use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't say that a private operator can impose a similar charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Schedule and itemised account:** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of the charges before you move in. If you use the services, it must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum number of residents the house can accommodate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask the operator** which legal basis it relies on for the charge, and whether the machines are part of a separately metered utility or a service charge.
2. **Check your paperwork.** Did you receive a schedule of services before you moved in? If the operator charges for services, it must have given you one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Request an itemised account** of your individual use of the machines, if you're being charged for them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Identify who runs the house.** If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or vary the service charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order the charge withdrawn, varied, or otherwise varied as it thinks fit [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Check the washing machine count.** If the house has fewer washing machines than the standard requires for its maximum number of residents, that is relevant to your rights [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out what remedy applies.

**Gaps:** The documents don't say whether a private operator can charge for coin-operated machines, or how a dispute with a private operator would be resolved. The Tribunal process I've described applies only to Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Version applied:** I used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version **v115** (file name rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf), the latest version in the documents and in force on 15 October 2026. The version number comes from the file name, as the excerpt doesn't show it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Rooming House Standards are from S.R. No. 10/2023, reprint dated 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the washing machine standard ('a washing machine, in good working order, for every 12 or fewer residents'), the schedule of charges required before moving in, and the next step of checking for that schedule. The hardest point, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is covered by 'The documents don't say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted: the answer limits the cost cap to Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies in declared rooming houses ("only in a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3)" and "The Act doesn't say that a private operator can impose a similar charge"), it states that the documents "do set limits on the charges an operator can make" rather than saying there are no rules, and it never says the machines must be free.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version v115" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations as the "reprint dated 1 December 2024" (link 23-10sra002, i.e. version 002). Both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies comes from them.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents suggest the provider may not advertise a property that they don't reasonably believe meets the minimum standards, but they don't confirm that this rule was in force on 1 October 2025. The documents also don't say whether photos are enough to prove a breach.

**Which versions apply on 1 October 2025**

- **Act:** The latest retrieved Act version dated before that date is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its text does not include the advertising provision. The advertising rule (s 65B) appears in the later Authorised Version No. 111 (25 November 2025), with a note that it was inserted by No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't show when No. 6/2025 took effect, so I can't confirm the rule applied on 1 October 2025.
- **Regulations:** The latest retrieved Regulations version dated before that date is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Mould standard:** Schedule 4, clause 8 provides: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The same wording appears in later versions [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to comply:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** In the later Act version, a provider or agent must not advertise premises to let unless, when advertising, they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is the same as above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Records:** The later Act version also requires providers who advertise to keep records "sufficient to demonstrate compliance" with s 65B, and says the Director may publish guidance on what those records are [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from the retrieved documents that these record-keeping rules applied on 1 October 2025.

**Is the photo enough?**

The documents don't answer this directly. They don't say that photos are proof of a breach or that they are insufficient. They also don't say how a mould breach is assessed. The clause 8 wording covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and a photo may show mould without showing its cause. That is my observation about the text, not a statement from the documents.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Request urgent repairs:** If the premises don't comply with the minimum standards on or just after the day the renter moves in, the renter "may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs to be carried out" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for maintenance:** The provider must ensure the premises are "provided and maintained in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies "whether or not the renter was aware of any disrepair" before moving in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for records:** Under the later Act version, the provider must keep compliance records for advertised premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The renter could ask about them, but the documents don't say whether renters have a right to request them.

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether the 1 October 2025 advertising rule was already in force.
- Whether photos alone are enough to prove a breach.
- How the Tribunal would handle a mould dispute, or any deadlines for filing one.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are present. The answer quotes the mould standard: 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'. The hardest point, that a photo alone doesn't prove a breach, is covered by 'They don't say that photos are proof of a breach' and 'a photo may show mould without showing its cause'. The answer also gives a next step, telling the renter they 'may issue a request ... for urgent repairs to be carried out'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the photo alone proves a breach. It says "The documents don't answer this directly" and "a photo may show mould without showing its cause." It also never says the advertising ban applied on 1 October 2025. It says the rule "appears in the later Authorised Version No. 111 (25 November 2025)" and "I can't confirm the rule applied on 1 October 2025." It notes the version in force before that date "does not include the advertising provision." The short answer's hedged wording ("suggest the provider may not advertise... but they don't confirm that this rule was in force on 1 October 2025") makes this a borderline case, but it does not assert that the ban applied on that date.

version-cited.reason: No — the answer names 'Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)' and 'Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)', but it relies on the later 'Authorised Version No. 111 (25 November 2025)' for the s 65B advertising rule (its short answer) and the record-keeping duty (offered as a step the renter can take); despite caveats, removing that material would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** Generally no. The provider or agent may only advertise the premises if they reasonably believe the premises meet the rental minimum standards. Visible mould in a bedroom suggests a possible breach. However, the documents don't say whether a photo alone is enough to prove non-compliance.

**Version applied:** For 1 February 2026, I used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file labelled v111, dated 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file labelled v005, dated 25 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Later versions in the search results, dated 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), postdate your date and I did not apply them.

---

### What the law says

- **Advertising rule:** A provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let" unless, when advertising, they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Mould that comes from something other than the building structure is not clearly covered by this clause.
- **Duty to comply:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," whether or not the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Is the photo enough?

The documents don't say. They don't set out an evidentiary test, say whether a photo is proof, or describe how a dispute is decided. A photo showing mould in a bedroom is a reasonable basis to question compliance, but whether it proves the breach depends on facts the documents don't address, such as whether the mould is related to the building structure.

### What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for information before signing:** The documents don't give a renter a specific right to ask for the advertising records in February 2026. Records rules for advertised premises (s 65E) and the Director's power to request them (s 65F) appear only in the 13 October 2026 version [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which doesn't apply on 1 February 2026.
- **Request urgent repairs after moving in:** If the premises don't comply with the minimum standards on or immediately after move-in day, the renter "may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask about the mould:** The renter can raise the mould with the provider. The documents don't set out a further step or timeframe beyond the urgent repair request.
- **Check whether the renter can withhold rent:** Under s 65, if premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day, the renter isn't required to move in, and rent isn't payable for the gap [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This covers cleanliness and vacancy, not mould specifically, so the documents don't support withholding rent over mould under this section.

**Not covered by the documents:** how to prove a mould breach, the dispute process at the Tribunal, and any remedies beyond the urgent repair request.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. The answer states the advertising rule ('reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards') and the mould standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'). It gives next steps: raise the mould with the provider, or request urgent repairs after moving in. The hardest point, that the photo alone doesn't prove a breach, is covered by 'The documents don't say. They don't set out an evidentiary test, say whether a photo is proof... whether it proves the breach depends on facts the documents don't address.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The output never says the photo alone proves illegality; it says "the documents don't say whether a photo alone is enough to prove non-compliance" and that a photo "is a reasonable basis to question compliance, but whether it proves the breach depends on facts the documents don't address". It never mentions an inspection certificate, describing the advertising rule only as requiring that the provider "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 'file labelled v111, dated 25 November 2025' (97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 'file labelled v005, dated 25 November 2025' (21-3sra005). Every rule it applies (advertising, the mould standard, compliance at move-in, the maintenance duty, urgent repairs and s 65) comes from those in-force versions. The later v115 (s 65E/65F) and v009 versions are mentioned only to say they postdate 1 February 2026 and do not apply, so the answer does not rely on them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the 2026 law, the only route in these documents to end an unauthorised occupancy is a notice to vacate for sub-letting or assignment without consent. The documents don't say how to remove someone who is not a party to the lease, so that part is unanswered.

**Which versions apply:** On 15 October 2026, the most recent Act in the documents is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file labelled v115, dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The most recent Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* file labelled v009, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm the Authorised Version numbers from the text itself, so those labels come from the file names.

**What the law says**

- The rental provider may give the renter a notice to vacate if the renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to assign or sub-let, all or part of the premises without the provider's consent. The notice must give a termination date at least 14 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations say the renter must not assign or sub-let without the rental provider's written consent. The provider cannot unreasonably withhold consent and must not charge a fee for it, other than reasonable expenses [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate must state the reason and the section of the Act. It must also be accompanied by documentary evidence where the Act requires it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must give the notice before applying to VCAT for a possession order. If the renter doesn't leave, VCAT decides whether to make a possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant. Rental providers cannot personally use force [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Establish the facts.** The notice-to-vacate ground is about sub-letting or assignment. Whether your friend's stay counts as that depends on whether they pay you or the agent rent or have exclusive possession. The documents don't define these terms, so this is a question for legal advice.
2. **Seek consent or end the arrangement.** If you want your friend to stay, you can ask the agent or rental provider for written consent. Consent cannot be unreasonably refused [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you want them out, you can ask them to leave.
3. **If you're the renter and want to end your agreement,** you can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This ends your agreement; it does not remove your friend.
4. **If the rental provider wants to act,** they must give you a notice to vacate with a termination date at least 14 days after notice is given, and they must give the reason and section number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you don't leave, they may apply to VCAT. You can challenge the notice at VCAT, and you should seek advice quickly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- How to remove an occupant who isn't a party to the agreement, including whether a notice to vacate can be used against them.
- Any timeframe for challenging a notice on this ground.

For these points, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting, 1300 558 181) or a community legal centre [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: both points are covered, and the hardest one is met by "Whether your friend's stay counts as that depends on whether they pay you or the agent rent or have exclusive possession," while the written-consent point is met by "the renter must not assign or sub-let without the rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer makes none of the prohibited assertions. Its 14-day periods apply only to the renter's own agreement, and it expressly says this "does not remove your friend" and that the documents don't cover "How to remove an occupant who isn't a party to the agreement." It never suggests a lockout, never says the friend has no rights, and never says the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file labelled v115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and relies only on in-force versions, including the Regulations 'v009, dated 30 June 2026' (21-3sra009).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A month-to-month arrangement is a **periodic tenancy**. The rental provider could generally give a notice to vacate without stating a reason, but the notice had to provide **at least 120 days’ notice**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

However, a notice under section 263 had **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise—or proposed exercise—of a right under the Act**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Reporting or pursuing repairs is supported by statutory repair rights: you could notify the rental provider in writing, and for non-urgent repairs apply to the Director after 14 days, or pursue a Tribunal order under the repair provisions. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The fact that the notice was given on the same day as your repair follow-up is relevant evidence of possible retaliation, but the documents do not say that same-day service automatically invalidates the notice. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What to check and do

1. **Check the termination date.** For a periodic tenancy, it should be at least **120 days after the notice was given**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Preserve the timing evidence:**  
   - your original repair report;  
   - your follow-up message;

   - timestamps, emails, texts and replies; and  
   - photographs or other evidence of the leaking fixtures.

4. **Check whether the rental provider actually pursued the repairs.** For non-urgent repairs, the Act allowed you to apply to the Director after the provider failed to repair within **14 days**, and to seek a Tribunal order in the circumstances set out in sections 74–75. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. The regulations document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (30 June 2026)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- You were required to notify the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable** about damage or a breakdown of fixtures or facilities supplied by the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- For non-urgent repairs, after you give written notice, the rental provider must carry out the repairs within **14 days** before you can apply to the Director or VCAT under the repair provisions. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, include required documentary evidence where applicable, and specify the termination date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed notice form says that you may challenge a notice if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter, or if it was not properly given or contains an incorrect or incomplete reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The Act provides that a notice given under **section 91ZK** has no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you should check and do

1. **Keep evidence of the timing and substance of your repair request**—for example, messages, emails, photographs, repair reports and the notice to vacate. The same-day timing may be relevant to whether the notice was retaliatory, but the retrieved documents do not state what evidence VCAT must accept. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the notice itself:**  
   - Is it the prescribed notice-to-vacate form?  
   - Is it addressed to you and signed?  
   - Does it identify the precise legal reason and explain why it was given?  
   - Is the termination date lawful and does it allow the required notice period?  
   - Is any required documentary evidence attached? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Check whether the notice cites section 91ZK or another section.** The documents do not provide the notice-period rule specifically for a month-to-month agreement or the full text of every possible notice ground, so they do not establish from the retrieved material what termination date applies in your particular case. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice** if you believe it was issued because you requested repairs. The prescribed form says to seek advice immediately, and the Act provides a specific challenge process for some notice grounds; however, the retrieved documents do not state the deadline or procedure specifically for a retaliation challenge under section 91ZK. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not stop paying rent or arrange repairs yourself solely because you received the notice** unless you follow the Act’s separate repair procedures. For urgent repairs, the Act requires reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to act immediately; for non-urgent repairs, the 14-day written-notice process applies. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can ask VCAT to determine whether the notice is invalid on the basis that it was retaliatory, and you should obtain tenancy-law advice promptly because the retrieved documents do not give the complete procedural details for that particular challenge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 February 2026. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 February 2026**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025**. The Act requires rental premises to be advertised or offered at a **fixed rent**. A rental provider or agent must not solicit or invite an offer above that amount, and must not accept an unsolicited or uninvited offer above it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore:

- If the agent or provider **asked for, encouraged, or accepted** a higher offer, that may breach the rental-bidding provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Relisting the property at a higher rent may also be unlawful if the original advertisement was false or misleading about the rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- However, the documents do **not** establish that an applicant must be offered the property at the advertised rent, or that rejecting your application is unlawful merely because another applicant offered more. The prescribed application information says an agent is **not required to give reasons** for an unsuccessful application. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The standard application information also confirms that rental bidding is prohibited and that the premises must be advertised or offered for a fixed amount. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Contact the agent in writing to say that you **did not withdraw your application**, ask them to correct their records, and ask whether your application was assessed at the advertised rent. Applicants are specifically told to contact the provider or agent to check the outcome. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether anyone was invited to offer more than the advertised rent, and whether the property was relisted because a higher rent was sought. If the answer confirms an invitation, solicitation, or acceptance of a higher offer, identify that conduct as potentially contrary to section 30F. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Keep the original advertisement, the higher-rent listing, your complete application and submission confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, all messages with the agent, and dated screenshots showing the rent and when each version appeared. **The retrieved documents do not prescribe an evidence list or explain a specific challenge process for this situation**, so they do not establish what forum, remedy, or deadline applies to a complaint about the alleged rental-bidding conduct.
- The documents also do not say that you can compel the agent to disclose another applicant’s offer. Do not assume that the report you heard is proof unless you can obtain supporting evidence.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer does not state that the false 'withdrawn' email isn't covered by a specific rental-law rule; it only says the documents do not 'explain a specific challenge process for this situation.' It also never clearly says that relisting at a higher fixed rent isn't illegal by itself, saying only that relisting 'may also be unlawful if the original advertisement was false or misleading.'

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**, you had to make the pet request using the approved form—which you say you did. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A simple refusal by the agent is not enough: the provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days** of receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you sent the request **three weeks ago**—more than 14 days ago—the documents indicate that you can treat consent as having been given **if the provider did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that an owner’s allergy automatically justifies refusal, nor do they say that the owner’s infrequent visits defeat that reason. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing, whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal under section 71D within 14 days of receiving your request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- **If no application was made within 14 days:** the Act says the provider is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
- **If an application was made in time:** the Tribunal decides whether refusal is reasonable, and may permit you to keep the dog or uphold the refusal. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not provide a specific process or form for you to challenge the agent’s refusal, so I cannot say more about that process from these documents.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer says the provider is taken to have consented unless they apply to the Tribunal within 14 days; it says that after three weeks 'you can treat consent as having been given if the provider did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days'; and it gives a next step: 'Ask the agent, in writing, whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal under section 71D within 14 days.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

A rental provider may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, **to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf) The Act does **not** expressly say in the retrieved text that a notice automatically becomes invalid when a buyer later withdraws from the purchase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

The notice is withdrawn only if the rental provider gives a **written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf) Therefore, the landlord’s failure to withdraw it does not, by itself, answer whether the notice remains valid—but you should not assume that the buyer’s withdrawal automatically cancels it.

If you do not leave by the termination date, the landlord cannot simply remove you personally: they must apply to VCAT for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf) VCAT must be satisfied that the provider was entitled to give the notice, that it **has not been withdrawn**, and that making the possession order is reasonable and proportionate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, using the statutory withdrawal process, and ask them to confirm that the tenancy continues. The withdrawal must be signed by both sides. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to VCAT challenging its validity; this applies to a notice given under section 91ZZB, the “premises to be sold” provision. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- Check whether the notice was in the prescribed form, gave the required reason and documentary evidence, and specified a termination date at least **60 days** after it was given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies to VCAT, attend the hearing and explain that the buyer withdrew and ask VCAT to determine whether the notice is still valid and whether possession would be reasonable and proportionate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

So, based only on the retrieved documents: **the buyer pulling out does not clearly or automatically cancel the notice, but the documents also do not establish that you must leave despite the failed sale. Obtain written withdrawal or challenge the notice at VCAT.**

The answer never says that whether the tenants must leave depends on the ground stated in the notice and its evidence, such as a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract. It only quotes the 'to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' ground and suggests checking the 'required reason and documentary evidence', without tying the outcome to that distinction. The other three points are covered: the 60-day minimum, withdrawal 'signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter', and the next steps of a written withdrawal or a VCAT challenge within 30 days.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **_Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021_, Authorised Version 004, effective 1 July 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider must use the prescribed **“Notice of proposed rent increase to renter of rented premises”** form, and **a valid notice is required for every rent increase**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) An ordinary email saying that the rent will increase is therefore not enough unless it is a valid prescribed notice; email delivery is permitted only if you have consented to receive notices by email. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The notice must give you **at least 60 days’ notice** and state the current rent, new rent, start date, and method used to calculate the increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, based on the facts given, **you do not have to pay the higher rent yet**. You continue paying the current rent unless and until a valid rent-increase notice is given. The higher rent cannot start before the valid notice’s stated start date, which must allow at least 60 days’ notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide the prescribed rent-increase notice, including the calculation method and proposed start date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Since no valid notice has been given, the documents do not establish any date from which the higher rent could lawfully be charged. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If they later give you a valid notice and you think the increase is excessive, you may apply in writing to the **Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days** after the notice is given for an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 February 2026. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?

You can tell the agent that you will continue paying the current rent until a valid notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The notice must state the new rent, start date, calculation method, and your right to seek an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

On **1 March 2023**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002** (*rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf*). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved law **does not specify a minimum number of power-point circuits** for a rental. Therefore, it does not establish a breach merely because most power points are on one circuit. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical minimum standard requiring all power-outlet and lighting circuits to be connected to specified circuit breakers and residual-current devices applied **“on and from 29 March 2023”**—not on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does not state that a breaker tripping when the kettle and heater run together is, by itself, a breach or an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can ask the rental provider **in writing** for:

- the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**; and
- an electrical safety check if one has not been conducted within the previous two years when you took possession, because the provider must arrange one **as soon as practicable** in that situation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The check must cover the electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by the rental provider and must be conducted every two years by a **licensed or registered electrician**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

You can also report the repeated tripping in writing and ask the provider to have a licensed or registered electrician investigate whether the circuit and electrical installation are safe and adequate. The retrieved documents do not specify that the provider must install an additional circuit, so you should ask for the safety problem to be assessed rather than demand a particular number of circuits. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?

1. The **separate schedule** showing the laundry charge; and

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On the documents retrieved, the relevant minimum-standard document for **1 October 2025** is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025**. It says each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved Act text is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025**, which is later than the date in your question. The documents do not include the Act’s Authorised Version that was in force specifically on **1 October 2025**. In that later version, section 65B says a provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless, at that time, they **reasonably believe** the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, a photo that appears to show mould does **not by itself establish** that the premises legally fail the minimum standard: the standard is specifically concerned with mould or damp **caused by or related to the building structure**, and the retrieved documents contain no rule saying that a photograph alone proves non-compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Nor do the retrieved documents say that displaying such a photograph is automatically unlawful. The key question is whether the provider or agent reasonably believed the premises complied when advertising them. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

- Ask the provider or agent whether the bedroom is free from structurally caused mould and whether they reasonably believe the premises meet the minimum standards. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether the provider has received, in the last three years, a repair notice relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure; that is information prescribed for disclosure before entering a rental agreement. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- If you enter the tenancy and the premises do not meet the minimum standards, section 65A(2) allows the renter to request **urgent repairs** to bring them into compliance. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved documents do not state that the rental advertisement photograph, without further evidence, is enough to prove a breach.

(3) It gives next steps: ask the provider or agent, and request urgent repairs under s65A(2) after moving in.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If your friend has been given part of the premises as a **sublet**, you must not sublet without the residential rental provider’s **written consent**. An unauthorised sublet is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV, specifying a termination date at least **14 days** after the notice is given. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** say that merely allowing a friend to stay is necessarily a sublet. They also do not provide a specific procedure for a renter to remove an ordinary guest or occupant. Therefore, the documents do not establish exactly what you must do to make this friend leave.

## What you can do or ask

- Check whether your friend has exclusive use of part of the property, pays you rent, or otherwise has an arrangement that could amount to a sublet. The retrieved documents do not define how those facts determine whether a particular arrangement is a sublet.
- If the friend’s conduct has caused a breach, VCAT can make a compliance order requiring you to remedy the breach and refrain from a further or similar breach. The Tribunal may also order that you do not permit the person responsible for the breach to enter or remain at the premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the rental provider applies for possession, VCAT must consider whether making a possession order is **reasonable and proportionate**, including whether the breach was caused by someone other than you and whether it has been remedied. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?

- a notice based on **threats or intimidation** if it was given in response to exercising a right under the Act; and
- a notice ending a **fixed-term agreement** at the end of its term if it was given in response to exercising an Act right or reporting damage or a breakdown under section 72AA. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate must nevertheless be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and state the termination date. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the stated reason is **repairs, renovation or reconstruction**, check that the provider has obtained all necessary permits and consents, that the work cannot properly be done while you remain, and that the notice gives at least **60 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The provider cannot simply evict you on the notice alone: the Act provides for an application to the Tribunal for a possession order after a notice to vacate is given. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the notice carefully:** its form, signature, stated reason, termination date, and—if repairs are claimed—the required documentary evidence and the 60-day period. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Preserve evidence of retaliation:** keep your repair requests, photographs of the leaking fixtures, replies, inspection or repair records, and the notice showing that it was issued the same day.

3. **Ask the provider in writing** to identify the precise statutory ground for the notice and, if it is based on repairs, provide the supporting permits, consents and other documentary evidence required by the Act. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Continue pursuing the repairs.** The provider had a duty to maintain the premises in good repair. For non-urgent repairs, after written notice and 14 days without repair, you could apply to the Director for an investigation or to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) For urgent repairs, you could apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring them; the application was to be heard within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved provisions expressly give a 30-day validity challenge for notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB and 91ZZC, but they do not state an equivalent general challenge procedure for an ordinary periodic-agreement notice. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
