question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer premises at a **fixed rent amount**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising the property at one rent and then making a **false or misleading representation about the rent** is prohibited in the circumstances covered by section 30G. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false or misleading representation about rent, when it is used to **induce someone to enter a residential rental agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do **not** say that merely receiving or accepting another applicant’s unsolicited higher offer was prohibited on 1 October 2025. The later Regulations document says that, but it is dated **25 November 2025**, so it does not establish the law on your stated date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- The Act provisions retrieved do not specifically say that sending an inaccurate “you have withdrawn” email to an unsuccessful applicant is unlawful, nor do they set out a specific challenge process for that conduct. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing, to confirm:

1. Whether your application was received and assessed;
2. Why they recorded or told you that you had withdrawn;
3. When and why the advertised rent changed; and
4. Whether anyone solicited or invited an offer above the advertised rent.

If the evidence shows that the agent invited a higher offer, or advertised a rent that was not genuinely available, you can raise the possible contraventions of sections **30F** and **30G**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not specify which body to complain to, a limitation period, or the precise remedy available for this situation, so I cannot state those from the documents.

## Evidence to preserve

The retrieved documents do **not** provide an evidence checklist. To preserve the facts, you should nevertheless keep—without altering them:

- Screenshots or a saved copy of the original advertisement showing the rent;
- The application you submitted, including its date and the advertised rent;
- All emails, texts and portal messages, especially the message saying you withdrew;
- Any message or record showing that the property was later listed at a higher rent;
- The property address, listing URL, agent’s name and relevant dates; and
- Any written statement or message from the person who said a higher offer was made.

The documents do not establish that hearsay about another person’s offer proves a breach; the key issue under section 30F is whether the provider or agent **solicited or invited** a higher offer. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026** (“the Act”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must request consent to keep the dog using the approved form, and give it to the residential rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Most importantly, the provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within **14 days** after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You sent the request about three weeks ago—approximately **21 days**—so, on the information provided, the 14-day period has passed.

The agent’s statement that the owner is allergic does not, by itself, establish that the refusal is reasonable. If the matter is before the Tribunal, it may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, its appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that an owner’s infrequent visits automatically make an allergy reason unreasonable, or that an allergy automatically justifies refusal.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or owner, in writing, whether the owner applied to the Tribunal **within 14 days of receiving your request**. If they did not, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do not rely only on the agent’s verbal refusal if you cannot confirm whether a Tribunal application was made. The Act states that a renter may keep a pet where the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not explain the procedure for confirming a deemed consent or obtaining a Tribunal determination, so they do not provide further steps.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
### What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider may give a notice to vacate for sale only if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the buyer pulling out does **not automatically cancel the notice** if the landlord is still genuinely offering the property for sale with vacant possession. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, if the landlord is no longer selling or offering it for sale, the documents do not say that the notice automatically remains valid. The notice can be challenged, and VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give it and that the notice has not been withdrawn before making a possession order. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice remains in force unless it is formally withdrawn. Withdrawal requires a **written notice signed by both the landlord and the renter**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

So, **you should not assume that you can simply stay past the termination date**, but the landlord also cannot personally evict you. If you do not leave, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, given that the buyer has pulled out. The withdrawal must be signed by both sides. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT** if it was given within the last 30 days: a renter may apply to challenge a sale-related notice under section 91ZZB within **30 days after it was given**. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

3. Keep evidence that the sale fell through and ask the landlord to confirm whether the property is still being offered for sale with vacant possession. The retrieved documents do not provide a separate automatic cancellation rule for a failed sale.

## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**, a rental provider may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The notice must give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The Act says a notice to vacate is withdrawn **only** by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the landlord’s failure to withdraw it means the notice has not formally been withdrawn.

However, the retrieved documents do **not** say whether a sale notice automatically becomes invalid merely because a prospective buyer later pulls out. So the documents do not establish that you definitely must leave, or that you definitely do not.

If you remain after the termination date, the landlord cannot simply evict you themselves. They may apply to VCAT for a possession order, and VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the order is reasonable and proportionate. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form also says VCAT decides whether you must leave and on what date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord **in writing** to give you a formal notice of withdrawal, signed by both sides. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to VCAT to challenge its validity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies to VCAT for possession, you may challenge the notice at or before that hearing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Do not assume the landlord can physically remove you: forcible eviction may be carried out only by Victoria Police acting on a VCAT possession order and warrant. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a definite answer on whether the buyer’s withdrawal alone cancels the notice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004 (1 July 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must use the prescribed **Form 5—Notice of Proposed Rent Increase** for a rent increase, and **a valid notice is required for every rent increase**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) An ordinary email saying that the rent will increase is not that prescribed notice on the facts you give. The form permits delivery by email only **if you have consented to receiving notices that way**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The notice must give at least **60 days’ notice** and state the current rent, new rent, proposed start date and calculation method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Therefore, you do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you or refused to negotiate. The documents do not support charging the higher rent from 1 October 2025—or from any earlier date—without a valid notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Continue paying the existing rent and ask the agent to provide a completed **Form 5** if they intend to increase it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If they later give a valid notice, the increase can take effect no earlier than the date allowed by the required **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If the increase appears excessive, you can apply in writing to the **Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria** for an investigation within **30 days after the notice is given**; you may also apply to **VCAT** within the time limits stated in the form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is required, at least 60 days' notice, the plain email is not a valid notice so the higher rent is not payable, and next steps are given. The hardest point is covered by 'An ordinary email saying that the rent will increase is not that prescribed notice... you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted. The answer says "you do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you", requires "at least **60 days' notice**", and says email delivery is permitted "if you have consented to receiving notices that way", so it never claims the increase runs from the email date or that email notice is never allowed.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

The retrieved documents **do not establish which version was in force on 15 October 2026**. The latest Act retrieved is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, incorporating amendments as at **6 August 2025**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The latest regulations retrieved are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version **v005**, dated **25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Under those documents, a renter must take care to avoid damaging the premises and must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed agreement summary says the same and states that only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The Act’s urgent-repair procedure does not allow a renter simply to arrange work secretly: the renter must first take reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or agent to carry out the urgent repairs, and be unable to get them to do so. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not say whether chewed skirting boards qualify as an urgent repair.

The retrieved documents contain **no information about the owner’s insurance policy or whether an undisclosed repair would affect insurance**. Therefore, that insurance question cannot be answered from them.

## What you can do or ask

- Notify the owner or agent **in writing now**, describing the damage and attaching photographs. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether they want to arrange the repair, or whether they consent to your proposed suitably qualified repairer. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- Keep the written notice, consent, quotation, invoice and photographs. The Act says a Tribunal considering repairs must consider whether the provider was notified, given a reasonable opportunity to repair, and whether the renter has documentary evidence of the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Do not conceal the damage or arrange a repair on the assumption that it will remove your responsibility. The Act permits the provider to give a repair notice requiring the renter to repair damage at the renter’s expense, or stating that the provider will arrange repairs and seek the reasonable cost. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says — 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002 (1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved law **does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental. It therefore does not establish that having most power points on one circuit is, by itself, unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical minimum standard in Schedule 4 clause 9—requiring power-outlet and lighting circuits to have a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device—applies **“on and from 29 March 2023”**, so it was not yet in force on **1 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider must arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide **every 2 years** through a licensed or registered electrician, and must give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you request it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

Write to the rental provider or agent and:

1. **Report that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together**, and ask them to arrange an inspection by a suitably qualified electrician. Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Request the date of the most recent electrical safety check**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. Ask the electrician to determine whether the circuit, breaker, power points and wiring are safe and compliant, and whether an electrical upgrade or additional circuit is required. **The retrieved documents do not say that you can require a particular number of circuits or automatically require installation of an extra circuit.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Give the notice in writing. The rental provider must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time; if they have not done so within **14 days** after receiving your notice, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents identify as urgent a failure or breakdown of an essential heating service supplied by the rental provider, but they do not specifically say whether a breaker that trips when a kettle and heater are used together is an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. The answer says the law 'does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits,' and as a next step it advises reporting the tripping breaker for an electrician's inspection and repair, and to 'Request the date of the most recent electrical safety check.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer avoids both failure conditions: it says the law "does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits" and "does not establish that having most power points on one circuit is, by itself, unlawful," and that the circuit breaker/RCD standard applies "on and from 29 March 2023" so it "was not yet in force on 1 March 2023."

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not state a minimum number of electrical circuits** that a rental must have. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

They do require, from **29 March 2023**, that **all power-outlet and lighting circuits** be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and a compliant residual-current device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

A breaker that repeatedly trips may indicate that the electrical installation needs checking or repair, but the documents do not say that this fact alone entitles you to demand installation of a separate circuit. The rental provider must maintain the premises in **good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition, and any repair work must be done by a **suitably qualified person**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can give the rental provider written notice describing the tripping and ask them to:

1. Arrange an inspection by a suitably qualified person; and [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. Carry out any electrical repairs needed to make the premises compliant and suitably usable. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the agreement does not contain the prescribed safety-related term, the provider must arrange an **electrical safety check every 2 years**. You may ask in writing for the **date of the most recent check**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record; under the Regulations, it must be provided within **7 days** of the written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not carry out non-urgent repairs within **14 days** after your written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate, or apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs in the circumstances set out in the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not establish whether your particular breaker problem is legally an “urgent repair.”

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. It says that a rooming-house operator who charges a resident for services must provide:

- a **separate schedule** of the amount for the services before the resident moves in; and
- an **itemised account** showing the resident’s individual use if the resident uses those services. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does not otherwise state in the retrieved material that an ordinary rooming-house operator is prohibited from charging for washing-machine use. The rooming-house standards also require, from **26 February 2024**, at least **one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the rooming house can accommodate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

If the operator is **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, a laundry service charge is allowed only where it is not possible or practicable to measure use accurately, and it must not exceed the cost of providing the facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator for:

1. the **separate schedule** showing the washing-machine charge; and  
2. an **itemised account** showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, ask how the charge complies with the requirements that use cannot practicably be measured and that the charge does not exceed the facility’s cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** specify a particular maximum coin charge for washing machines operated by an ordinary private rooming-house operator.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the standard's "at least one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents"; that the Act does not state "an ordinary rooming-house operator is prohibited from charging for washing-machine use"; the "separate schedule" requirement before the resident moves in; and the next step to "Ask the operator for... the separate schedule showing the washing-machine charge."

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant retrieved documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, 1 July 2025**; and
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, 25 November 2025**. The retrieved Act is later than the date asked about, so the documents do not provide an Act version dated on or before 1 October 2025. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standard is that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) A rental provider or agent **must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless, at the time of advertising, they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, advertising the property with a photograph that appears to show mould is **not automatically unlawful merely because the photograph shows it**. It may indicate a problem, but the legal question is whether the provider or agent reasonably believed the premises complied when advertising them. If the pictured substance is structural mould or damp, and they did not reasonably believe the property complied, the advertisement may contravene the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

A photograph alone is **not conclusive proof** that the minimum standard is breached. The standard concerns mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure, and the retrieved documents do not say that a photograph by itself establishes that cause or proves non-compliance. The prescribed condition-report form says photographs **“may be useful in a dispute”**, rather than making them conclusive evidence. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

The renter can:

- save the advertisement and photograph, and ask the provider or agent to explain whether the apparent mould has been inspected, removed and whether the premises meet the mould-and-damp standard; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- ask for the issue to be addressed before entering into the rental agreement; and
- if they enter the premises and they do not comply with the minimum standards **on or immediately after occupation**, issue a request to the provider for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** specify that a renter can treat the advertisement photograph alone as definitive proof, or set out a specific pre-tenancy complaint procedure for this situation.

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?

On the later provisions only, you could ask the rental provider or agent:

The later Act requires records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the advertising requirement, but that requirement appears in the later **v115** document and cannot safely be treated as applying on 1 February 2026. question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the relevant version is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

A renter must **not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider’s written consent**. An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent is not required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the arrangement with your friend amounts to assigning or sub-letting part of the premises, the residential rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV. The notice must specify a termination date **at least 14 days after it is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current Act document does not state that merely allowing a friend to live with you is necessarily a sub-letting; that depends on the arrangement.

## What you can do or ask

The retrieved documents do **not** set out the procedure for a renter to remove a friend or other occupant from the premises. They therefore do not establish whether you must give your friend a particular notice, or what notice period applies.

You should not represent yourself as the rental provider when using the prescribed notice-to-vacate form: that form identifies the rental provider or mortgagee as the person giving the notice, and says the rental provider’s name cannot be the agent’s name [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents also do not authorise you to use force to remove your friend.

You can ask the rental provider or agent for written consent to the friend’s occupation, or ask for advice about the friend’s legal status and the proper process to end it. If the arrangement is a sub-let, the Act says the rental provider must not unreasonably withhold written consent, and you may apply to VCAT if you believe consent was unreasonably withheld [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The first point is therefore missing, even though the written-consent point is covered ('must not assign or sub-let... without the residential rental provider's written consent').

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019** (“renter” terminology was already in force). The later **Authorised Version 089, dated 4 December 2019**, was after the date in your question and is not used here. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A renter had to notify the residential rental provider **in writing, as soon as practicable**, about damage or a breakdown of supplied fixtures or facilities. For non-urgent repairs, the renter could apply to the Director for an investigation if the provider had not repaired them within **14 days** after receiving written notice, and could apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[15]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Check the notice carefully:

- **What section and reason does it give?** A notice to vacate had to be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and state the termination date. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- **Does it claim the premises need repairs, renovation or reconstruction?** Under section 91ZX, the provider needed the necessary permits and consents, the work had to require you to leave, and the notice had to allow at least **60 days**. It also needed approved documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- **Does it claim threats or intimidation under section 91ZK?** A notice under section 91ZK had no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Is the notice simply relying on your month-to-month status?** The retrieved documents do not contain the full rule governing every possible notice ending a periodic/month-to-month residential rental agreement, so they do not establish from these documents alone whether such a notice was retaliatory or valid.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Preserve evidence:** keep the repair requests, dates, photographs, replies, the notice to vacate, and proof of when and how the notice was delivered.
2. **Ask in writing** which statutory section and factual reason the provider relies on, and request any required supporting documentary evidence.
3. If the leaking fixtures are non-urgent and remain unrepaired for **14 days after your written notice**, consider applying to the Director or VCAT for repairs. [[15]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
4. If the notice appears to be a section 91ZK notice issued because you pursued repairs, raise that retaliation ground with VCAT. The retrieved documents do not state a general application deadline for challenging that type of notice; seek advice promptly. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
5. Do **not** assume that the notice is valid merely because it was issued on the same day as your repair follow-up: check the stated reason, required notice period, form, signature, delivery and evidence against the requirements above. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)[[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer is missing the first point: it never says a no-reason notice was allowed with at least 120 days' notice, and instead says the retrieved documents do not contain the rule for notices ending a month-to-month agreement. It also misses the other two points. It ties the 'no effect if given in response to exercising a right' rule to a section 91ZK threats/intimidation notice rather than to a no-reason notice. It does not give the 60-day window to challenge at VCAT, saying instead that 'the retrieved documents do not state a general application deadline.'

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer asserts that the landlord needed to give a reason, stating that a notice to vacate had to "state the reason, and state the termination date" and advising the user to ask "which statutory section and factual reason the provider relies on"; it does not assert a non-60-day VCAT challenge deadline, saying instead that "The retrieved documents do not state a general application deadline."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names "Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019", but it also relies on Version 089 (link 97-109aa089), which was not yet in force, for the notice-to-vacate requirements: prescribed form, signature, stated reason and termination date. That rule is cited only to version 089, so deleting it would change the substance of the answer.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- You must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of a fixture. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- For **non-urgent repairs**, if you gave written notice and the rental provider has not completed the repairs within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director for an investigation or to VCAT for a repair order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed notice-to-vacate form says you may challenge a notice at VCAT if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The notice must state the **termination date**, allow the minimum notice required by the Act, state the reason and relevant Act section, explain why it was given, and include any required documentary evidence. It must also identify how it was delivered and be signed and dated. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The documents provided do **not** state the specific minimum notice period for a month-to-month residential rental agreement, so that period cannot be confirmed from these documents. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you should check and ask

1. **Compare the timing and communications.** Keep your repair request, the notice, emails, texts, photographs and any reply showing that the notice was issued the same day. These may help show that the notice was connected with exercising your repair rights. The documents do not set out a separate evidentiary test for proving retaliation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the notice itself:**  
   - Is your full name and the correct premises address included?  
   - Is the rental provider—not merely the agent—identified?  
   - Does it give a specific reason, the relevant Act section and supporting details?  
   - Is any required documentary evidence attached?  
   - Is the termination date long enough?  
   - Was it delivered by an approved method—personally, registered post, or email only if you consented to email service?  
   - Is it signed and dated? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for repair action separately.** For non-urgent repairs, check whether 14 days have passed since your written request; if so, you can ask the Director to investigate or apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask VCAT to determine whether the notice is valid.** The form specifically identifies exercising renter rights as a possible basis for challenging the notice. You should seek advice immediately; the form says you may challenge validity at VCAT and that specific timeframes can apply. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not assume you must leave immediately.** A notice is not itself a possession order. If you do not leave by the stated date, the rental provider may apply to VCAT, and VCAT decides whether the provider was entitled to give the notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Its closest wording, 'The documents do not set out a separate evidentiary test for proving retaliation', concerns proof rather than whether retaliation voids the notice.

None of the three failure statements is made: the answer does not call a retaliatory notice automatically void (it says "VCAT decides whether the provider was entitled to give the notice"), does not say a no-reason notice is allowed (it says the notice must "state the reason and relevant Act section"), and gives no VCAT deadline other than 30 days (it says only that "specific timeframes can apply").

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer the premises at a **fixed rent** and must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, if the agent or provider encouraged someone to offer more than the advertised price, that may contravene section 30F(3); the Act provides penalties of **60 penalty units for a natural person** and **300 penalty units for a body corporate**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The fact that another applicant independently offered more, without being solicited or invited, is not by itself enough on the retrieved material to establish a contravention. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also not make a **false or misleading representation about the rent** when advertising the premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Relisting the property at a higher rent could therefore be relevant, but the documents do not say that every later rent increase is automatically unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The Act also prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct that induces a person to enter a residential rental agreement, including a false or misleading representation about the rent; the retrieved provision applies to certain providers and agents **not acting in trade or commerce**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The documents do not specifically address an application being falsely recorded as “withdrawn” or provide a rule requiring an applicant to be offered the property at the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing, to:

- confirm who marked your application as withdrawn and when;
- explain why it was recorded as withdrawn despite your not withdrawing it;
- confirm the advertised rent, any later rent, and whether the agent or provider requested or invited offers above the advertised amount; and
- preserve the application and communications relating to the property.

The retrieved Act states that the **Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT)** may make orders on an application or in proceedings concerning a contravention of section 30E. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do **not** specify a VCAT procedure or remedy for this particular application dispute, nor do they state how to challenge a rental provider’s selection decision. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents also do **not** specify what evidence an applicant should save. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) As a practical matter, preserve the advertisement showing the original rent, your completed application and submission confirmation, the “withdrawn” email, all messages with the agent, screenshots or records showing the later higher rent, and any direct evidence that the agent or provider solicited or invited a higher offer; but the documents supplied do not prescribe these items or establish what each would prove.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) Relisting at a higher rent is not illegal by itself: 'the documents do not say that every later rent increase is automatically unlawful.' (2) Soliciting or inviting offers above the advertised rent is prohibited. (3) An unsolicited higher offer is not banned: 'another applicant independently offered more, without being solicited or invited, is not by itself enough... to establish a contravention.' This is the hardest point because it does not say 'accepting' explicitly, but its meaning is clear. (4) The false 'withdrawn' email: 'The documents do not specifically address an application being falsely recorded as "withdrawn".'

must-not-say.reason: Yes — none of the prohibited claims are made: the answer says "the documents do not say that every later rent increase is automatically unlawful," that an applicant who "independently offered more, without being solicited or invited, is not by itself enough on the retrieved material to establish a contravention," and that the documents do not "provide a rule requiring an applicant to be offered the property at the advertised rent."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110), which is the version in force on 1 October 2025, and every rule it applies comes from that version.

question: It is 1 February 2026. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 February 2026**, the relevant version is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025** (“rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf”). The application-form requirements are in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005, dated 25 November 2025** (“rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

- The property must be advertised or offered at a **fixed amount of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- They must also not **accept an unsolicited or uninvited** offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising or promoting the property with a **false or misleading representation about the rent** is prohibited. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed application information says that rental auctions and rental bidding are prohibited and repeats that providers and agents must not invite or accept higher offers. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent or provider encouraged someone to offer more than the advertised rent, that appears inconsistent with section 30F. If someone independently offered more, the documents state that accepting such an unsolicited or uninvited higher offer is also prohibited. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do **not** establish whether the other applicant’s offer was solicited, invited, or genuinely unsolicited, nor do they say that merely relisting at a higher rent is automatically unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The documents also do not contain a specific rule about falsely recording that an applicant “withdrew”, or a specific process for challenging that decision. They do state that applicants should contact the rental provider or agent to check the outcome of an application. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do and save

You can ask the provider or agent, in writing:

1. to confirm whether your application was treated as withdrawn;
2. to identify who withdrew it and when;
3. to provide the reason or record supporting that claim; and
4. to explain the change from the advertised rent and whether any higher offer was invited or accepted.

Save:

- the original advertisement showing the rent;
- screenshots or saved copies showing the date, time, property address and advertised amount;
- your completed application and submission confirmation;
- the email saying you withdrew;
- all emails, texts and messages with the agent or provider;
- the later advertisement showing the higher rent; and
- any written evidence or witness information about a higher offer.

The retrieved documents do **not** prescribe an evidence list or identify a particular complaint or tribunal procedure for this situation. They do, however, support preserving evidence relevant to whether the rent was fixed, whether a higher offer was invited or accepted, and whether the advertising was misleading. question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider may apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you gave the request **three weeks ago**, more than the statutory **14 days** has passed. The provider is taken to have consented **unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they applied to the Tribunal**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act allows the Tribunal to consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does **not** say whether an owner’s allergy—or the fact that the owner rarely visits—makes refusal reasonable.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing, whether the owner or provider made a Tribunal application within the 14-day period. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If no application was made within that period, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You may also ask for written confirmation of consent, or apply to the Tribunal for an order permitting you to keep the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state the Tribunal application form, process, or timeframe.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the output says 'more than the statutory 14 days has passed. The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they applied to the Tribunal,' and gives the next step 'Ask the agent, in writing, whether the owner or provider made a Tribunal application within the 14-day period.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate for sale may be given where the premises are to be **“sold or offered for sale with vacant possession”** immediately after the termination date. It must give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the buyer pulling out does **not automatically cancel** the notice if the landlord is still entitled to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice is withdrawn **only if a notice of withdrawal is given**. That withdrawal must be **in writing**, signed by the landlord or person who gave the notice, and signed by the renter. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Since the landlord has not withdrawn it in that way, the notice remains on foot unless it is invalid for another reason or the Tribunal determines otherwise. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

So, **you may still have to leave on the termination date**, but the documents do not provide enough facts to determine whether your particular notice remains valid—for example, whether it was properly issued, accompanied by the required documentary evidence, and based on a legally sufficient reason. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord to give you a **written notice of withdrawal**, signed by both the landlord and the renter. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check whether the notice was in the **prescribed form**, addressed to you, signed, stated the reason, specified the termination date, and included documentary evidence supporting the sale reason. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- You may apply to the Tribunal to challenge the notice’s validity **within 30 days after it was given**, on or before the hearing of any application for a possession order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord seeks possession, the Tribunal must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that it **has not been withdrawn** before making a possession order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The 60-day minimum, the written withdrawal signed by both landlord and renter, and the next steps (written withdrawal; a Tribunal challenge within 30 days) are all covered. The first point is missing: the answer only addresses the 'sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' ground and never explains that the outcome depends on which ground the notice states and its evidence, such as a planned sale versus a signed contract of sale that has now fallen through.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing statements is made: the answer says the buyer pulling out "does not automatically cancel" the notice, requires a withdrawal "signed by the landlord or person who gave the notice, and signed by the renter" (not the landlord alone), and states "at least 60 days' notice."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)', links to 97-109aa110, and takes every rule it applies from that version alone.

question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 February 2026**, the relevant document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 110, 6 August 2025_**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Under section 91ZZB, a rental provider may give a notice to vacate if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. The notice must generally give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not specifically say that a notice automatically ends when a buyer withdraws**. Therefore, they do not establish that you must leave—or that you may remain—merely because the buyer pulled out.

If the landlord applies to VCAT for possession, VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that the notice **has not been withdrawn**, among other requirements. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form also says that you may challenge the notice if you disagree with the reason given or the information is incorrect or incomplete. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord **in writing to withdraw the notice**, explaining that the proposed sale has fallen through. The Act expressly refers to whether a notice has been withdrawn, but the retrieved documents do not provide a separate withdrawal procedure. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask the landlord whether the property is still genuinely **being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. That is the statutory basis for this type of notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord does not withdraw it, you can **challenge its validity at VCAT**, particularly if the stated sale reason is no longer accurate or the property is not being offered for sale. The documents do not specify the precise application process or deadline for this situation. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- Do not assume the landlord can physically remove you: the notice form states that VCAT decides whether you must leave, and forcible eviction requires a VCAT possession order and warrant carried out by Victoria Police. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer states a 60-day minimum notice period instead of 90 days. It does not say the outcome depends on whether the notice is based on a planned sale with vacant possession or a signed contract of sale. It also says the documents give no withdrawal procedure, rather than stating that withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both the landlord and the renter. Only the next-step point is covered.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer states a minimum notice period other than 90 days: "The notice must generally give at least **60 days’ notice**." It does not claim the buyer pulling out cancels the notice automatically, and it does not assert that the landlord can withdraw the notice alone.

Its citation of the Regulations (21-3sra005) is the in-force version and is fine.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days’ notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase. The notice must state the increase, how it was calculated, and your right to challenge it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed **Form 5** says that a valid notice is required for **all** rent increases. It must identify the current and new rent, the start date, and the calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The form may be sent by email **only if you have consented to email delivery**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent’s email was only an informal statement that the rent would increase—not a completed Form 5 delivered in an authorised way—you do **not** have to pay the higher rent. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Continue paying the existing rent unless and until you receive a valid notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Ask the agent to provide the prescribed **Form 5** and confirm the proposed start date.
- If a valid notice is later given, the increase cannot start until **at least 60 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If you think the proposed rent is excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within **30 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is required for all rent increases, at least 60 days' notice applies, and the hardest point is covered by "if the agent's email was only an informal statement... not a completed Form 5... you do not have to pay the higher rent. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid," with "Continue paying the existing rent" given as a next step.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions is asserted. The answer says "you do **not** have to pay the higher rent", that any increase "cannot start until **at least 60 days after the notice is given**", and that the form "may be sent by email **only if you have consented to email delivery**", so it neither requires payment now, nor dates the increase from the email, nor gives a notice period other than 60 days, nor bans email delivery.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and every rule it applies is cited only to those versions.

question: It is 1 February 2026. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 February 2026**, the applicable document retrieved is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v005 (25 November 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider **must use Form 5** to notify a renter of a proposed rent increase, and **a valid notice is required for every rent increase**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The notice must state the current rent, new rent, proposed start date, and the method used to calculate the increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The renter must receive **at least 90 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Therefore, an email merely saying that the rent will increase—without a valid Form 5 notice—does not establish a rent-increase start date on the documents provided. You do **not** have to pay the higher rent yet; continue paying the existing rent unless and until a valid notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that negotiating, or refusing to negotiate, changes these requirements. They also state that rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months, and cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement allows it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide the required **Form 5 notice**, including the calculation method and proposed start date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) If they provide a valid notice, the higher rent can begin no earlier than **90 days after the notice is given**; the exact date cannot be calculated from the facts provided. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

If you think the proposed increase is excessive, you may apply in writing to the **Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria** within **30 days after the notice is given** for an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers every point: Form 5 is required, at least 90 days' notice is needed, an email without Form 5 means 'You do not have to pay the higher rent yet', and it gives next steps such as 'continue paying the existing rent' and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria once a notice is given.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "You do **not** have to pay the higher rent yet," gives "at least 90 days' notice" as the notice period, and objects only to an email "without a valid Form 5 notice" rather than saying a notice can never be sent by email.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names only 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v005 (25 November 2025)' (link 21-3sra005) and never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 or its Authorised Version No. 111, which the rubric requires, even though it applies rules that come from the Act (90 days' notice, the 12-month limit, the fixed-term restriction and the 30-day application to the Director).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable Act is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- You **must give the rental provider written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The regulations state that renters must avoid damaging the premises and, where damage occurs, must notify the rental provider in writing. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Skirting-board damage appears to be a **non-urgent repair**, not an urgent repair. The Act’s provision allowing a renter to arrange repairs applies only to **urgent repairs**, and only after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent arrange them and being unable to get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs**, including non-urgent repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, you should **not simply arrange a quick repair secretly**. The documents require you to notify the owner or agent first, and they do not say that a renter may independently arrange a non-urgent repair without the rental provider’s involvement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Write to the owner or agent promptly, describe the damage, and ask whether they want to arrange the repair or approve a suitably qualified repairer. Keep photographs, written communications and any repair documentation; the prescribed condition-report material says photographs may help resolve disputes about damage. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not address whether an undisclosed repair would affect the owner’s property insurance**, so I cannot say what effect it would have on the insurance.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer is missing the second point: it never says the renter is responsible for damage they or their pet cause (as opposed to fair wear and tear) or that they must leave the home in the same condition. It only says renters 'must avoid damaging the premises' and must notify in writing. The other three points are covered: written notice 'as soon as practicable', insurance 'not address[ed]' by the documents, and the next step of writing to the owner or agent.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer rejects a secret repair ("you should **not simply arrange a quick repair secretly**"), states no insurance outcome as fact ("I cannot say what effect it would have on the insurance"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.
