It identifies the Regulations as "the regulations" through the link 21-3sra009, which is version 009. Both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and the answer relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says — 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002 (1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved law **does not specify a minimum number of power circuits** for a rental. It therefore does not establish that having most power points on one circuit is, by itself, unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical-safety minimum standard requiring all power-outlet and lighting circuits to have a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device applied **from 29 March 2023**, so it was not yet in force on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider must arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide **every 2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The provider must also maintain the premises in good repair, and any repairs must be carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can write to the rental provider or agent and ask them to:

1. **Arrange a licensed or registered electrician to investigate the breaker tripping**, including whether the circuit, wiring, outlets and appliances are safe and adequately rated. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
2. **Provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. **Provide a copy of the most recent electrical-safety-check record within 7 days** of your written request. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. **Carry out any repairs identified by the electrician**, using a suitably qualified person. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that the provider must install an additional circuit merely because the kettle and heater trip the breaker. Do not bypass or reset the breaker repeatedly; report the problem in writing and stop using the combination that causes it to trip until it has been checked.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The output says the retrieved law 'does not specify a minimum number of power circuits' for a rental. Its next steps include asking the provider to 'Arrange a licensed or registered electrician to investigate the breaker tripping', to 'Carry out any repairs identified by the electrician', and to 'Provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing'.

answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version 009 (30 June 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not specify a minimum number of power circuits** for a rental. They do require all power-outlet and lighting circuits to be connected to a compliant switchboard-type **Circuit Breaker** and **Residual Current Device (RCD)**. The law requires an electrical safety check at least every **2 years** where the rental agreement does not contain the prescribed safety-related term; if no check was done within the previous two years when you first moved in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable. question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (dated 13 October 2026). It does **not expressly say that a rooming-house operator may or may not charge for coin-operated washing machines**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does say:

- If a rooming-house operator charges for services, they must give you a **separate schedule of the service amounts before you move in**, and an **itemised account showing your individual use** if you use those services. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the rooming house is operated by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, it may impose a service charge for laundry facilities only where it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure individual use. The charge **must not exceed the cost of providing the facility**, and written notice is required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, version 002** require, from 26 February 2024, at least **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, but the retrieved regulation does not say that use must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

1. **What is the legal basis for the charge?**
2. **Where is the schedule of service charges** that should have been provided before you moved in? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. For any use-based charge, ask for an **itemised account showing your individual use**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. Whether the operator is **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**; if so, ask for the written notice explaining the charge and how it is limited to the cost of providing the laundry facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

So, based on these documents, a coin charge is **not expressly prohibited**, but the documents also do not establish that an ordinary rooming-house operator is automatically entitled to impose one.

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?

## What the law says

This applies to the advertisement, including its photographs. The penalty stated is **60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 penalty units for a body corporate**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standard is that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Therefore, if the pictured mould is structural mould or damp, advertising the premises without a reasonable belief that the standard is met may breach the Act. However, the documents do not say that every visible mark that appears to be mould necessarily establishes a breach—for example, they do not determine from a photograph what caused it.

**A photograph alone is not stated in the retrieved documents to be conclusive proof** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The documents do say that photographs may be useful in a dispute about the condition of rented premises, but they do not set an evidentiary rule that one photograph proves non-compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Before entering into the rental agreement, ask the provider or agent in writing:

1. **Whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**; and  
2. **Whether the provider has received, in the last three years, a repair notice relating to mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure.** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If your friend’s arrangement legally amounts to an unauthorised sub-letting, the rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV, with a termination date at least **14 days** after the notice is given. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A notice to vacate must use the relevant prescribed form, be addressed to the renter, be signed, state the reason, and specify the termination date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved regulations identify **Form 6** as the notice-to-vacate form. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If your friend is occupying under a sub-residential rental agreement and your head agreement ends, your friend may become a renter directly of the rental provider on the same applicable terms, unless the sub-agreement has ended. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

The retrieved documents **do not state a procedure allowing you, as the head renter, to forcibly remove a friend or occupant**, nor do they say what notice you must give that person. Therefore, I cannot say from these documents that you may change the locks, remove their belongings, or physically evict them.

You can ask the rental provider for **written consent** to the arrangement or ask your friend to leave voluntarily, but the documents do not prescribe the steps or notice period for doing so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do not assume that ending your own tenancy will remove your friend: under section 91R, your friend could become the rental provider’s renter if the sub-residential agreement continues. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?

Based on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version v009 as of 30 June 2026), which is the law in force on 15 October 2026, you may challenge a notice to vacate at VCAT if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter (such as requesting repairs) or due to unlawful discrimination [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

Here is exactly what you should check on your Notice to Vacate (Form 6):

1. **The Stated Reason and Details (Clause 11)**: Check if the rental provider has inserted a specific legal reason, the relevant section number of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, and a clear explanation of why the notice was given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The regulations require specific details; it is not enough to just quote general reasons. VCAT may find the notice invalid if it lacks sufficient detail [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Documentary Evidence**: Check if any required documentary evidence (approved by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria) is attached to the notice, as some grounds require it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **The Termination Date and Notice Period (Clause 10)**: Verify that the termination date allows for the minimum number of days' notice required under the Act, taking into account how the notice was delivered and when you are expected to receive it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Grounds for Challenge**: Confirm whether your suspicion aligns with the valid grounds listed on the form—specifically, that you believe the notice was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter or due to unlawful discrimination [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

If you find discrepancies or believe the notice is retaliatory, you should seek advice immediately from a community legal organisation or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria at 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. ### What the law says about your situation
*   **Higher Rent Offers:** A residential rental provider or their agent is strictly prohibited from soliciting or inviting an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, they must not accept an unsolicited or uninvited offer that exceeds the advertised rent [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
*   **False Advertising & Misleading Conduct:** It is illegal for a provider or agent to make false or misleading representations regarding the rent for the premises [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Additionally, inducing a person to enter into a rental agreement through conduct that is misleading or deceptive—including making false representations about the rent payable—is prohibited [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
*   **Tribunal Orders:** You may be able to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for orders regarding a contravention of the provisions against misleading or deceptive conduct [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Consumer Law Rights:** The Act explicitly states that these tenancy provisions do not limit your rights under the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria), meaning you may have additional avenues for redress depending on how the provider's actions were conducted [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What evidence to save
The retrieved documents do not contain specific guidance or instructions on what evidence you should save for this situation.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version **v115** as of **13 October 2026** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can they refuse?
**No, not unilaterally.** Under section 71C(1), a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If the owner wishes to refuse your request based on their allergy, they are legally required to apply to the Tribunal for an order stating that it is reasonable to refuse consent [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Crucially, under section 71C(2), if the provider does not make this Tribunal application **within 14 days** of receiving your official request form, they are automatically **taken to have consented** to you keeping the pet [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Because three weeks have passed and the agent simply said "no" without applying to the Tribunal within that 14-day window, the law considers your consent as already granted. The owner's allergy (and the fact that they hardly visit) would be a factor the Tribunal considers under "any other matter... relevant" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but it does not give them the right to unilaterally refuse after the statutory deadline has passed.

### What you can do:
1. **Notify the agent in writing:** Inform the agent that because more than 14 days have passed without a Tribunal application, section 71C(2) deems their consent as granted. You are legally permitted to keep the dog. 
2. **Keep the pet:** You may proceed with keeping the dog on the premises under section 71A [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Seek Tribunal confirmation if necessary:** If the agent continues to object or threatens eviction, you can apply to the Tribunal for a formal declaration confirming your right to keep the pet [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes, technically the notice is still in effect.** Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate cannot simply be ignored or cancelled verbally. It can only be formally withdrawn if a written **notice of withdrawal** is provided that is signed by both you and your landlord [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because the buyer pulled out and no formal withdrawal was issued, the original notice remains legally valid until it expires or is successfully challenged.

### What you can do
You have the right to challenge the validity of this notice at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). 

1. **Apply to VCAT within 30 days:** You must apply to challenge the notice within 30 days after it was given to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If the sale fell through, your landlord may no longer have a valid legal ground (such as selling with vacant possession) or the required evidence to back up their claim. 
3. **Attend the hearing:** If you apply within the 30-day window, VCAT will determine whether the notice is valid. If they find it invalid because the sale collapsed, the notice will be set aside and you can stay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

*Note: If your landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order before you challenge the notice, you still have the right to challenge its validity at that hearing, but acting within the initial 30-day window is the standard and safest approach.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**What the law says**

If you do receive the official Form 5, the law requires the provider to give you **at least 90 days' notice** before the new rent can start [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The increase cannot take effect until that 90-day period has passed.

*   **Continue paying your current rent:** You are legally entitled to keep paying your existing rent amount until a valid Form 5 is properly served and the 90-day notice period expires.
*   **Request the official notice:** Ask your agent in writing for the official Form 5. If they cannot provide it, they cannot legally enforce the increase.
*   **Challenge an excessive increase:** Once you receive the official notice, if you believe the amount is too high, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation within 30 days [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT to have the proposed rent amount declared excessive [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021)** in force on 1 March 2023:

**Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?**
No. The retrieved documents do not contain any rule, minimum standard, or limit specifying how many electrical circuits or power points a rental property must have. The regulations focus entirely on safety compliance and inspection frequency, not on circuit quantity or load distribution.

**What can you ask for?**
While the law does not regulate how many appliances can run on one circuit, it does give you specific rights regarding electrical safety documentation and maintenance:
* **Request your most recent safety check record:** Your rental provider must provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing upon request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you submit a written request for a copy of the full report, they must provide it within 7 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Ask for an immediate inspection if overdue:** The provider is legally required to have all electrical installations and fittings checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If one hasn't been conducted in the last 2 years, you can ask them to arrange one as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* **Note on upcoming standards:** On and from 29 March 2023 (just over a month after your question), all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, along with a Residual Current Device meeting specific safety standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

**Regarding the tripping breaker:**
If the breaker trips specifically when you run two high-draw appliances (like a kettle and a heater) together, this is generally the **normal and correct safety function** of a properly rated circuit breaker. It is designed to cut power to prevent wires from overheating and causing a fire. Under tenancy law, a correctly functioning breaker that trips under an electrical overload is not considered a breach or a maintenance defect—it means the system is working as intended to protect the property. 

If you experience frequent tripping during normal single-appliance use, or if the breaker feels hot, makes burning smells, or fails to reset, those would be valid safety concerns to raise with your provider for an urgent inspection.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?**
Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 111 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), a residential rental provider or their agent **must not advertise or offer premises to let** unless, at the time of advertising, they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

Whether the ad is lawful depends entirely on the *cause* of the mould. The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 4 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), set the specific minimum standard that "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
- If the photo shows mould stemming from a structural issue (e.g., leaking walls, poor ventilation, or rising damp), advertising it would likely breach section 65B because the provider cannot reasonably believe it meets the standards.
- If the mould is superficial or caused by the tenant's lifestyle (e.g., drying clothes indoors without heating), the property may still technically meet the minimum standard, though the ad could be considered misleading.

**2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?**
The retrieved documents **do not specify** whether a single photograph is legally sufficient on its own to prove that a rental property fails to meet the mould and dampness standard. While the Act requires providers to keep records demonstrating compliance [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), it does not outline what evidence a renter must provide to successfully challenge an ad or prove non-compliance in a tribunal setting.

**What you can do:**
- **Request clarification/photos:** Ask the agent for more recent, high-resolution photos of the bedroom and ask specifically about the cause of the visible mould.
- **Check mandatory disclosures:** On or before the occupation day, the provider must give you a written statement and disclose if they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by the building structure [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
- **Inspect before signing:** Do not sign a lease or pay a bond until you have physically inspected the property. If structural mould is present upon inspection, you can refuse to move in without penalty.
- **Report if necessary:** If you discover structural mould after moving in, you can issue a request for urgent repairs under section 65A of the Act [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: This information applies to Victorian residential tenancy law as it stood on 1 October 2025.)*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version v115, as at 13 October 2026), which is the law in force on your date of 15 October 2026, the agent and owner **cannot simply refuse your request outright**. 

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

**1. They cannot unreasonably refuse consent**
The law states that a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to you keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). An allergy alone does not automatically make a refusal reasonable, especially if the owner rarely visits the property.

**2. The 14-day rule and deemed consent**
If the agent simply said "no" without taking further legal action, their refusal may be invalid. Under the Act, the provider is legally **taken to have consented** to your request unless they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within **14 days** of receiving your official form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If 14 days have passed since you sent your request and they haven't applied to the Tribunal, you are legally allowed to keep the dog.

**3. The Tribunal process**
If the owner/agent wants their refusal to be legally binding, they must apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days and prove that it is "reasonable" to refuse [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). When deciding this, the Tribunal will look at factors such as:
* The type of pet you propose to keep [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
* The character and nature of the rented premises (your apartment) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* Any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

While an allergy could theoretically be raised as a factor under "any other matter," the fact that the owner "hardly ever visits" is highly relevant to mitigating that risk. The Tribunal will weigh the health impact against your right to keep a pet and whether the apartment can reasonably accommodate it.

**What you can do:**
* **Check the timeline:** If it has been more than 14 days since you submitted your official request form and they have not applied to the Tribunal, their refusal is invalid and consent is deemed granted. You can proceed with keeping the dog.
* **If they applied to the Tribunal:** Prepare for the hearing by providing evidence that the owner's absence minimizes the allergy risk, and that you will maintain the apartment to prevent any damage or nuisance. 
* **Apply to the Tribunal yourself:** If the agent is blocking your request without applying to the Tribunal within 14 days, you can apply to the Tribunal directly for an order permitting you to keep the pet [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?

A notice to vacate **does not automatically expire or become invalid** just because the buyer pulled out of the sale. The notice remains legally valid until it is formally withdrawn [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

To officially withdraw the notice, the landlord must provide a **notice of withdrawal** that meets strict requirements:
* It must be in writing;
* It must be signed by the person who gave the notice (the landlord); and
* It must be signed by the person to whom the notice was given (you, the tenant) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

Until this dual-signed document is provided, the original notice to vacate remains in full force [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask For
1. **Ask for a Formal Withdrawal:** Request that your landlord provide you with a written notice of withdrawal that you both sign. Do not consider the matter closed until you have physically received and signed this document [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the Notice at the Tribunal:** If the landlord refuses to withdraw the notice, you can apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity. You must make this application within 30 days after the notice to vacate was given to you [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: While a failed sale may give you grounds to argue the notice is invalid because the original reason for eviction no longer applies, the Act explicitly states that a notice is withdrawn **only** through the formal written process described above [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).)*

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes.** A notice to vacate for the sale of a property does not automatically expire or become invalid just because the buyer pulls out [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice remains legally binding until either:
1. The landlord formally withdraws it; or

> * In writing;
> * Signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice); and
> * Signed by you (the person to whom the notice was given) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

2. **Challenge the Notice at VCAT:** If you believe the notice is invalid for a legal reason (for example, if it wasn't given in the correct prescribed form or lacks required documentary evidence), you can apply to VCAT to challenge its validity. This application must be made within **30 days** after the notice was given [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

If the landlord simply changed their mind about selling but refuses to sign a withdrawal notice, your only options are to negotiate an extension with them or prepare to vacate by the specified date.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (**Authorised Version v004**, effective 1 July 2025), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about your situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, an informal email from an agent does not legally trigger a rent increase. The regulations explicitly state that **"A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases"** and that the rental provider **"must use this form [Form 5: Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises] to notify the renter"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

Regarding when the increase can take effect, the law mandates that **"The rental provider must give you at least 90 days notice of any rent increase"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This means the higher rent cannot legally start until a valid official notice has been served and 90 full days have passed from that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Additionally, providers are strictly prohibited from increasing rent more than once every 12 months, and they generally cannot increase it during a fixed-term agreement unless your contract specifically allows for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
Because you never received an official notice:
1. **Do not pay the higher amount yet.** You are legally entitled to continue paying your current rent until a valid 90-day notice period has been properly served.
2. **Ask for the official Form 5.** Reply to your agent in writing and request they provide the formal "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
3. **Verify the timeline.** Once you receive the form, check that the proposed start date is at least 90 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Escalate if necessary.** If the agent refuses to provide the form or tries to enforce the increase immediately, you can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation or apply to VCAT to have the increase declared excessive or invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: This advice is based on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (v004) which was in force on 1 October 2025.)*

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:

### What the law says & what you can do
**1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?**

* **Duty to notify:** You must give written notice to the landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **No unauthorised work:** You must not make any alteration, renovation, or addition to the rented premises without the landlord's consent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
* **Repair liability:** Because the skirting boards were damaged due to a failure to take reasonable care (s 61), the landlord can issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). If you do not, or if they prefer to handle it, the landlord may carry out the repairs themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs, provided they give you written particulars of those costs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). 

**Recommendation:** Notify your landlord/agent in writing immediately about the damage. Discuss whether they want to hire a tradesperson or allow you to arrange the repair (with their prior consent) to avoid disputes over workmanship or costs later.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), here is what the law states regarding your situation as of 1 March 2023:

### What the law says about circuits
There is **no rule in Victorian tenancy law that specifies a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points** a rental property must have. The regulations focus entirely on the *safety standards* of the electrical installations rather than their quantity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

A breaker tripping when you run high-power appliances (like a kettle and heater) together simply means the circuit is overloaded, which is exactly what the safety device is designed to do to prevent overheating and fires.

### What you can ask for
While you cannot legally demand a specific number of circuits, you can ask your landlord for the following:

1. **Upgrades to meet imminent safety standards (effective 29 March 2023):** 
   Just two weeks after your current date, on **29 March 2023**, new electrical minimum standards come into force [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can ask your landlord to ensure that all power outlets and lighting circuits are connected to:
   * A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000; and
   * A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
   If your current switchboard is old and lacks modern RCD protection, it will need to be upgraded to comply with this new standard.

2. **A recent electrical safety check:**
   Your landlord is legally required to have all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings checked by a licensed or registered electrician every 2 years [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can ask them in writing for the date of the most recent safety check [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If one has not been conducted within the last 2 years, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

3. **A professional assessment:**
   Because the law does not mandate extra circuits, your best course of action is to ask your landlord to have a licensed electrician assess whether the existing wiring and circuit capacity are adequate for modern living. While they aren't forced to add new circuits just because one trips, an electrician's report can help demonstrate if the property's electrical infrastructure is outdated or unsafe.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the Victorian laws in force on **15 October 2026**, here is what the legislation says about your situation:

### 📜 What the Law Says
**1. You are entitled to a washing machine, but it can be charged for.**
Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (S.R. No. 10/2023), rooming house operators are legally required to provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). However, the regulations do not state that this facility must be free of charge.

**2. Private operators can charge for laundry services, but must disclose it.**
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115-2026-10-13.pdf), if a rooming house operator charges you for services (which includes laundry facilities), they are legally required to:
* Provide you with a separate schedule of those service charges **before** you take up residency [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you use the machines, provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of those services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Strict cost limits apply only to government/registered housing.**
Section 109A of the Act specifically governs *Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies*. It states they may impose a laundry service charge only if it is not practicable to measure your exact usage, and **the charge must not exceed the actual cost** of providing the facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal to have such a charge withdrawn or varied if it exceeds that cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. No explicit per-use cap for private operators in these documents.**
The retrieved documents do not explicitly mention "coin-operated" machines, nor do they place a specific price-per-load cap on laundry charges for *private* rooming house operators beyond the requirement to disclose them in your pre-move-in schedule [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ What You Can Do
1. **Check your move-in paperwork:** Look for the "schedule of services" you were given before moving in. The operator should have listed the laundry charges there [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Request an itemised account:** If you have been using the machines, ask the operator for a breakdown of your individual usage. They are legally required to provide this if they charge you for the service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Verify the operator type:** 
   * If your rooming house is managed by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, and the coin-operated charges exceed the actual cost of providing the laundry facility, you can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   * If it is a **private operator**, your primary recourse is to ensure the charges were properly disclosed in your original schedule and that they are not breaching any terms of your residency agreement.

*Note: This answer is based strictly on the provided statutory documents dated 15 October 2026. For personalised legal advice or dispute resolution, you may need to consult VCAT or a community legal centre.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**What the law says**
Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), a rental provider or their agent must not advertise premises to let unless they **reasonably believe** the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at the time of advertising. The law does not explicitly ban showing mould in photos, but if the provider knows (or should reasonably know from the photo) that the property has structural mould, advertising it while claiming compliance would likely breach this duty.

Regarding proof of non-compliance, Schedule 4, clause 8 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* sets the minimum standard for mould: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp **caused by or related to the building structure**" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

A photo alone is **not enough** to prove the place doesn't meet this standard. The law specifically ties the breach to mould caused by the *building structure*. A photo cannot determine the cause of the mould; it could easily be lifestyle-related (e.g., condensation from daily activities, poor ventilation, or drying clothes indoors), which would not violate this specific minimum standard.

**What the renter can do or ask**
1. **Ask for disclosure:** Before signing a lease, you can ask the provider to confirm if the premises comply with rental minimum standards and whether they have received any repair notices in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Request urgent repairs:** If you move in and discover structural mould, section 65A(2) of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* allows you to issue a formal request to the provider for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to standard [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence:** To prove a breach of the minimum standard, you would need more than a photo—such as an inspection report from a qualified professional confirming the mould is structural in origin. 

*(Note: This answer applies the law as set out in the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version v111) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v005) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), which reflect the law in force on 1 October 2025.)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer states the mould standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), says 'A photo alone is not enough to prove the place doesn't meet this standard', and gives next steps such as asking the provider to confirm compliance before signing and requesting urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: No: the answer presents the advertising ban as law in force on 1 October 2025, stating that 'a rental provider or their agent must not advertise premises to let unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at the time of advertising', but that rule does not apply on this date.

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on **1 February 2026**, here is how the situation is addressed:

### 1. Advertising & Minimum Standards
The law does not explicitly ban showing photos of mould in a rental advertisement. However, under **section 65B** of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version v111, dated 25 November 2025), a residential rental provider or their agent **must not advertise or offer premises to let unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards** at the time of advertising [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

If the property actually contains structural mould, it breaches the minimum standards. Under **Schedule 4 clause 8** of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version v5, dated 25 November 2025), *"each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Therefore, if a provider knows about structural mould but advertises the property as compliant, they would be violating the "reasonable belief" requirement in section 65B [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?
The retrieved documents **do not contain any provision** stating that a photo in a rental ad is sufficient proof that a property fails to meet the minimum standards. 

To legally prove a breach of the mould standard, it must be established that the mould is *"caused by or related to the building structure"* rather than tenant-caused (e.g., poor ventilation or lifestyle habits) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents do not specify that an advertisement photo alone constitutes legal proof of this structural defect.

### 3. What the renter can do
If a renter moves in and discovers that the premises actually do not comply with the rental minimum standards, they may **issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs** to be carried out to ensure the premises comply [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the provider fails to address structural mould or dampness after moving in, the renter can pursue this through the standard dispute resolution processes under Part 5 of the Act.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), **Authorised Version No. 088 as at 2 July 2019** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and the standard tenancy regulations/forms applicable to your month-to-month agreement, here is what you should check and do if you suspect a retaliatory notice:

### 🔍 What to Check
1. **The "Challenging this notice" section on your form**: Review the information provided on the notice you received. It explicitly states that you may challenge the notice at VCAT if *"you believe you were given this notice due to unlawful discrimination or because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter"* [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Following up on repairs is a protected legal right, making the timing of the notice (issued the exact same day) a critical detail to check.
2. **The stated reason for termination**: Look at the specific ground listed on the notice. Does it align with a legitimate legal reason under Victorian tenancy law, or does it appear fabricated to cover up retaliation? VCAT will decide whether the rental provider was actually entitled to give you the notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### ⚖️ What You Should Do
* **Apply to VCAT immediately**: If you believe the notice is retaliatory, file an application with VCAT to challenge its validity. The burden will be on your rental provider to prove they had a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for issuing it.
* **Document the timeline**: Keep all written records of your repair requests, follow-up communications, and the date/time the notice was served. This evidence is crucial for demonstrating that the notice was issued in direct response to you exercising your rights [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

*(Note: The provided excerpts from the 2019 Act focus on rooming houses, but the standard **Form 6 Notice to Vacate** applies to periodic residential tenancies and outlines your explicit right to challenge retaliatory notices at VCAT [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).)*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version as of 30 June 2026), here is what you should check and do if you believe your notice to vacate is retaliation for requesting repairs:

### 🔍 What to Check on the Notice
1. **The Stated Reason & Details**  
   The rental provider must provide specific details explaining why the notice was given, rather than just quoting generic text from an information sheet [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT may find a notice invalid if it lacks sufficient detail or required documentary evidence [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Look closely at whether their stated reason aligns with reality (e.g., is "repairs" or "renovation" listed as the official reason, which might actually be the pretext for retaliation?).

2. **Your Right to Challenge for Exercising Rights**  
   You may challenge this notice at VCAT if you believe it was given **"because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter"** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Requesting repairs is a protected tenancy right, so the timing of the notice relative to your repair requests is a key factor in proving retaliation.

3. **Procedural Compliance**  
   - **Termination Date:** Ensure the notice allows for the minimum notice period required under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - **Delivery Method & Dates:** Verify that the notice was delivered properly (e.g., personally, by registered post, or by email if you consented) and note the date it was sent versus when you received it [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🛡️ What You Can Do Next
- **Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice** on the grounds that you were exercising your rights as a renter, or because the notice was not given properly or contains incorrect/incomplete information [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek immediate advice** from a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or call 1300 558 181 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Attend any VCAT hearing** if the rental provider applies for a possession order. VCAT will decide whether the provider was entitled to give the notice and whether it is "reasonable and proportionate" to make a possession order [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*Note: This guidance is based on the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version as of 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For binding legal advice, consult a qualified tenancy lawyer or community legal centre.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on your query date of 1 October 2025, the relevant legislation is the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (No. 109 of 1997), **Authorised Version v110 dated 6 August 2025** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Can you challenge what happened?
Yes, the actions you described appear to breach several specific provisions in the Act:
* **Fixed Rent & Higher Offers:** The law requires that rented premises be advertised or offered at a fixed rent amount [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It is illegal for a rental provider or agent to solicit or invite offers higher than the advertised amount (s 30F(3)) or to accept unsolicited offers higher than the advertised amount (s 30F(4)) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **False Withdrawal & Misleading Conduct:** Sending a false email claiming you withdrew, or advertising rent in a way that misleads applicants, breaches section 30G (which prohibits false or misleading representations about rent) and section 30E (which prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct to induce someone to enter an agreement) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Penalties & Tribunal Action:** These are offences carrying penalties of up to 60 penalty units for individuals or 300 penalty units for corporations [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can challenge this by applying to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), as section 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make regarding contraventions of these sections [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, these provisions do not limit your rights under the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What should you save as evidence?

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** as it stood on 15 October 2026 (Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about your situation
*   **Refusals must be reasonable:** A residential rental provider (the owner) cannot *unreasonably* refuse consent for you to keep a pet on the rented premises [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **You have likely already been approved by default:** Because you submitted your official request form three weeks ago, the law states that the owner is legally **taken to have consented** to your request. This automatic approval happens unless the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since they only gave a verbal refusal and did not apply to the Tribunal in time, their refusal is invalid under the Act.
*   **Allergies do not automatically justify a refusal:** Even if the owner had applied to the Tribunal within the 14-day window, an owner's personal allergy does not guarantee they can refuse consent. When deciding such applications, the Tribunal weighs this against other factors—such as the type of pet and the nature of the apartment—under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
*   **Inform the agent in writing:** Send a formal message to the agent stating that under section 71C(2) of the Act, they are taken to have consented because more than 14 days have passed without a Tribunal application [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Ask for written confirmation:** Request that the agent provide you with written confirmation of this deemed consent so you can legally keep your dog in the apartment [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Apply to VCAT if they continue to block you:** If the owner persists in their refusal, you can apply directly to the Tribunal (VCAT) yourself for an order permitting you to keep the pet under section 71A(b) of the Act [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer says the owner is 'taken to have consented to your request... unless the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your form', ties this to the three weeks that have passed, and gives a reasonable next step ('Send a formal message to the agent... Request that the agent provide you with written confirmation'). It does wrongly assume no VCAT application was made, but it still states the conditional.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted. The answer calls the refusal "invalid under the Act" rather than final. It treats VCAT as optional ("you can apply directly to the Tribunal (VCAT) yourself" only "if the owner persists"). It says "an owner's personal allergy does not guarantee they can refuse consent," so the allergy does not automatically decide it either way.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic) as 'Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026' and cites only the in-force link 97-109aa115, without relying on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the provided documents, here is how Victorian residential tenancy law applies to your situation as of 1 October 2025:

### **Does the notice remain valid?**
**Yes.** The provided documents do not contain specific rules stating that a notice to vacate becomes invalid if a buyer withdraws from a sale. A landlord is legally entitled to give you a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). Once a notice is properly issued, it remains legally effective until it expires or is formally withdrawn by the landlord. 

### **What happens if you do not leave?**
If you do not vacate the property by the termination date stated in the notice, your landlord can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). At the hearing, VCAT will decide whether your landlord was entitled to give the notice and will determine if you must leave and on what date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### **What can you do?**
Because your landlord has not withdrawn the notice, it remains in force. Your options are:
*   **Negotiate with your landlord:** You can ask your landlord to formally withdraw the notice or agree to a new lease term so you can stay. 
*   **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If you believe the notice is invalid for other reasons (for example, if it lacks sufficient details or required documentary evidence), you may challenge its validity when the landlord applies for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

*Note: The documents do not provide specific guidance on whether a failed sale automatically voids a notice. In practice, standard tenancy law treats the notice as valid once given, meaning you would need to reach a new agreement with your landlord or face a VCAT hearing if you choose to stay.*

question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the provided documents, the relevant law in force on 1 February 2026 is the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version No. 101 dated 28 September 2022) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What the law says about your situation
Under the Act, a notice to vacate remains legally valid and enforceable until it is formally withdrawn or its termination date passes [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The law explicitly states that a notice can only be withdrawn if a formal **"notice of withdrawal"** is given in writing and signed by both the landlord (who gave the notice) and you (the tenant to whom it was given) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

If the buyer pulls out and your landlord fails to issue this signed withdrawal, the notice stands. Therefore, **yes, you are still legally required to vacate by the termination date on the notice** unless you take action to challenge it or secure a formal withdrawal.

### What you can do or ask
1. **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** Because the sale has fallen through, the original reason for the notice may no longer apply. You have the right to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the validity of the notice [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). This application must be made **within 30 days after the notice was given** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will then determine whether the notice is valid [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Formally request a withdrawal:** Ask your landlord in writing to issue the required signed notice of withdrawal, as they are legally obligated to do so when the sale no longer proceeds [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of this request for your records.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, here is the information you need:

**What the Law Says**
Under **Authorised Version No. 4 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf):
* A valid official notice is required for all rent increases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* The rental provider must use the official **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)** to notify you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). An informal email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement.
* The provider must give you at least **60 days' notice** before any rent increase takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to pay the higher rent, and from when?**
No, you do not have to pay the higher rent yet. Because you never received an official Form 5, the increase is not legally valid. The new rent can only start on the specific "Start date" listed on that official notice, provided at least 60 days have passed since it was properly served [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Until a valid notice is served, your current rent remains the legal amount you must pay.

**What You Can Do or Ask**
* Reply to your agent in writing and state that under Victorian law, a rent increase cannot take effect without an official **Form 5** being properly served [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* Ask them to provide you with the completed Form 5 showing the calculation method and the valid start date.
* If they continue to demand the higher amount or threaten action over unpaid rent, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for guidance on your rights.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is required, at least 60 days' notice is required, the informal email is not valid so 'you do not have to pay the higher rent yet', and next steps are given, including replying 'to your agent in writing' and contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims are made: the answer says "No, you do not have to pay the higher rent yet," ties the start date to a properly served Form 5 rather than the email, states "at least 60 days' notice," and says only that "an informal email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement" without claiming a notice can never be sent by email.

It also cites the Regulations through the link 21-3sra005, which is version 005 and not the in-force version 004, even though the text says "Authorised Version No. 4 ... (dated 1 July 2025)".

question: It is 1 February 2026. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:

No. A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The rental provider must use the official "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" form to notify you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). An informal email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement.

**From when would the increase apply?**
The rent can only be increased from the **"Start date"** explicitly listed on that valid official notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Because no official notice was served, there is no legally valid start date for the increase, and you are not obligated to pay the higher amount.

**Key regulatory requirements:**
*   **Notice Periods:** The law mandates a minimum notice period before the start date can take effect. Under the 2022 version of the regulations, this was at least 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Under the 2026 version of the regulations, this requirement increased to at least 90 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Frequency:** Rental providers must not increase the rent more than once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
*   **Email Delivery:** While rental providers are permitted to deliver the *official* notice by email, this is only valid if you have previously provided consent for electronic communication [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Even then, it must be the formal Form 5 document containing all required details (such as the calculation method and start date), not just a casual email.

Since you never received the official form, the agent's attempt to increase your rent is invalid. You should continue paying your current rent until a compliant notice is properly served.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version v115 (updated 13 October 2026) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?
**No.** You are legally required to notify your residential rental provider about the damage. Under section 72AA of the Act, a renter must give written notice to the residential rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Additionally, under section 61, you have a duty to take reasonable care to avoid damaging the rented premises [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). Because your dog caused the damage, the owner is entitled to issue you with a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the skirting boards at your own expense within 14 days, or they may choose to arrange the repairs themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).

### 2. Would it affect the owner's insurance?
The provided legal documents **do not contain any information** regarding how tenant-caused damage affects a property owner's insurance policy. You would need to consult the owner's specific insurance policy or an insurance professional for details on that matter.
