question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not by a simple refusal. Under the current law, the owner cannot unreasonably refuse, and if they did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, the law treats the request as approved. Whether the allergy is a reasonable ground is a question the Tribunal decides, and the documents I retrieved don't address allergies specifically.

**Which law applies:** The current Authorised Version is No. 115 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version applies on 15 October 2026. The earlier Authorised Version No. 111 (25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) is superseded.

### What the law says

- **Your request:** A renter who asks for consent to keep a pet must use the form approved by the Director and give it to the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No unreasonable refusal:** The provider "must not unreasonably refuse" consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent:** The provider is taken to have consented unless, "within 14 days after being given the request," they apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal route:** The provider may apply to the Tribunal for an order that it is reasonable to refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances and fittings, "whether refusing consent... is permitted under any Act," and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Written consent or order:** A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Applying this to your situation

- Your request was made three weeks ago, so the 14-day window has passed. Unless the owner or agent applied to the Tribunal within that window, the law treats consent as given.
- An agent's "no" is not, by itself, a Tribunal application. The documents I retrieved don't say whether any application was filed, so you should check with VCAT (vcat.vic.gov.au or 1300 018 228) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The Act does not list an owner's allergy as a ground. If the owner did apply, the Tribunal would decide whether refusal is reasonable, and the documents don't say how an allergy would be weighed.
- If the dog is an assistance dog, the regulations state that refusing accommodation because of an assistance dog may be unlawful [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Keep your evidence:** Keep a copy of the form, proof of delivery, and the agent's refusal.
2. **Ask in writing:** Ask the agent or owner to confirm in writing whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days. The documents don't set out a specific renter process for this, so I can't confirm the exact steps.
3. **Get advice:** Victoria Legal Aid can advise on rental discrimination and existing agreements at 1300 792 387 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 1 October 2025, the notice is not withdrawn just because the buyer pulled out. It stays in effect unless a formal written withdrawal is signed. You should still check whether the notice was valid to begin with.

**Which version applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file dated 6 August 2025 (labelled v110 in its filename) is the version in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't state an "Authorised Version number" in any other form, so I'm relying on that filename label. Later versions (v111, dated 25 November 2025, and v115, dated 13 October 2026) postdate your date, so I haven't applied them [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If a contract of sale is subject to conditions, the landlord must give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not subject to such conditions, the landlord must give it within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text of this provision comes from the later versions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm its exact wording in the 1 October 2025 version.
- **Validity:** A notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, specify the reasons, and specify the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a sale notice, it must also be accompanied by documentary evidence approved by the Director, which supports the reason for the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed terms:** If you're on a fixed-term agreement, a sale notice is of no effect if it specifies a termination date earlier than the end of the term (unless the agreement has an early-termination clause that the notice complies with) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for a written withdrawal** if you want the notice ended. Under the withdrawal rule, it needs to be signed by the landlord and by you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the notice itself.** Confirm the termination date is at least 60 days after it was given, the form is correct, the reason is stated, and the required documentary evidence is attached [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge it at VCAT if you have grounds.** You can apply to the Tribunal challenging the validity of a sale notice, but only within 30 days after the notice is given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may determine whether the notice is valid [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The right to challenge is limited: if VCAT finds the notice valid, you generally can't challenge it again unless exceptional circumstances exist [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek advice quickly.** The 30-day deadline is short.

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't say whether a landlord who no longer intends to sell can still rely on a sale notice, or how VCAT would treat that.
- They don't include the possession-order rules in force on 1 October 2025. The retrieved Part 7 text is from a 2021 version and may have changed [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these documents whether VCAT must make a possession order while a sale notice remains unwithdrawn.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations documents I retrieved are dated after 1 October 2025, so I can't confirm the regulation forms in force on that date.

If you tell me the date the notice was given, the termination date, and whether your agreement is fixed-term or periodic, I can check those points against the text above.

It also requires 'documentary evidence approved by the Director, which supports the reason for the notice', so validity turns on the stated ground and its evidence. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A buyer pulling out is not mentioned as a form of withdrawal.
- **Validity requirements:** A notice to vacate for sale is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reason, is accompanied by the documentary evidence approved by the Director, and states the termination date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations' Form 6 is in a later version (dated 30 June 2026) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm what applied on 1 February 2026.
- **Landlord's restriction:** After obtaining possession under a sale-type notice, the landlord must not let the premises for use as a residence within 6 months of the notice date, unless an exception applies [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice's date.** You may apply to VCAT to challenge the validity of a sale notice within **30 days after the notice to vacate is given** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 5. **Get advice.** Contact a tenancy advice service promptly. The documents don't say whether a landlord can still rely on the notice if the sale does not go ahead, so a legal opinion on your specific facts is worthwhile.

question: It is 1 February 2026. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not yet. An email saying the rent is going up, followed by a refusal to negotiate, is not a formal rent increase notice. Under the documents I found, a rent increase needs a valid notice, and an increase made in breach of the rules is invalid.

- A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase. The notice may provide for only one increase and must state the amount, the method used to calculate it, and a statement of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Act says a rent increase made in contravention of these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Under a fixed-term agreement, the rent generally cannot be increased before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations' Form 5 states that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Conflict in the documents:** The Act requires at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current Form 5 in the regulations says the provider "must give you at least 90 days notice" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't explain how these fit together, so check the notice period carefully with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

A version dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) postdates your question, so I haven't relied on it. I haven't seen an "Authorised Version" number in the documents, so I can only identify the Act by its file name (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the regulations by file name (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the formal notice.** Ask the agent or owner to provide a Form 5 notice. Check that it states the current and new rent, the start date, and the calculation method [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the timing.** If the start date is earlier than the required notice period after the notice is given, the increase may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Also check that it is no more than once in 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't give a single answer. You would only owe the increase from the start date in a valid notice, and that date must allow for the notice period. question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The renter should not quietly arrange the repair. The law requires you to tell the owner about the damage in writing, and the owner can choose to have it fixed and charge you. The documents do not address insurance.

**What the law says (as at 15 October 2026)**

- **Your duty to avoid damage:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Damage from a dog chewing skirting boards would likely fall within this duty, though whether it was negligent is a question of fact.
- **Duty to notify:** A renter must give written notice to the provider "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice must state that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This applies regardless of whether you plan to fix it.
- **Provider's option to charge you:** If damage results from the renter's failure to take care, the provider may give a written repair notice. It must state the nature of the damage, that the renter caused it, and whether the renter must repair it within 14 days or the provider will do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter doesn't repair it in a proper and tradesman-like manner within 14 days, the provider may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The renter is liable for the reasonable cost if the provider gives written particulars of that cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who may do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This applies to any repair you arrange.
- **Leaving the premises:** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the renter can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage (for example, "skirting boards chewed by our dog, in [rooms]"). This satisfies the notice duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask whether they want to repair it themselves** or have you arrange it. If the owner agrees, get the agreement in writing.
3. **If you arrange the repair yourself with the owner's agreement**, use a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Do not rely on the urgent-repair route.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider cannot or does not do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards are not an obvious urgent repair, and the documents don't list them as one.
5. **Ask about the dog.** A renter may keep a pet only with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether consent was given here, so check your agreement.

**Insurance:** The documents do not address whether the owner's property insurance would be affected by damage, repairs, or a repair done without notice. You should ask the owner or your insurer directly.

**Gaps:** The retrieved documents don't say what the repair would cost or how a skirting board repair would be assessed. The Act text I found also doesn't say what happens if a renter repairs damage without telling the provider, beyond the notice duty and the repair-notice process above.

---

**Sources and versions**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, dated 13 October 2026). This is the most recent Act version in the documents, so it applies on 15 October 2026. Its Authorised Version number is not shown in the text, only the file label "v115".
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, dated 30 June 2026). This is the most recent Regulations version retrieved.
- [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 6 August 2025). I used this older version only for the pet provisions, because the newer version's pet text wasn't retrieved. Please confirm it against the current Act.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a limit on how many circuits a rental must have, or how many appliances can share one. They do contain an electrical safety standard that starts on 29 March 2023, which is 28 days after your date, and a right to ask for electrical safety check records.

**What the law says**

- The electrical safety standard in Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 says that "on and from 29 March 2023, … all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device meeting one of the listed AS/NZS standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). On 1 March 2023 this standard isn't yet in force.
- The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations I used are the reprint file named "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" (dated 1 June 2022). It is the earliest version in the documents and the closest to your date. I could not confirm which Authorised Version number was in force on 1 March 2023 from the documents provided.

**What you can ask for**

- **Electrical safety check date:** You can ask the rental provider to provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A later version of the Regulations also requires a copy of the most recent check to be given within 7 days of a written request, but that version isn't in force on your date [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety check:** If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you moved in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Circuit standard:** From 29 March 2023 you can point to the clause 9 requirement that power outlets and lighting circuits be connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual current device [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a single circuit serving most power points meets that standard, so an electrician would need to check it.

**What the documents don't cover**

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a number of circuits or a maximum load. They do require every power outlet and lighting circuit to be protected by a switchboard-type circuit breaker and residual current device (RCD). Your renter's options are mainly to request an electrical safety check and a repair.

## What the law says

- **Protection devices:** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type RCD that complies with one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This is in Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file labelled v009, dated 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standards at the start of the tenancy:** The provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act text I retrieved for this section is from an earlier version (file labelled v111, dated 25 November 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so please check it against the current version.
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** Where the agreement has no prescribed safety term, the provider must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. They must also give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask, and arrange a check as soon as practicable if none has been done in the last 2 years when you moved in [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** Any repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have or what load each circuit must carry. I can't confirm whether one circuit feeding most outlets breaches the rules. A breaker that trips under combined load may be operating as designed, but the documents don't address that.

## What you can ask for

1. **A written electrical safety check.** Ask the provider in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If none was done in the last 2 years, ask them to arrange one as soon as practicable [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **A copy of the check record.** On a written request, the provider must give you a copy of the most recent electrical safety check within 7 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Repairs.** Ask for the wiring and circuits to be inspected and repaired, relying on the duty to keep the premises in good repair [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the premises don't meet the minimum standards, you can make a request for urgent repairs [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I'd suggest putting these requests in writing and keeping a copy. Note that the documents don't give a specific deadline for a general repair request, beyond the "as soon as practicable" wording above.

On next steps, it advises asking in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check and requesting repairs, including urgent repairs.

That presents a non-in-force version's rule as law and as a step the user can take, despite the caveat.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't directly address coin-operated washing machines in a rooming house, so I can't confirm whether your operator may charge for them.

**What the law says**

The version in force on 15 October 2026 is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file labelled Authorised Version v115 (dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its provisions on charges are these:

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in the room only if the operator pays for those utilities and the room is separately metered. The charge must not exceed the supplier's charge, and this does not apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses the services, the operator must provide an itemised account of their individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency:** These bodies may charge for laundry services only in a declared rooming house, and only where use cannot practically be measured. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This provision does not cover private operators.
- **Excessive usage caused by faults:** If you are charged for excessive usage caused by a fault in the premises, the operator is liable for the excess above ordinary usage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

On facilities, the Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023 (version dated 1 December 2024) require, from 26 February 2024, one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether that machine must be free.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the schedule of services.** Under section 109, your operator should have given you a separate schedule of any charged services before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check whether the washing machines are listed.
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you are being charged for laundry use, you can ask for an account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the house rules and your agreement.** The Regulations' rooming house form says you must be given a summary of your rights and duties and a copy of the house rules [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Check these for any laundry terms.
4. **Check whether the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency.** If so, the cost-based cap in section 109A may apply, and you can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary a service charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep records and report faults.** If a machine is broken, notify the operator in writing as soon as practicable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If a fault causes excess charges, notify the operator promptly, as the operator's liability depends on that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

For a definite answer on whether your specific charge is lawful, you should get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or Victoria Legal Aid. The retrieved documents reference these bodies, but they don't give a full answer for coin-operated laundry [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

---

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, v002 (1 December 2024)
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Form 7 (version dated 30 June 2026)

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents clearly set out the mould standard. They don't settle whether the advertisement was allowed on 1 October 2025, and they don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

## Which versions apply on 1 October 2025

- **Act:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), is the version in force on that date. Later versions (v111, dated 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and v115, dated 13 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)) postdate the question.
- **Regulations:** The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), is the version in force on that date. The v005 version (25 November 2025) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) postdates it.

## What the law says

- **Mould standard:** Schedule 4, clause 8 of the Regulations says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- **Duty to comply:** Under s 65A(1), the provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Advertising:** The v110 text I retrieved does not include s 65B. Its s 65A refers only to "sections 65, 68 and 70" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The later v111 text adds s 65B, which says a provider or agent must not advertise premises to let unless, at the time, they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. The penalty is the same as in s 65A. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The documents don't say when s 65B commenced, so I can't confirm it was in force on 1 October 2025. If it was, a mould problem visible in photos would make it hard for the provider to show a reasonable belief of compliance. That is my inference, not something the documents state.

## Is the photo enough?

The documents don't say what evidence proves a breach. The later v115 text requires providers to keep records sufficient to show compliance with s 65B and allows the Director to publish guidance on what records are sufficient [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version is dated after 1 October 2025, and the guidance itself is not in the documents.

A photo shows that mould appears to be present. The standard also requires that the mould be "caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether a photo can show that cause. That is my reading, not something the documents state.

## What the renter can do

- **Request urgent repairs:** If the premises don't meet the rental minimum standards on or immediately after the move-in day, the renter may send the provider a request for urgent repairs under s 65A(2). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Rely on the general repair duty:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. This applies whether or not the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents don't cover how a mould dispute would be taken to the Tribunal, what remedies are available, or how the bond or rent would be affected. You would need to check those points in other sources.

It gives a next step: 'the renter may send the provider a request for urgent repairs under s 65A(2)'.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**The law on the situation**

The version in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under it, a renter must not assign or sub-let all or part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An assignment or sub-letting made without that consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider may give a notice to vacate if the renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to assign or sub-let, without consent. The notice must give a termination date at least 14 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask for consent.** The rental provider must not unreasonably withhold consent to sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider also cannot demand a fee for giving consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT if consent is refused.** If the provider withholds consent and you believe that is unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not answer**

- **Whether your friend's arrangement is a sub-letting.** The excerpts do not define "sub-let" or say whether a friend living with you without paying rent falls within s 81. Check this before relying on s 91ZV.
- **How you can remove your friend.** The documents do not set out a procedure for a renter to remove a non-party occupant. The notice to vacate form in the Regulations is issued by the rental provider to the renter [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say what you must do to end your friend's occupancy.
- **Your exposure to a notice.** The documents do not state the consequences beyond the notice to vacate.

If you receive a notice to vacate, you may be able to challenge it at VCAT, and the form suggests seeking advice promptly [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For guidance, the Regulations' form refers renters to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or 1300 558 181 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law bars one kind of retaliatory notice outright, but that bar does not clearly cover a month-to-month notice to vacate. Check the stated reason and the notice period first, then the 30-day challenge deadline.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the Act, the owner's refusal must not be unreasonable, and if they did not apply to VCAT within 14 days of your request, they are taken to have consented.

**Governing version:** The most recent Act document in the search results is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, dated 13 October 2026 and labelled v115 in its file name [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm its official Authorised Version number beyond that label. Its pet provisions (ss 71A–71E) match the earlier versions in the results [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so the rules below don't depend on which version applies.

### What the law says

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director and given to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say you used the official form.
- A provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under s 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- To refuse, the provider must apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the Act as it stood on 1 October 2025, the notice is not withdrawn just because the buyer pulled out. Unless the landlord gives a formal written withdrawal, the notice stays in place. The documents do not say what happens to a sale-based notice when the sale falls through, so this is not a final answer.

**Which law applies:** The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A later version, v111 (dated 25 November 2025), postdates your date, so I have not relied on it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A buyer falling through is not a withdrawal under this section.
- **Form:** A valid notice must be in the relevant prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, state the reason, and state the termination date. For a sale notice, it must also be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice.** Under s 91ZZQ, a withdrawal needs to be in writing and signed by both of you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the landlord won't sign, the notice remains effective.
2. **Check whether the notice was valid.** You can apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity "on or before the hearing of an application for a possession order." The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This 30-day window is critical, so check the date on your notice.
3. **Know what happens if you stay.** The regulations' notice form says the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Note that this regulation text is from a version dated 25 November 2025, after your date, so I cannot confirm it was the wording in force on 1 October 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice quickly.** The form suggests contacting community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a sale notice remains valid if the landlord is no longer selling or offering the property for sale. The retrieved sections state the requirement but don't address this scenario.
- The date your notice was given and its termination date. I need these to tell you whether the 30-day challenge window is still open and when the notice takes effect.

If you can share the date the notice was given, the termination date stated on it, and whether it came with documentary evidence, I can check those points against the Act.

question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice is not withdrawn just because the buyer pulled out. Only a formal withdrawal ends it. You may still be able to challenge it, though, so don't ignore it or assume you can stay.

**What the law says**

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession." If the landlord has a sale contract, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into, or after its last condition is satisfied. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) These provisions appear in Authorised Version 110 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf). The Authorised Version 111 excerpts I retrieved (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf) do not include this section, so I can't confirm from them that the wording is unchanged in Version 111, which was the version in force on 1 February 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Because the landlord hasn't done this, the buyer falling through does not, on the documents, end the notice by itself.
- **Challenging the notice:** A renter who receives a notice to vacate under the sale provision may apply to VCAT challenging its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Letting after a sale notice:** If the landlord obtains possession after a sale notice and then lets the premises for use as a residence within 6 months of the notice, the penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person or 750 for a body corporate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice's date and form.** Work out whether you are still within 30 days of when it was given, since that is the deadline to challenge it at VCAT. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. **Check the timing.** Ask when the sale contract was entered into and whether the notice was given within 14 days of that (or of the last sale condition being met). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
3. **Check the termination date.** It must be at least 60 days after the notice was given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
4. **Ask the landlord in writing** whether they intend to withdraw the notice. If they do, the withdrawal must meet the requirements in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep records** of the sale collapse, the notice, and any communications.
6. **Seek legal advice promptly** if you think the notice is invalid or the sale was never genuine.

**What the documents don't cover**

- The documents don't say whether a sale notice stops being valid automatically when a sale falls through before the termination date.
- They don't set out the VCAT possession-order process or what VCAT must consider in that hearing for a sale notice, because the Part 7 possession provisions I retrieved are from 2021 and are superseded.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** On the documents I have, an emailed rent increase that you never received as a formal notice is not a valid increase, so you don't have to pay the higher rent yet. Your rent can only go up after a valid notice is given, and the earliest start date depends on when that notice is given.

## What the law says (as at 1 October 2025)

I've applied the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf") and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf"), since these were the versions in force on that date.

- **Notice is required:** A rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Content:** The notice "must include" the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and a statement of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed form:** The notice must use Form 5. It states that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" and that rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases:** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements:** The provider "must not increase the rent before the term ends" unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for a written notice in Form 5.** An email saying the rent is going up is not the prescribed notice. Ask the rental provider (not just the agent) to give the formal notice. Form 5 says the provider's name "cannot be the agent's name," although the address for service can be the agent's [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the dates.** The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If it is given on 1 October 2025, the earliest possible start would be 30 November 2025. Any notice that gives less time would be in breach of s 44 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the amount and method.** The notice must state how the increase was calculated, and the increase "cannot be greater than the amount calculated using this method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge it if needed.** Within 30 days after the notice is given, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate and report on whether the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says this is free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). After the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT directly, with leave, if you have reasonable grounds for not first asking the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 notes that you will generally need to pay the increased amount from the date in the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Important caveats

- **Later versions don't apply yet.** A later version of the Regulations (file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf") changes the notice period to 90 days [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). It was not in force on 1 October 2025, so it does not govern this question.
- **I don't have your tenancy agreement.** I can't tell whether your agreement is fixed-term or what it says about rent adjustments. The documents I have don't cover that, so check your agreement or get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- A rent increase made in contravention of s 44 is invalid [1, s 44(5)].
- The provider must not increase rent during a fixed term unless the agreement provides for it [1, s 44(4)], and must not increase rent at intervals of less than 12 months [1, s 44(4A)].

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No, the renter can't just arrange a repair without telling the owner. The documents also don't address the owner's insurance.

I've applied the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 in the version dated 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"), the latest version in the search results and the one in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I'm citing the Regulations from the version dated 25 November 2025 (file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf") because it's the most recent one retrieved [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't state an Authorised Version number, so I've used the version identifiers from the file names.

**What the law says**

- **Damage duty:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a dog's chewing counts as damage caused by a visitor or as something else is not addressed in the documents.
- **Duty to notify:** A renter must give written notice to the owner as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This applies even if you plan to fix it yourself.
- **Urgent repairs only:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do them immediately and the owner can't be reached or won't act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter does this, they must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost, and the owner must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Skirting boards are not obviously an urgent repair, and the full list of urgent repairs is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website rather than in the retrieved documents [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** The renter must notify the owner in writing as soon as practicable. The owner must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Moving out:** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The damage therefore needs to be dealt with before you leave, or the owner may claim the cost.
- **Pets:** A renter may keep a pet only with the owner's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether you had consent for your dog.

**What the renter can do**

1. Put the damage in writing to the owner or agent now, describing the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Offer to have a suitably qualified person repair it, and agree the timing and cost with the owner in writing. This avoids a dispute over the cost at the end of the tenancy.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found set an electrical standard for power outlets and lighting circuits, but they say nothing about how many circuits a rental must have. They also don't cover what to do about a breaker that trips under load. The renter can ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check, and can ask the provider to meet the minimum standards.

**Version used:** For 1 March 2023 I used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), in the copy labelled v002, dated 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't show a separate "Authorised Version" number, so I can't confirm one beyond that label and the S.R. number. Later versions (2024–2026) contain amendments that don't apply on 1 March 2023 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Electrical standard:** Schedule 4, clause 9 says that "on and from 29 March 2023," all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of the listed AS/NZS standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That date is 28 days after 1 March 2023, so the standard was not yet in force on the day you asked.
- **Number of circuits:** The retrieved documents don't set a minimum number of circuits or say how circuits must be divided among outlets.
- **Overloading:** The documents don't address breakers tripping when appliances run together.

**What you can ask for**

1. **The date of the latest electrical safety check.** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. They must give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A check now, if none has been done in the last 2 years.** If no electrical safety check has been done within the 2 years before you moved in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Repairs to meet the standards.** The standard form agreement says the provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and must maintain them in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Gaps:** The retrieved excerpts don't include the 2023 text on how and when to request urgent or non-urgent repairs, and I didn't find the 2023 version of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*. The Act document I found is dated 13 October 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so I haven't relied on it for the position on 1 March 2023.

**Practical next step (general advice, not from the documents):** Ask the provider in writing for the electrical safety check date and for an electrician to inspect the circuits, and keep a record of when the breaker trips. Tripping under normal use can indicate a wiring or capacity problem, so an electrician is the right person to assess it.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental, and they don't say how much load a circuit must carry. They do set electrical safety standards you can rely on.

## What the law says

- **Electrical standard:** From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in a rental must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, plus a switchboard-type residual current device meeting one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This standard doesn't specify how many circuits there must be [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards:** A provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** If your agreement doesn't contain a prescribed safety term, the provider must have an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by them every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. They must also give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If no check was done within the 2 years before you moved in, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Records:** On your written request, a copy of the most recent electrical safety check must be given to you within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **Written confirmation of the date of the last electrical safety check**, which the provider must give you on request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **A copy of the most recent electrical safety check report** within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Urgent repairs:** If the premises don't meet the rental minimum standards, you may make a request to the provider for urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved mention this right but don't set out the urgent repairs procedure or timeframes, so I can't confirm those details.
4. **Qualified repairs:** Any repairs or maintenance must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether one circuit feeding most outlets meets the standard. The rule only requires the circuit breaker and RCD protection described above.
- Whether tripping when the kettle and heater run together is a breach. The documents don't address circuit loading.

A licensed electrician can check whether the wiring and protection comply with the standard and whether the circuit is adequate for your normal use. Ask the provider in writing to arrange this as a repair.

**Documents used:**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf (dated 30 June 2026). Version identifier v009.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf (dated 13 October 2026). Version identifier v115.

Both are the most recent versions in the retrieved set and were current on 15 October 2026. The documents show these version identifiers in their file names. They don't use the words "Authorised Version," so treat v009 and v115 as the version numbers.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. The only laundry-charge rule I found applies to Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies, not to private operators.

**Version applied:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file dated 13 October 2026 (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) is the latest version and was in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The file name identifies it as v115. The document text doesn't print a version number, so please confirm the number against the official source.

**What the law says**

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays those bills, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge. This doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This section doesn't mention laundry or washing machines.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must give an itemised account of that individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Coin-operated machines would seem to fall under this rule if they are charged as a service, but the document doesn't say so directly.
- **Laundry service charges:** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry or utility services in a declared rooming house. This is allowed only if it isn't possible or practicable to measure the individual use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service, and written notice is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Reduced services:** If a rooming house stops providing a service, the operator must reduce the rent by the agreed amount or by an amount set by the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Facility standards:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum number of residents it can accommodate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This comes from the 2023 Regulations, version dated 1 December 2024, which may not be the current version.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the written schedule of charges.** If the operator charges for the machines, it must have given you a separate schedule before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised account** of your own use if you are charged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check how many machines there are.** The standards require one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, so two machines may be compliant depending on the number of residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check whether the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency.** Only those bodies can impose the laundry service charge under s 109A, and only where the use can't practicably be measured. Any such charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the machines stop working or the operator reduces the service,** ask for a rent reduction. If you can't agree, the Tribunal can set the amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** whether a private operator may charge a coin-operated rate for washing machines, what a fair rate is, and whether a coin charge counts as a "service charge" under the Act. For these questions, you would need to check the full Act, any applicable regulations, or get advice from the Tribunal or a tenancy service.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** On 1 October 2025, the retrieved law requires that rented premises be free of mould, but the advertising ban I found is not in the version in force that day. The documents also don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

**Which versions apply on 1 October 2025**
- Act: *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file version **v110** (dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I took the version number from the file name, as the text itself doesn't state it.
- Regulations: *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file version **v004** (dated 1 July 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Later versions (Act v111 dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)) are not in force on that date, so I haven't relied on them for the answer.

**What the law says**
- **Minimum standards:** A provider must ensure rented premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould:** Schedule 4, clause 8 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** The version in force on 1 October 2025 (v110) doesn't include a section 65B. The advertising rule appears in the later version: a provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless" they "reasonably believe[] the premises comply with the rental minimum standards," with the same penalties [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That text was inserted by No. 6/2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say when No. 6/2025 commenced, so I can't confirm whether that ban applied on 1 October 2025.

**Is the photo enough to prove a breach?**
The documents don't say. Nothing I retrieved sets an evidence standard, or says a photo alone proves non-compliance. The condition report form notes that photos "may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the rented premises" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), but that document is the 2022 version of the Regulations, not the 2025 one. Whether mould is "caused by or related to the building structure" would be a matter for the dispute decision-maker, and the documents don't say how that is decided.

**What the renter can do**
- **Urgent repairs:** If the premises don't meet the standards when the renter moves in, the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance duty:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for occupation. This applies even if the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in, and despite the rent or the age of the property [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Written record:** Recording the mould in the condition report and attaching dated, labelled photos is advised [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If repairs aren't done within a reasonable time, the renter can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This guidance comes from the 2022 form, so check it against current guidance.

All three points are covered: the mould standard is quoted ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'); the photo point is addressed by 'Nothing I retrieved sets an evidence standard, or says a photo alone proves non-compliance'; and a next step is given ('the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance').
