question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** No, not if the landlord or agent doesn't reasonably believe the place meets the minimum standards. The documents don't say whether a photo alone proves a breach.

**Which versions apply:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 version in force on 1 February 2026 is the one dated 25 November 2025, "rta-1997-v111" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Versions dated after that date, such as v115 from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), don't apply. For the Regulations, the mould standard appears in the 2022 version [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and the 2026 version [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I could not retrieve the Regulations version in force on 1 February 2026, so I can't name its Authorised Version number. The mould wording is the same in both retrieved versions.

**What the law says about advertising**
- Section 65B says a provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless" they reasonably believe, at the time of advertising, that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 65E requires the provider or agent who advertises to keep records "sufficient to demonstrate compliance with section 65B" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Director may publish guidance on what records are sufficient [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include any such guidance.

**The mould standard**
- Schedule 4, clause 8 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough?**
The documents don't answer this directly. They don't say whether a photo is conclusive, how a breach must be proven, or what the Tribunal would accept. Two points matter:
- The standard is about mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould but may not show its cause.
- The test in section 65B is what the provider or agent reasonably believed when advertising [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A photo showing mould would make it hard to argue they reasonably believed the premises complied, but the documents don't say how that would be decided.

**What the renter can do or ask**
- If the premises don't meet the standards when the renter moves in, the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs under section 65A(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must also keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," regardless of whether the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The renter can ask the provider for the records kept under section 65E, though the documents don't say the renter can compel them. Only the Director can require production, under section 65F [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover what a renter should do if the advertising breach happened and the renter has already moved in, or how the Director or Tribunal would assess mould evidence.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current Act, letting someone move in without the landlord's written consent is a breach. The documents I found don't say how you remove the friend, so you should get advice before taking steps.

**What the law says (as at 15 October 2026)**

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", which is Authorised Version 115 according to its file name and is dated 13 October 2026. That is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- A renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Such an assignment or sub-letting without consent "is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord's side is limited too: a provider "must not unreasonably withhold consent" to assignment or sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether a friend moving in and living there is a "sub-let" under the Act. That depends on the facts, such as whether you've given them exclusive use of part of the property or are charging them anything.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for written consent.** Under the Act, consent must be in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must not unreasonably withhold it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and cannot demand a fee for giving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to VCAT if consent is refused.** If the provider withholds consent and you believe that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent is not required. If the Tribunal agrees, the arrangement may go ahead without consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Tell the agent.** The agent is the provider's representative, and the Act's rules on consent apply to them as well.

**What the documents don't cover**

- **How to get the friend out.** The retrieved documents don't set out the steps for removing an occupant who isn't a party to your agreement. They also don't cover what happens to the friend's rights if they are removed.
- **Consequences for you.** An older version of the Act, dated 7 September 2022, does list a notice-to-vacate ground for sub-letting without consent, requiring at least 14 days' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). That version is superseded, and the retrieved current version doesn't include that provision, so I can't confirm that it applies now. Check the current Act or get advice before relying on it.

**Next steps:** Consider getting advice from a tenancy service or the Consumer Affairs Victoria renting line on 1300 558 181. This is the number given in the regulations' forms [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They can advise on removing the friend and on the risk to your tenancy.

---

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025**—not the later v111 document dated 25 November 2025. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer premises at a **fixed amount**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not **solicit or invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising rent must not be **false or misleading**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- However, the v110 version does **not** contain the later rule expressly prohibiting acceptance of an unsolicited higher offer; that rule appears in v111 and was inserted by the 2025 amendment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved law does not say that an applicant is entitled to the property, or give a specific right to appeal a rejection, a claimed withdrawal, or the selection of another applicant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent withdrew your application because someone offered more, that could support a concern that the agent invited higher rental bidding, but the documents do not establish that this happened merely because the property was later advertised at a higher rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The documents also do not specifically address an email falsely saying that you withdrew.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing, to confirm:

1. whether your application was actually withdrawn and, if so, who withdrew it and when;
2. the rent at which the property was first advertised and the date it changed;
3. whether the agent or provider invited, requested, or relied on an offer above the advertised rent; and
4. whether the property was leased, and at what advertised or agreed rent.

The retrieved documents do not state a specific challenge procedure, regulator complaint process, remedy, or compensation available for these facts. They also do not specify what evidence an applicant should preserve.

As a practical matter, preserve the original advertisement, later listing, your completed application and submission confirmation, all emails and messages (including the withdrawal email), and a dated record of what you were told. These particular evidence-preservation steps are **not stated in the retrieved documents**.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**, a renter must request consent to keep a pet using the approved form. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must not **unreasonably refuse** consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A refusal is not automatically valid merely because the owner says they are allergic. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the nature of the apartment and its fixtures, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not state whether the owner’s allergy, or the fact that the owner rarely visits, would specifically justify refusal.

Importantly, the provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days after receiving the request**, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Since you sent the form about three weeks ago, the 14-day period appears to have passed—unless the provider applied to the Tribunal within that period. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing:

1. **Whether the rental provider applied to the Tribunal within 14 days**, and for the application details; and  
2. If not, confirm that consent is taken to have been given under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do not rely only on the agent’s verbal refusal. The Act says you may keep the dog if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it; the Act’s note provides that consent is taken to have occurred if no timely Tribunal application was made. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If a timely Tribunal application was made, the Tribunal decides whether refusing consent is reasonable and may permit the dog or order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate because the premises are to be sold is permitted only where, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The notice must generally give at least **60 days’ notice** and include supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The landlord’s notice is **not automatically withdrawn** just because the buyer pulled out. Under section 91ZZQ, it is withdrawn only if the landlord gives you a written withdrawal notice, signed by the landlord and by you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, based only on the documents, the notice remains on foot unless it is formally withdrawn or successfully challenged. However, the documents do not say that you must leave automatically merely because the landlord has not withdrawn it: if you do not leave, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order, and VCAT decides whether the notice is valid and whether you must leave. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, using a written withdrawal signed by both the landlord and you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the property is no longer genuinely going to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession, you may have grounds to challenge whether the notice was valid under section 91ZZB. The documents do not decide whether a failed sale, by itself, invalidates an already-issued notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice within **30 days after it was given**, and VCAT can determine whether it is valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Do not assume the landlord can physically remove you: if you do not leave, the landlord must obtain a possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a warrant for possession. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, 1 June 2022**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

It did **not specify a minimum number of separate electrical circuits** for a rental. The electrical minimum standard instead provided that, **from 29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits had to be connected to compliant switchboard-type circuit breakers and residual-current devices. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) That requirement was therefore **not yet in force on 1 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The breaker tripping when the kettle and heater run together is not, by itself, addressed by a circuit-number rule in the retrieved document. The document does not say that you are entitled to demand an additional circuit or rewiring for that reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can ask the rental provider, in writing, for:

- **The date of the most recent electrical safety check.** The provider had to arrange a check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided every two years, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician, and provide the date on request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- **A copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record.** The provider had to provide it within **7 days** after receiving your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- If no check had been conducted within the previous two years when you moved in, **arrangement of an electrical safety check as soon as practicable**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

You should describe the repeated tripping and ask that the electrician assess whether the circuit, breaker, power points and connected appliances are safe and compliant. The retrieved documents do not state a specific right to require extra circuits or a particular repair, so I cannot say that the provider must install another circuit based on these documents alone.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (13 October 2026)**. It does **not specifically say whether coin-operated washing machines are allowed**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act requires a rooming house to provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the rooming house’s maximum capacity. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) It does not state that use must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

However, if the operator charges an amount for services, they must give you a separate schedule of the service charge before you take up residency and, if you use the service, an itemised account showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents therefore do not establish that coin-operated machines are unlawful, but any laundry charge must comply with those requirements if it is a charge for a service. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

- what service the coin payment covers;
- for the separate schedule of charges given before you moved in; and
- for an itemised account of your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the machines are not in good working order, notify the operator in writing, because the required laundry facilities must be maintained in good working order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state what remedy applies specifically if the operator fails to provide the required schedule or itemised account.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

For **1 October 2025**, the relevant retrieved versions are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standard says **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. Therefore, if the bedroom actually has that kind of mould, it does not meet that minimum standard. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act version in force on that date does **not contain section 65B**, which would prohibit advertising premises unless the provider reasonably believed they met the minimum standards. The later Act version—**Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025**—does contain section 65B, but that is a later document and cannot be applied to 1 October 2025. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

A photograph that appears to show mould is **not, by itself, enough under these documents to prove** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The standard depends on whether there is mould or dampness **caused by or related to the building structure**, and the documents do not state what evidence is sufficient to prove that. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

The documents do not specify what a prospective renter may demand about a photograph in an advertisement. You can ask the provider or agent whether the mould has been inspected and remedied, and whether the room complies with the mould-and-dampness standard; the documents do not prescribe a particular response or proof.

If you have already moved in and the premises do not comply with the minimum standards **on or immediately after the occupation day**, you may issue the residential rental provider a request for **urgent repairs** to bring the premises into compliance. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said

The retrieved historical document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 089, dated 4 December 2019**—the closest document retrieved to **1 November 2019**. The documents do not establish whether the exact version in force on 1 November differed. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate had to be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, state the reason, and state the termination date. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

If the notice said the landlord intended to carry out repairs, check that it stated all of the following:

- the landlord genuinely intended to repair, renovate or reconstruct;
- all necessary permits and consents had been obtained; and
- the work could not properly be done unless you vacated. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

A repairs-based notice had to give at least **60 days’ notice** and be accompanied by approved documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

The Act expressly made certain notices ineffective if retaliatory: a notice under **section 91ZK** was ineffective if given because the renter exercised, or proposed to exercise, a right under the Act. The document does **not** state a general retaliation rule for an ordinary month-to-month agreement merely because the renter requested repairs. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the notice’s stated section and reason.** If it relies on repairs, compare it with the requirements above and check for the supporting evidence. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Preserve evidence of retaliation:** your repair requests, dates, replies, photographs, contractor messages and the notice. The same-day timing may be relevant evidence, but the retrieved documents do not state that timing alone invalidates a notice.

3. **Check whether the repairs were urgent or non-urgent.** The retrieved documents state that a renter may notify the rental provider in writing about damage or breakdown of fixtures and may apply to the Tribunal for repairs if non-urgent repairs have not been done within **14 days** of notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) However, that repair material comes from **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**, not the 2019 document, so I cannot confirm that those details were identical on 1 November 2019. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

4. If the notice is a notice under **section 91ZX** (repairs), the 2019 document says a renter may challenge its validity at the Tribunal, but the application must be made within **30 days** after the notice was given. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not assume you must leave immediately or that the notice is valid.** The 2019 document states that, except in accordance with the Act, a rental provider must not require or compel—or attempt to compel—a renter to vacate. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf) Seek urgent tenancy advice and consider a Tribunal challenge within the stated time limit. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days' notice. It also says the document 'does not state a general retaliation rule,' which contradicts the point that a no-reason notice has no effect if given in response to the tenant exercising a right. Finally, it gives a 30-day challenge window for repairs notices instead of the 60-day VCAT challenge.

It also presents a repair-application step drawn from 'Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025' as an option for the user, and the caveat does not stop that from counting as reliance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

A renter must use the Director-approved form and give the request to the residential rental provider [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days** of receiving the request, it applies to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say the request was sent three weeks ago—about **21 days**—so, if it was properly made and received, the documents indicate that consent is now deemed to have been given unless the provider applied to the Tribunal within that 14-day period [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The Act does not specifically say whether an owner’s allergy, or the fact that the owner rarely visits, makes refusal reasonable. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises and their fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters and any other relevant matter [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Therefore, the agent cannot simply rely on “the owner is allergic” as an automatic refusal; whether that makes refusal reasonable is for the Tribunal if an application was made [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal **within 14 days** of receiving your request, and request the application or case details [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If no such application was made within 14 days, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, the Act also states that a renter may keep the pet where the provider has consented **in writing** or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Ask for written confirmation of the deemed consent before bringing the dog into the apartment [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the provider did apply within time, you can rely on the Tribunal process: the Tribunal may order that you are permitted to keep the pet, or may uphold refusal only if satisfied that refusal is reasonable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?

The applicable document on **1 March 2023** is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 2 (1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, from **29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and residual-current device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) That requirement was **not yet in force on 1 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide **every 2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

Write to the rental provider or agent explaining that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and ask them to:

- arrange an inspection and repair by a **licensed or registered electrician**; and [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- provide you, in writing, with the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

You can also request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record; the rental provider must provide it within **7 days** of receiving your written request. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The record must include the electrician’s name, licence or registration number, inspection date, results, repairs required and actions taken. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that this particular tripping problem is automatically an urgent repair. If treated as a non-urgent repair, you must notify the provider in writing; if it is not repaired within **14 days**, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?

The documents **do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental. They require all power-outlet and lighting circuits to be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and a compliant residual-current device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

However, the rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition, and any repair work must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

You can write to the rental provider or agent asking them to:

2. **Provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Provide a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record within 7 days of your written request**; the record must include the electrician’s details, date, results, repairs required and actions taken [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm whether installing an additional circuit or other electrical upgrade is necessary**, based on the electrician’s assessment. Do not keep using the kettle and heater together if doing so repeatedly trips the breaker; report the problem in writing and describe exactly what happens.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?

- The renter could also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring non-urgent repairs after written notice and **14 days** without repairs; the Tribunal had to hear that application within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If the notice to vacate claimed that the provider intended to repair, renovate or reconstruct the premises, it was subject to specific requirements: necessary permits and consents, work that could not properly be done while the renter remained, at least **60 days’ notice**, and supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved 2019 Act expressly made a notice invalid if a **section 91ZK** notice—based on threats or intimidation—was given in response to exercising a right under the Act. It did **not**, in the retrieved provisions, state a general rule making every notice invalid merely because it followed a repair request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should check or ask for

1. **Check the reason and section stated on the notice.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and specify the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

2. **If it relies on “repairs”, check the 60-day period and evidence.** Ask for the permits or consents and other documentary evidence supporting the claimed repair work, and check whether the work genuinely requires you to leave. question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Because you sent the form three weeks ago, more than 14 days have passed. - the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**; and

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 February 2026**, the applicable versions are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v111 (25 November 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v005 (25 November 2025)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider or agent **must not advertise or otherwise offer premises for rent unless, at the time of advertising, they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

One of those standards is that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Therefore, if the apparent mould is structural mould or damp, advertising the property without a reasonable belief that it complies may breach the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

A photograph that appears to show mould is **not, according to these documents, automatically conclusive proof** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The documents do not prescribe a photographic test or say that one photo is sufficient evidence. They also do not state what evidentiary threshold proves non-compliance. **So the documents do not establish that the photo alone proves the property fails the standard.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

The renter can ask the rental provider or agent:

- whether the apparent mould has been inspected;
- whether it is caused by, or related to, the building structure; and
- whether the provider reasonably believes the premises comply with the mould standard before offering them for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The renter can also provide the photograph and ask for the mould or dampness to be investigated and remedied before entering into an agreement. The retrieved documents do not contain a specific procedure for challenging a rental advertisement or establish what further evidence is required.

All four points are covered: the advertising rule ('must not advertise... unless... they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards'), the structural mould and damp standard, the photo point (hardest: 'the documents do not establish that the photo alone proves the property fails the standard'), and a next step (ask the agent whether the mould has been inspected and request remediation before entering an agreement).

You can ask your friend to leave voluntarily and contact the rental provider or agent about the unauthorised arrangement. If the rental provider gives you a notice to vacate and you do not leave, the rental provider may apply to VCAT for a possession order; only Victoria Police may carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant for possession. question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?

Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. v110 dated 6 August 2025 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
* **Rental Auctions are Prohibited:** A rental provider or agent must not solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They also cannot accept an unsolicited offer that exceeds the advertised amount [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **False/Misleading Conduct is Illegal:** Agents must not make false or misleading representations about the rent payable, nor engage in conduct likely to mislead or deceive someone regarding entering a rental agreement [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). While the Act does not explicitly name "false withdrawal" emails as a standalone offense, falsely claiming you withdrew to manipulate the application process falls under these broader prohibitions against deceptive conduct.

### What You Can Do
* **Report to Consumer Affairs Victoria:** The behaviors described (soliciting/accepting higher offers, false representations) are criminal offenses under the Act [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Penalties include up to 60 penalty units for individuals and 300 penalty units for corporations [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Apply to VCAT:** You may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal for orders regarding contraventions of the misleading conduct provisions (section 30E) [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Evidence to Save
To support a challenge, you should preserve:
1. The original property advertisement showing the fixed advertised rent.
2. Proof of your application submitted at that price (e.g., submission confirmation, emails).
3. The email falsely claiming you withdrew.
4. Screenshots or records of the new listing at a higher rent.
5. Any proof or communication regarding the other person's offer above the advertised price.

**Can you challenge what happened?**
Yes. Under this version of the law, rental providers and their agents are strictly prohibited from conducting "rental auctions" or price negotiations above the listed price:
- **Fixed Rent Requirement:** Premises must be advertised and offered at a fixed rent amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **No Higher Offers:** It is an offence for a provider or agent to solicit/invite, or accept unsolicited offers of rent that are higher than the advertised amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). - **Misleading Conduct:** Sending you an email claiming you withdrew when you did not, and then relisting at a higher price, may constitute misleading or deceptive conduct intended to induce people into agreements, which is also prohibited [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, making false or misleading representations about the rent is illegal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

You can challenge these actions by applying to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). The Tribunal has the authority to make orders regarding contraventions of these sections under section 472(1A) of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

While the Act does not provide a specific checklist for this scenario, you must gather proof to demonstrate the statutory breaches outlined above. You should save:
- **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or archived links showing the property was advertised at the fixed price.
- **The false withdrawal email:** The exact email claiming you withdrew, proving the misleading conduct [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Proof of the new listing and higher offer:** Evidence of the relisted higher rent and any communication showing the agent solicited or accepted an offer above the advertised price (contravening section 30F) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **All correspondence:** Keep a complete record of your original application and all subsequent communications with the provider or agent.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to you keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 

Crucially, because you submitted the official request form three weeks ago, you are likely already legally approved to keep the dog. The law states that if the residential rental provider does not apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within **14 days** of receiving your request, they are automatically taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). A simple verbal or written "no" from an agent is not enough to override this rule.

Even if the owner did file a formal application with VCAT to try and block the dog, an allergy does not automatically make a refusal "reasonable." When deciding the case, the Tribunal will look at factors such as the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, and **any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The fact that the owner hardly ever visits is highly relevant to whether refusing consent is reasonable in your specific circumstances.

### What You Can Do
1. **Confirm if they applied to VCAT:** Did the agent file an application with the Tribunal within 14 days of your request? 
   - **If NO:** Their refusal is legally invalid. You are deemed to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). Send a written notice to the agent stating that because they failed to apply to the Tribunal within the 14-day window, they are taken to have consented under section 71C(2) of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). You may then keep the dog.
   - **If YES:** The owner has initiated a formal process to prove their refusal is reasonable. You will need to attend the VCAT hearing and present your case. Highlight that the owner rarely visits, meaning their allergy poses no practical issue for you as the tenant, which supports why their refusal is unreasonable.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110 as at 6 August 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about your situation
Under section 91ZZQ, a notice to vacate is withdrawn **only** if a formal notice of withdrawal is given. This withdrawal notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the original notice (the landlord) and the person to whom it was given (you) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because your landlord has not provided this signed withdrawal notice, the original notice remains legally valid on its face, even though the buyer pulled out of the sale. Therefore, you are still technically required to vacate by the termination date unless you successfully challenge the notice or reach a new agreement with the landlord.

### What you can do or ask
1. **Challenge the validity of the notice at VCAT:** You have the right to apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge whether the notice is valid. This application must be made within **30 days** after the notice was given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the landlord's reason for the notice (e.g., selling the property) no longer applies because the sale fell through, this could be grounds to argue the notice is invalid [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge it at a possession order hearing:** If your landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order because you haven't left by the termination date, you can challenge the validity of the notice on or before that hearing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
3. **Seek advice:** You should seek immediate advice if you are considering challenging the notice. You can contact community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website or call 1300 558 181 for further information [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v004 dated 1 July 2025), which was in force on your query date of 1 October 2025:

### What the law says
Under Victorian tenancy regulations, a valid official notice of a proposed rent increase is legally required for **all** rent increases [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Specifically, the rental provider must give you at least **60 days' notice** of any rent increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

Because you never received an official notice (Form 5), your agent's email and verbal refusal to negotiate do not satisfy this legal requirement.

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Since a valid notice was never provided, the agent cannot legally enforce the higher rent. You are only obligated to continue paying your current rent amount until proper legal procedures are followed.

### From when can they increase the rent?
The new rent can only take effect after a valid official notice is properly served and **at least 60 days have passed** from the date of that notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### What you can do or ask
* **Ask for the official form:** Request that your agent provide you with the official *Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises* (Form 5). 
* **Know your rights regarding the amount:** If you believe the proposed increase is excessive, you have the right to apply for a free investigation by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT to declare the amount excessive [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Wait out the notice period:** Once you receive the official Form 5, the 60-day countdown begins. You do not need to pay the increased amount until those 60 days have elapsed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

All four points are covered: the official form ('you never received an official notice (Form 5)'), the 60-day minimum ('at least 60 days' notice'), the email not being valid notice ('your agent's email and verbal refusal to negotiate do not satisfy this legal requirement... No'), and a next step ('You are only obligated to continue paying your current rent amount', plus requesting Form 5 and a Consumer Affairs Victoria investigation).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, specifically **Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?
**No, you are legally required to report the damage.** Under section 72AA of the Act, a renter must give written notice to the residential rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard tenancy agreement also explicitly states that "Where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Attempting to fix it secretly without informing them would breach this obligation.

### 2. What happens next?
Because the skirting boards were damaged by your dog (which is considered a failure to take care to avoid damaging the premises), the owner has the right to issue you a formal repair notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). This notice can require you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner, or the owner can arrange for someone else to do it and charge you for the reasonable costs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). It is generally best to report it promptly so you can agree on a repair method before moving out, rather than risking a dispute over the condition report at the end of your tenancy.

### 3. Would it affect the owner's insurance?
The provided legal documents **do not contain any information** regarding how reporting or repairing this damage would affect the owner's property insurance. You may need to ask your real estate agent, the owner directly, or a local legal advice service for clarification on that specific point.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021) in force as of 1 March 2023:

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The retrieved regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points that a rental property must have. 

### What can you ask for?
While the documents do not explicitly mandate upgrading circuits to handle higher appliance loads, you can take the following steps based on the regulations:

* **Request an electrical safety check:** You can ask your rental provider to arrange an electrical safety check if one has not been conducted by a licensed or registered electrician within the last 2 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
* **Note upcoming standards:** On **29 March 2023** (just over a month after your query date), new minimum standards will come into effect requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, as well as a switchboard-type Residual Current Device [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Report the tripping breaker:** Frequent tripping indicates an overloaded circuit. You should formally report this to your rental provider. While the provided text does not explicitly state they must add more circuits for capacity reasons, ensuring electrical installations are safe and compliant with the upcoming 29 March 2023 standards is their legal responsibility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on **15 October 2026**, here is what the law says about your situation:

### 🔌 Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
**No.** The current regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have. 

The only electrical requirement in force is that **all existing power outlets and lighting circuits** must be connected to compliant safety equipment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Specifically, they must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 ("Electrical Installations") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The law does not mandate upgrading circuits to handle more simultaneous appliances (like a kettle and heater running together) unless the existing circuit is defective or unsafe.

### 📝 What can you ask for?
Even though there is no rule on circuit *count*, you have specific rights regarding electrical safety and maintenance under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (v115, dated 13 October 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (v009, dated 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):

1. **Request proof of the last electrical safety check:** Your rental provider is legally required to have an electrical safety check of all provided installations conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. You can ask them for the date of the most recent check in writing, and they must provide it [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Report the tripping as a fault/repair:** If the breaker is tripping due to a defect, overload from faulty wiring, or an unsafe installation, you can report it to your provider. 
   * If it poses an immediate safety risk (e.g., sparking, burning smell, or complete loss of power), you can request **urgent repairs**, which the provider must immediately arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   * If it is not an immediate danger but still requires attention, you can apply to the Tribunal or the Director to investigate the need for non-urgent repairs [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Request a professional assessment:** Since the provider must ensure all electrical installations are safe, you can ask them to have a licensed electrician inspect the circuit to determine if the tripping is caused by a compliance issue (which they must fix) or simply an overloaded circuit (which may require a voluntary upgrade or usage adjustments).

*Note: While you cannot legally force a provider to add new circuits solely for convenience, you can absolutely demand that any existing electrical work meets the mandatory safety standards and is properly maintained.*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the Victorian laws in force on **15 October 2026**, here is what the retrieved documents state regarding your situation:

### 📜 What the Law Says
**1. The operator must provide a washing machine**
Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (S.R. No. 10/2023), rooming house operators are legally required to provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). 

**2. Can the operator charge you?**
The documents do not explicitly ban private rooming house operators from charging for laundry services, but they do set out strict rules for how any charges must be handled:
* **For all operators:** If a rooming house operator charges you for services (which can include laundry), they are required to provide you with a separate schedule of the service amounts *before* you take up residency. Additionally, if you use those services, they must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **For Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies:** These specific operators are explicitly permitted to impose a service charge for laundry facilities if it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure your use of the machine. However, this charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the service to you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ What You Can Do
* **Check your initial paperwork:** Ensure you received a separate schedule of service charges before you moved in. If you were not provided one, the operator may be breaching their obligations under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Request an itemised account:** If you are being charged, ask for a breakdown of your individual usage to ensure the charges align with what was agreed upon.
* **Verify the cost limit (if applicable):** If your rooming house is run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you have the right to ensure the charge does not exceed the actual cost of providing the laundry service [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: The retrieved documents do not contain specific provisions that explicitly allow or prohibit private operators from using coin-operated machines specifically, nor do they set maximum price limits for private operators beyond the general requirement to provide a schedule and itemised account.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on **1 October 2025**, here are the answers to your questions:

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?
**Yes, but only if they genuinely and reasonably believe the property meets the minimum standards at the time of advertising.** 

Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v111 as of 25 November 2025), a rental provider or their agent must not advertise premises to let unless they **reasonably believe** the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at that time [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

Regarding mould specifically, Schedule 4, clause 8 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (v004 as of 1 July 2025) sets the following standard: *"Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"* [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* If the mould visible in the photo is structural (e.g., from leaks, poor insulation, or building condensation), advertising the property would breach section 65B because the provider cannot reasonably believe it complies.
* If the mould is superficial and caused by tenant lifestyle factors (like drying clothes indoors), it may not breach this specific minimum standard, but the provider must still have a reasonable basis for believing the property complies before listing it.

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
**The retrieved documents do not specify whether a single photograph is legally sufficient on its own to "prove" non-compliance.** 

However, the law does impose related obligations that work in your favour:
* The provider has a legal duty to keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the advertising rule (section 65E of the Act) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* If the provider has received a repair notice relating to structural mould or damp in the last 3 years, they are legally required to disclose this fact to you as an applicant (regulation 16 of the Regulations) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

While a photo may raise reasonable doubt about compliance, the documents do not provide a specific evidentiary rule stating that a photo alone definitively proves non-compliance. If you suspect the property fails to meet the standards, you can request the provider's compliance records or ask for clarification on the cause of the mould before signing any agreement.

It says 'the documents do not provide a specific evidentiary rule stating that a photo alone definitively proves non-compliance', which covers the hardest point. As a next step, it suggests to 'request the provider's compliance records or ask for clarification on the cause of the mould before signing any agreement'.

question: It is 1 February 2026. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:

### What the Law Says About Advertising
The law does not explicitly ban showing mould in a rental advertisement. However, under **section 65B** of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a provider or their agent must not advertise premises unless they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" at the time of advertising [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider is aware that the property has structural mould, they cannot legally hold this "reasonable belief," making the advertisement non-compliant regardless of the photo's presence.

A photo alone is **not enough** to prove the place fails to meet the minimum standards. Because the regulation focuses on the *cause* of the mould, a photo only proves its presence, not its origin. The mould could be caused by tenant behavior (such as poor ventilation or drying clothes indoors) rather than a structural defect. Therefore, further investigation is required to determine if the standard is actually breached.

If you move into the property and discover that the mould is indeed caused by the building structure:
*   **Request Urgent Repairs:** If the premises do not comply with the minimum standards on or immediately after your occupation day, you may issue a formal request to the provider for urgent repairs to ensure the premises comply [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

You can ask the provider if they have kept records proving their "reasonable belief" that the property was free from structural mould at the time of advertising [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

It also bans making false representations concerning the rent payable or the application process itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
*   **False Advertising:** Promoting or advertising premises with a representation about the rent that is false or misleading is explicitly prohibited [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

*   **Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT):** The Act notes that the Tribunal may make orders on an application regarding a contravention of the misleading/deceptive conduct provisions (s 30E) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can they refuse?
The owner (or their agent) **cannot unreasonably refuse** your request to keep a pet [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, if they do refuse, they cannot simply say "no" and leave it at that. They must take legal action to justify their refusal. 

Specifically, under the law:
* If the agent refuses consent, they must apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving your official request form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* The residential rental provider must ask the Tribunal for an order that it is *reasonable* for them to refuse consent based on their allergy [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* When deciding this, the Tribunal will consider factors such as the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, and any other relevant matters (like the fact that the owner hardly ever visits) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Wait for the 14-day period:** If the agent or owner does not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request, they are automatically taken to have **consented** to you keeping the dog [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Prepare for a Tribunal hearing (if necessary):** If the agent *does* apply to the Tribunal to refuse consent, you can attend the hearing and explain why their refusal is unreasonable. You can highlight that the owner's allergy is unlikely to affect you since they rarely visit the premises [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will then make a final decision based on all relevant factors [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

In short, the agent cannot unilaterally block your request without going through the Tribunal, and if they do nothing for 14 days, your dog is legally approved.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?

Yes, the notice to vacate remains legally valid and **does not automatically lapse or become invalid** just because the buyer pulled out of the sale. 

**What you can do:**
1. **Request a formal withdrawal:** Under the Act, a notice to vacate is withdrawn *only* if a written notice of withdrawal is given, which must be signed by both the person who gave the notice (the landlord/agent) and you [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). You should formally ask your landlord to provide this signed document immediately.
2. **Attend any VCAT hearing:** If the landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order because you haven't vacated, VCAT will decide if you must leave and on what date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You are encouraged to attend the hearing to explain that the sale fell through. 
3. **Ask for more time if in hardship:** If being required to move out by the termination date would cause you financial or personal hardship, you can ask VCAT for an extension of time to stay in the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Important protections:**
* Your landlord cannot personally use force to remove you if you refuse to leave [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT possession order (a warrant for possession) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
