A notice to vacate given because a landlord intends to sell the property does **not** automatically become invalid or expire just because the buyer pulls out of the sale. The original notice remains legally valid and has full force and effect until it is formally withdrawn [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

Under the Act, a notice can only be withdrawn if a formal "notice of withdrawal" is provided. This notice of withdrawal must meet strict requirements:
* It must be in writing;
* It must be signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice); and
* It must also be signed by you (the renter) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

* **Upcoming Mandatory Safety Standards:** On and from 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000, as well as a compliant Residual Current Device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Practical next steps:** When a breaker trips from running high-draw appliances (like a kettle and heater) on the same circuit, it usually indicates the circuit is overloaded rather than broken. You can ask your landlord to have a licensed electrician perform the required safety check [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The electrician can then assess whether the switchboard needs upgrading or if the circuits need splitting to safely handle modern appliance loads and meet the AS/NZS 3000 standards that take effect on 29 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on Victorian tenancy law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how the situation is handled:

### What the law says about the situation

**Advertising with mould photos:** 
Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), a rental provider or agent **must not** advertise premises unless they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" at the time of advertising [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because Schedule 4 clause 8 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021) requires that every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure, posting a photo that clearly shows mould strongly suggests the provider does not hold this reasonable belief, making the advertisement potentially unlawful [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?**
The documents do not state that a single photo is automatically sufficient proof that the property fails the minimum standards. To legally prove a breach, it must be demonstrated that the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure" rather than resulting from tenant lifestyle factors (such as poor ventilation or drying clothes indoors) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). While the photo raises a serious concern and justifies further investigation, proving structural non-compliance typically requires evidence of the mould's origin, not just its presence.

### What you can do or ask

*   **Ask for compliance records:** You can request that the provider provide documentation showing they reasonably believe the premises meet the minimum standards and that any mould is not structurally caused [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Request disclosure of past repair notices:** Under regulation 16(2)(c) of the Regulations, providers are legally required to disclose if they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to structural mould or damp [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can explicitly ask them to confirm whether such a notice exists.
*   **Request an inspection or urgent repairs:** If you view the property and confirm structural mould before signing, you can request urgent repairs under section 65A(2) of the Act to bring the premises up to standard [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you have already signed a lease and discover structural mould, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the necessary repairs.
*   **Report misleading advertising:** If the ad continues to display mould while claiming compliance, you may report the advertisement to Consumer Affairs Victoria or the relevant consumer protection body for investigation under section 65B [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:

*   **The Reason for the Notice:** Check if the notice was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act (such as requesting repairs) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it was given in response to this, the notice is **of no effect** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
*   **The Termination Date & Agreement Terms:** Verify that the termination date complies with the notice period required by your residency agreement. If your agreement allows you to determine it by notice, the termination date must match the dates allowed under that provision [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). ### 2. Timeframe to Challenge
If you believe the notice is invalid for the reasons above, you must apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge its validity **within 14 days** after the date the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Victoria), **Authorised Version No. 110**, which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### 🔍 What the Law Says About Your Situation
* **Fixed Rent Advertising & Prohibited Offers:** A rental provider or agent must advertise rent as a fixed amount. They are strictly prohibited from soliciting or inviting offers higher than that advertised price, and they cannot accept unsolicited offers that exceed the advertised rent [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Misleading Conduct:** Providers and agents must not engage in misleading or deceptive conduct to induce you to enter an agreement, nor make false representations concerning the rent payable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Sending a fraudulent email claiming you withdrew your application when you did not constitutes a false/misleading representation [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Penalties:** Contravening these rules carries penalties of 60 penalty units for natural persons and 300 penalty units for body corporates [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### ⚖️ What You Can Do
Yes, you can challenge this behavior. The agent's actions appear to violate Sections 30E and 30F of the Act [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You should:
1. **Report the Conduct:** Lodge a formal complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria regarding the misleading advertising and false withdrawal notice [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to VCAT:** You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders addressing the provider's or agent's contravention of Section 30E (misleading/deceptive conduct) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### 📂 Evidence to Save Immediately
To substantiate your challenge, preserve the following:
* **Original Advertisement:** Screenshots or archived links showing the property was advertised at the original fixed price.
* **The False Withdrawal Email:** The complete email claiming you withdrew, plus any proof that you never withdrew (e.g., application submission receipts).
* **New Listing Details:** Screenshots of the property now listed at a higher rent.
* **Communication Logs:** All correspondence with the agent/landlord regarding your application and the price change.
* **Proof of the Higher Offer:** Any documentation, screenshots, or agent statements confirming that another party offered more than the advertised price.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), version v115, which was in force on 15 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about your situation
Under section 71C(1) of the Act, a residential rental provider (the owner) **must not unreasonably refuse** your request to keep a pet [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Because you submitted the official request form three weeks ago (more than 14 days ago), if the owner did not formally apply to the Tribunal within those first 14 days, they are legally **taken to have consented** to your dog [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If the owner wishes to refuse consent, they cannot simply say "no" through an agent. They must apply to the Tribunal under section 71D within 14 days of receiving your request [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they do, the Tribunal will decide whether the refusal is reasonable by considering factors such as the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, and any other relevant matters [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While an owner's health concerns are a factor, it does not automatically grant them the right to block the pet without Tribunal approval.

### What you can do or ask
1. **Ask for proof of a Tribunal application:** Contact the agent in writing and ask if the owner filed an application with the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **If they did NOT apply to the Tribunal:** Inform the agent that under section 71C(2), consent is legally deemed given because the 14-day period has passed without a Tribunal application [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You are entitled to keep the dog.
3. **If they DID apply to the Tribunal:** You will need to attend the hearing and argue why the refusal is unreasonable. You can highlight that the owner "hardly ever visits," which minimizes the impact of their allergy, and present your case for why keeping the dog is reasonable given the nature of the premises [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_ (Authorised Version No. v110 as of 6 August 2025)** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes.** Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate given because the landlord intends to sell the property remains legally valid even if the buyer pulls out or the sale contract falls through [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The Act does not automatically cancel or void the notice just because the underlying sale has been terminated. 

### How can the notice be withdrawn?
A notice to vacate cannot simply lapse, expire early, or be withdrawn by implication. It can only be formally withdrawn if a specific **"notice of withdrawal"** is given [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For this withdrawal to be legally valid, it must:
* Be in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* Be signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
* Be signed by you (the tenant) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### What can you do?
1. **Request a formal withdrawal:** Ask your landlord to sign and provide you with a written notice of withdrawal [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they do this, the notice to vacate is officially cancelled and you no longer have to leave based on that notice.
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** If the landlord refuses to withdraw the notice or ignores your request, you have the right to challenge its validity at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
   * You must apply to VCAT within **30 days** after the notice was given [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   * At the hearing, VCAT will decide whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice. If VCAT determines the notice is invalid, it will make an order declaring it so [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Do not ignore the termination date:** If you stay past the termination date and the landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order, VCAT may grant the order if it is satisfied that doing so is reasonable and proportionate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: You should seek immediate legal advice from a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria if you are considering challenging the notice.)*

question: It is 1 February 2026. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Authorised Version v101** of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), dated **7 September 2022** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), which was the version in force on 1 February 2026, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes.** Even though the buyer pulled out of the sale, your original notice to vacate remains legally valid and enforceable until it is formally withdrawn. The Act does not automatically cancel a notice just because the underlying reason (the sale) falls through. You are still required to vacate by the termination date specified in the notice unless you take further action.

### What can you do or ask?
1. **Ask for a Formal Withdrawal**
   You can request that your landlord sign a written notice of withdrawal. Under the law, a notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a written notice is given that is signed by both the landlord and you [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Without this dual-signed document, the eviction process continues.

2. **Challenge the Notice at VCAT**
   You have the right to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the validity of the notice. This application must be made **within 30 days** after the notice was given and on or before the hearing of a possession order [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). While challenging it because the sale fell through can be complex, raising the issue with the Tribunal is your legal avenue to contest it.

3. **Negotiate More Time**
   Even if the notice remains valid, you can ask your landlord for additional time to find a new home and move out. Landlords are often willing to grant a short extension (e.g., an extra few weeks) in exchange for the property being left in good condition, especially if they no longer intend to sell it immediately.

*Note: The later version of the Act (Authorised Version v115, dated October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) is not yet in force and does not apply to your situation.*

The answer says the opposite of automatic cancellation ("The Act does not automatically cancel a notice just because the underlying reason (the sale) falls through") and of unilateral withdrawal ("a notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a written notice is given that is signed by both the landlord and you"), and it never states a minimum notice period, since "within 30 days" is the deadline for a VCAT challenge, not a notice period.

Its substantive rules (dual-signed withdrawal, the 30-day VCAT challenge) are drawn from that earlier version, so it never names the required version and applies rules from a version not in force on that date.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v004, effective 1 July 2025)**, which was in force on your query date of 1 October 2025:

**What the law says about the situation**
A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The rental provider must give you at least 60 days' notice of any rent increase [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). An email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement.

**Do you have to pay the higher rent?**
No. Because you never received an official notice, the agent's email is not legally sufficient to enforce a rent increase. You are only required to pay your current agreed rent until a valid notice is properly served.

**From when does the increase apply?**
The new rent can only take effect after the rental provider gives you at least 60 days' notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The increase would start on the specific "Start date" listed in that official notice, provided that date is at least 60 days after the notice was given to you.

**What you can do or ask**
You should request that your agent provide the official **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)**. Once you receive it, you will have the full 60-day period before any higher rent is due. If you believe the proposed increase is excessive, you can apply for a free investigation by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days of receiving the notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: every required point is covered. The hardest one, that a rent increase needs notice on the official form, is met by the answer's request for 'the official Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)' together with its statement that 'An email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement'. The answer also states the 60-day minimum notice, says the higher rent isn't payable because the email is not legally sufficient, and gives next steps: pay the current rent, request Form 5, and seek a Consumer Affairs Victoria investigation.

The answer says the renter does not have to pay ('No. Because you never received an official notice, the agent's email is not legally sufficient'), that the increase starts on the 'Start date' in a valid notice 'at least 60 days after the notice was given', and that the notice period is 'at least 60 days'. The line 'An email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement' refers to this informal email, which lacked an official notice, and does not claim a notice can never be sent by email.

answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version v005 (updated 25 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), which was in force on 1 February 2026:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under Victorian law, a valid official notice is required for all rent increases [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). An informal email from your agent does not satisfy this legal requirement. Until you receive and are given the proper statutory notice, you continue to pay your current rent.

### From when would it apply?
The new rent would only apply from the specific start date listed on that official notice. However, the law mandates that the rental provider must give you **at least 90 days' notice** of any rent increase [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This means the earliest the new rent could legally start is 90 days after you receive the valid notice. 

### What you can do or ask:
*   **Request the official form:** Ask your agent for the formal "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (Form 5). 
*   **Check the calculation details:** Once provided, ensure the notice includes the method used to calculate the increase and that the new rent does not exceed the amount calculated using that method [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   **Challenge the increase:** If you believe the proposed increase is excessive, you can apply for a free review by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days of receiving the notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT to declare the amount excessive [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent cannot produce this official notice, or if they claim the rent is increasing in less than 90 days from when you receive it, the increase is not legally valid.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 15 October 2026, here is how your situation is handled:

**Can you fix the damage without telling the owner?**
No. You are legally required to report the damage to your landlord (referred to as the "residential rental provider" under the current Act). 
* Under section 72AA of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026), you must give written notice to the residential rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* The standard rental agreement form under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025) also explicitly states that where damage occurs, you must notify the rental provider in writing [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* Because your dog caused the damage, you are responsible for it. Under section 61 of the Act, you have a duty to ensure care is taken to avoid damaging the premises [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). If you do not report and fix the skirting boards, the landlord can issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days, or they can repair it themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

**Would it affect the owner's insurance?**
The retrieved documents do not contain any information regarding how a tenant secretly repairing property damage would affect the landlord's property insurance.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), here is what the law says regarding your situation as of 1 March 2023:

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have. 

### What are the electrical safety rules?
While there is no set number of circuits, there are strict safety standards for the equipment installed on those circuits. From **29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 ("Electrical Installations") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with specific Australian/New Zealand safety standards (such as AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What can you ask for?
Since the new electrical safety standards come into force in just over a month (29 March 2023), you can take the following steps:
1. **Request an Electrical Safety Check:** You can ask your landlord to provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing. Landlords are legally required to have all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings checked by a licensed or registered electrician every 2 years [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Ask for Compliance Upgrades:** If the frequent tripping is caused by an outdated or non-compliant switchboard, you can ask your landlord to upgrade the installation to meet the new minimum standards that take effect on 29 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Ask your rental provider to have a licensed electrician inspect the circuit to determine if it is simply overloaded (requiring you to stagger appliance use) or if there is an underlying fault that needs repairing under their maintenance obligations. question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version **v115** (dated 13 October 2026), which is the law in force on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

### Are they allowed to charge you?
Yes. Rooming house operators are permitted to charge residents for specific services provided, which can include the use of laundry facilities like coin-operated washing machines. 

### What the law says about these charges
Under **Section 109** of the Act, if your rooming house operator charges you for a service (such as using the washing machines), they are legally required to:
* Provide you with a separate schedule detailing the amount relating to those services *before* you take up residency in the room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you use any of those services, provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Ask for the Schedule of Services:** Request a copy of the schedule of services provided that was given to you before you moved in. This document should clearly list the cost of using the laundry facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Request an Itemised Account:** If you use the machines, ask the operator for an itemised account showing exactly how much you owe based on your usage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Dispute Improper Charges:** If the operator never provided a schedule of service charges before you moved in, or if they are charging amounts not listed in that schedule, you can raise this with them. You may also apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to have the charge reviewed or withdrawn if it is deemed unreasonable or was not properly disclosed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how your situation is addressed under Victorian residential tenancy law:

**Applicable Documents:**
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. v004, effective 1 July 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. v115) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?
**No, not if the property genuinely fails to meet the minimum standards.** Under section 65B of the Act, a residential rental provider or agent **"must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless at the time the premises are advertised or otherwise offered to let, the residential rental provider or the provider's agent reasonably believes the premises comply with the rental minimum standards"** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If the property actually contains structural mould (which breaches the minimum standards), advertising it without addressing the issue would violate this rule. Furthermore, providers are legally required to keep records sufficient to demonstrate that they reasonably believed the premises complied with these standards at the time of advertising [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
**No, a photograph alone is generally not enough to prove a breach.** 

The relevant minimum standard states that **"Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The legal threshold specifically hinges on the *cause* of the mould. 
* A photo showing visible mould does not, on its own, prove that the mould stems from a structural defect.
* Mould can also arise from non-structural factors (such as inadequate ventilation or moisture generation), which would not constitute a breach of this specific minimum standard.

Because a photograph cannot determine the underlying cause of the dampness or mould, further investigation into the building structure and maintenance history would be required to prove that the property actually fails to meet the legal minimum standards.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), which is the version in force on your date of 15 October 2026, the provided documents **do not contain information** on how a renter can remove an unauthorized friend or guest who has moved into their rental without telling the agent.

The retrieved text consists entirely of statutory forms for notices to vacate that are issued *by* landlords, operators, or site owners *to* tenants or residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It outlines processes for:
- Serving a notice to vacate and applying to VCAT for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Challenging a notice at VCAT on specific grounds (e.g., discrimination, improper service, family violence) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Warrants for possession that can only be carried out by Victoria Police acting on a VCAT order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because the documents only cover landlord-to-tenant eviction procedures and do not address a renter's rights or obligations regarding unauthorized occupants, I cannot provide steps on how to remove your friend based solely on this material.
